---- - On the window ledge he stood, With a bright inquiring eye; 'Twas a compact that he should Always call in passing by, Just to show we might pretend Each to entertain a friend. When I saw my tiny guest Waiting for his daily crumb, Dainty, trim, and self-possessed, Never doubting it would come, I could almost hear him say, "Mistress, food is scarce to-day."

And my heart made sad reply, As the little dole I threw, " Strange that one so poor as I Should have store enough for two ! Robin, if the thing could be, Would you throw a crumb to me Not a sound disturbed the hush, Save my own impatient sigh— Robin to a neighbouring bush Darted off without good-bye. How 1 you leave me, faithless bird. As I waited for a word. Ah ! I wronged that heart of flame: Through the silence, sweet and clear, Forth his cheery carol came, And I held my breath to hear, For that dear familisz strain Woke my better self again, 'Twas a benediction sweet, Chaunted in a foreign tongue, Like those graces after meat, By the warbling s.cholars sung, Where the reverend customs;hold, Handed down by men of old. Did I dream that, as he sang, Some one entered at the door, That some childish laughter ran, And small footsteps crossed the floor? Who bath touched my lips with wine, Mellow juice of Auld Lang Sync? Suddenly the music ceased, Yet the silence breathed of balm; Art thou flown then, small Ledge priest, Somewhere else to ran:o the ylealta. ? 't Man," the Master finely said, "Doth not live alone by bread." C. 8., in Good Inn*, for February.

Being en- gaged as courisel for the defendant, it was his duty to prove that the horse was sound in wind and limb. The most important wituees was an elderly clergyman. herjeant IrLkins: "Well, you're a parson; you don't know much about horse!, I suppose ?" Witness: "Well, yes, Ido ; my fattier was a laege breeder, and I do know something about them." Serjetrit (in an off-hand style): "0, I da.reeay you think yourself very clever. Can you tell my hid and the turt the difference between a horse end a cow ?" Witness: "Why, there are so many points of difference. One is the some difference as between a bull and a bully ; the bull has horns and the belly has not !" This was said with a polite and significant bow to the Serjeant, who sat down forth- with. Art6IBISROP TAIT.—If I were called on to give In a few Words the character of the late Archbishop of Canterbury, sheuld do so by quoting a text of Scripture: "God hath not given us the spirit of fear, but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind." There was in him nothing of this timorousness which often characterises the life and policy tV. Churchmen. His piety was eseeatially of a manly type. 0! no one could the proverb that no man is a hero to his valet be less truly quoted than of him. His character was eminently equable. To his servants, his friends, his family, his chaplains, and his fellow-workers, he was as truly great and as truly Most Reverend as in public and official rela- tions. It was recognised that he was a real man, and that he had a high spiritual influence over men: not over the clergy only, but over the laity generally. He was listened to and followed, not only in assemblies for Church purposes, but in Parliament, and in other places of general influence. It is felt, now that he is gone, that a blank is left which it is peculiarly difficult to fill; and the reason Is that he was not an ecclesiastic of the ordinary type, but one with a far- reaching mind, who saw that in matters of conduct which are often thought common and secular, as well as with what is strictly celled religions, the kingdom of God was con- cerned. He was a statesman as well as a Churchman, be- cause he saw that the common and public life of men can- not be separated from religion, and that if religion is to make progress it must influence the public and general life. He said on one occasion, when opposing the claim of the Convccations to legislate on all religious questions, that every question of deep conviction affecting the interests of Men must be religions. And this saying represents the ruling conviction of his life.— Hon. and Rev. Canon Fre- mantle, in "Good Wards." COMMIRCIAL " GENTS."—I have been in the booksellicg line many years, when 2d. and 31. in the is. discount had net even been thought about. It may be fancy, but I can- not help thinking that the " traveller " of years ago and the "Commercial gent" of the present day are a different rate of men. The " traveller " was patient, courteous and affable, and, as a rule, knew something of the inside of the booxs he exhibited. The "commercial gent" of the pre- sent day, as a rule (there are exceptions), Is pert, dictato- rial: always in a hurry, always wanting "to catch the next tram," priding himself upon the number of towns he can (to" in a day. Remaining in a town for a couple of hours, say twice a year, he knows more about what will "tell" than the tradesman who, most likely, has been years in the place; he tells fabulous tales of the number of books he has aOld on the tourney, and he is surprised and annoyed if, after all his chatter, he does not get a line, and does not scruple to show that he is so. The "commercial gent" ittitotte be has done his duty towards his employer if he hurriedly allows the whole of hie samples, and calls attention to the showy " casts," and occasionally to the illustrations. The contents and merits of a book . " ac no concern of his. And so he rushes from town to town, an activ6, fussy, getting "over the ground," but missicommercial gent," eg many an order, which, with a little more tact and a little less hurry, might have been secured. The same remarks, so far as my experience goes, also apply to the " stationery commercials;" they, as a rule, know more of the suitability of their goods to the wants of their customers, and what be ought to buy, than the customer himself, and are full of push and in- judicious energy. There is one other subject I would like to mention, and that Is" handshaking." lam a Viet in- offensive man, who would like, if it could be managed, to shake hands only with my own particular friends and ac- quaintance, and with those whom I esteem, when such a process is deemed necessary. lam not allowed to use my -own discretion ; perhaps during the day two or three, or even more, "commercials," some of them hardly arrived at maturity, do mo the favour at calling upon me; some of them I ha:e never seen before, and others for about half an hour twice a year. In they come with outstretched palm, as they were my dearest friends. Some will give me just tho tip of their fingers (to those I am very grateful), others pride themselves on giving the "hearty" grip, and (oh, the bor. or of it!) some hands are hard and horny, cold and 2a1i07, soft and limp, warm and soft, wet, cold, and slimy (the last makes my flesh creep while I write). CLOVER SICIINESS.—I remember a few years ago, a friend of mine, who occupies a farm where the soil is mestly black topped, complained that his clover came up with a one braird, and then died out. He was advised to dress with potash early in the spring, and the result is that he now has splendid crops of clover. I have since known a dressing of I potash have the desired effect on many occasions.—T. I Farrell. WORTHLESSNESS OF SEEDS OF WEEDS AS FODDER.---. Weed-seeds ate sometimes used as food, but as a rule it would be much better to burn them and scatter the ash on theta-ad.. F. Nobbe examined a mixture of swill weed-seeds which had been used as fodder for cattle, and he found it to contain 20 per cent. of sand, dust, mouse-dung, and other such rubbish, the rest bring seeds of tho abominable goose. foot and other weeds. Such a mixture IA absolutely useless Bs foal, for it is qeite indigestible, the Ste+.ls passing through the animals unaltered. il A few night's ago a remarkable instance of the fecundity of a Dorset horned sheep occurred on the farm of Mr. Campbell, F.S , sanctuary of Powersteck, Dorset. During the night one of hie ewes gave birth to four lambs, all of largo siz,e and in a strong and healthy condition. The 1110illEr is do- ing well, and is qeite'equal to supporting two of them, the remaining two being raised by hand. Of the four other ranee which lambed during the same night three had twins and the other one, showing a total of eleven lambs to five ewes. All the ewes are young sheep, and in every case both they and their limbs are healthy and strong. This is a most remarkable case of prolific breeding. SI7CCEES WPM & BAY-DRYING FAN.—With respect to recent remarks regarding the unsatisfactory`,,' official reports on the artificial hav-rirying machine trials at Beading, Mr. Streeter, cf Sackville Piece Farm, Bnxted, Sussex, who has been using GiWts's exhaust fan, has published some par- ticulars of his exnerienee which we are asked to repeat. On one clay the haa 'from a field of twelve acres was carried, carted, and stacked, the rain being so incessant that the men employed were all wet through. The temperature of the resulting stack after a short time rose to 180 degrees; the fan was then set to work, and quickly reduced it to 80 deg. This rite and reduction of temperature by the fan went on for three weeks, when the hay was dry and in first-rate con- dition. A field of clover and two or three stacks of oats were treated in the same way, which under ordinary condi- tions would have been quite spoiled. Mr. Streeter speaks very highly of the action of the little machine, the coat of which is (rely £B. THE DEMANDS OF Court CHOPS ON WATER.—In Bieder- riarat'S Cemrallelattliir AgoikulPir Chemie P. Sorauer pub. lishe.a the results of a series of investigations on this sub- ject. Wheat, rye, barley, and oats were grown in solutions of varicueerreogths, and it was found that oats required for efficient growth a weaker solution than the other three cereals, and this is said to agree with the fact that a crop of oats on a soil in poor condition is ellen better than that grown on the same soil which has been improved by manuring. A genera law is enunciated that each kind of plant requires a definite strength of solution to produce the maximum yield, as when the solution of plant food in the soil is too weak, a large quantity must be absorbed te allow of complete 1 nourishment; on the other hand, when the solution is too strong, the plants; do not increase much in size, but are considerably richer in ash ingredients. Wheat and rye flourish in strong solution?, hence these two crops may pre- cede barley and oats, which thrive better on land which is not teo rich in soluble matter; on the other hand, barley and eats should flourish on toils in which wheat and rye might starve. While the deposit of dry matter in the roots of cereals appears to be fairly uniform, it seems that the portions of the plant above ground are shorter the greater the concentration of the solution of mineral food. Soraner claims that his numerical results afford a clue to much that has been inexplicable in practical agriculture. He compares the stronger solutions to a heavy soil that has been well worked and well manured, and the dilute solutions to a poor, light, sandy soil. Plants cultivated on soils that have been heavily manured, and which are, therefore, rich in soluble material, are smaller, feebler, of lees rapid growth, and richer in ash than if they had grown upon less rich soils, while their roots remain short and do not occupy much ground; on such soils, therefore, heavy manuring is a loss, as is also deep ploughing. But, he argues, in poorer and more open soils the roots:extend themselves further, absorbing a much greater quantity of water so as to provide food for the plant, so that if there is a sufficiency of food in the soil the yield will he satisfactory, and this, he rays, is why light sandy soils are remunerative in wet seasons, and why some plants flourish only on certain soils. The Chicago Times does not believe that the limit of the exportable power of the United States has yet been reached with regard to its live stock. That journal, in the course of a long article on the subject, remarks as follows r—" Up to the present time animals in this country have been kept almost entirely on grass and corn. It requires a large amount of land to raise enough of these to support a given number of animals. In a near future more attention will be given to the production of root crops, of which a larger amount of food can be produced from the same amount of land. More cottonseed and flax-seed meal will be employed in feeding stock. By the judicious Use of ensilage it is likely that the cattle Population of the entire States can and will be doubled. Neither IS it true that the great plains are now covered with flocks and herds. It is likely that the number of cattle and sheep on them will increase fourfold in a short time. They will receive much batter care and attention than they now de and will have, in addition, some shelter from the storms and some harvested food. The animals will not be scrubs or ' natives ' They will be fall bloods, or at least high grades. They will eat no more food than inferior animals, but will produce much more meat, and it will be of a better nuality. Much is being done to hasten the matu- rity of all classes of meat-prcducirg animals. Three-year- old beeves weigh as much as five-year-old 'Peeves did a few years ago. They consume but about half as much food and produce a better quality of meat. Improvements in live stock are now going on more rapidly than ever. A more judicious system of feeding is also being practised. The art of preserving fresh meat for transportation is only in its in- fancy. The inland transportation of fresh meat in large quantities and over long distances was regarded as chimerical even a few months ago. The business has now assumed im- mense proportions and is rapidly increasing. At present most of the dressed meat shipped is from one large city to another, as from Chicago to New York. In the course of a few years dressed meat may be shipped from every point where live stock is now shipped, and consigned to every vil- lage in the country where fresh meat is procured from a dis- tance. When we consider the vast numbers of cattle and sheep in countries south of the equator, the ease with which they can be multiplied, and the low cost of keeping them, we are forced to the conclusion that fresh meat will be com- paratively plentiful and cheap as soon as means for preserv- ing and transporting it are prefected." STRUCTURE OF A Cow's HORN.—It IS frequently the case, says prank Buckland, that in the commonest objects we may see, if we like, beautiful examples of engineering structures. I take the anatomy of the cow's horn as a good example. A few days since I was inspiriting the tanneries of the Messrs. Hamlyn, Buckfastleigh, on the river Dart, Devonshire. In one of the backyards was a mountain of the skulla and horns of cows of all sorts and kinds. Here there was a treasure worthy of investigation; so I got on to the mountain of horns and skulls and picked out some beau- tiful specimens, which Mr. Hamlyn kindly gave me, in or- der to make sections, &a. I find that over the brain of the cow a etrong roof of bone is thrown in the shape of an arch, so as to form a substantial foundation for the horns. It is not solid, however, but it is again strengthened below by a series of bony arches, that are so distributed as to form a series of hollow chambers, thus forming a structure uniting streooth with lirttness. The Problem now ie, how to fasten Q . the horns On each side on to this butirese. The horn itself !oust be formed of horn proper, i.e., hardened hair. In the ' rhinoceros we find a horn corripOetal entirel.7 of a potid marts! of what 111 really a bunch of hair, agglaitinated together; but this kind of a horn would have been much too heavy for the cow's convenient use. What is to be done? Why, hollow out the centre of the horn, of course; but stay—this will not do, because how is the horn to be supplied with blood vessels—in fact, how is it to grow? Let us see how It is done by the Great Designer. Cat the horn right more with a saw, and you will find inside another horn, only made of bone. If the section is made about one-third of the way down the length of the horn, you will be able to pick out a piece of bone in the shape of a cone, on which, or rather around which, the horn proper has shaped itself. This bona fits the cavity with the greatest accuracy; it is as light as the thinnest paper, and yet as strong as a cone of tin. It is everywhere perforated with holes, which in life contained the nerves, the veins and arteries, and we know a cow has all these in her horns; nerves, proved by the fact that cows do not like their horns touched, and that they can scratch a fly off their bides with the tip of the horn; arteries and veins, proved by the fact that a born, when broken, will bleed, and that the horn of a living cow feels quite warm when held in the hand, besides which the nerves and arteries form a union between the internal core of bons and the external covering of horn paper. If we now cut the rest of the horn into sections, we shall find that the , inside of the body part is really hollow, but thatvery strong greatest of bone are thrown (about every inch or so) across the cavity of the horn in inch a manner as to give it the ea Possible support and strength. I have cut a cow's horns and skull into several sections to show these buttresses ' of bone, and now that the preparation is finished, I have another specimen to show that there is design and beauty in all created objects.

I agree with him to the extent of Bug- , pelting the desirability of occasionally mopping house floors ' with this solution. Its visible effects on the wood are first to stain it with a faint green tinge, which gradually tones down to a brown stain, giving to deal the appearance of oak, ; a change which has no disadvantage from an artistic point of view. If the wood is already tainted with organic mat- ter capable of giving off sulpharetted hydrogen, the darken- ing change is more rapid and decided, owing to the forma- tion of sulphide of copper. The solution of sulphate should not be put into iron or zinc veseels, as it rapidly corrodes them, and deposits a non-adherent film of copper. It will even disintegrate common earthenware by penetrating the glaze, and crystallising within the pores of the ware, but this is a work of time (weeks or months). Stoneware resists this, and wooden buckets may be used safely. It is better to keep the crystals and dissolve when required. Ordinary earthenware may be used with impunity if washed imme- diately afterwards.

THE ABOLITION OF THE CONTROL IN EGYPT

The Foreign Office has issued the correspondence res- pecting the Anglo-French financial control in Egypt. The only despatch subsequent to the presentation of Lord Gran- ville's Circular Note is from his Lordship to Viscount Lyons, dated January 25. In this letter Earl Granville comments on M. Duclerc's reply to the despatch of Decem- ber 30 regarding the abanJonmeut of the Anglo-French financial control. His Lordship refers particularly to the portion in which M. Duelerc questions the right of England and Egypt to withdraw from or to modify the arrangement without the consent of France. After recapitulating the history of the negotiations prior to the decree of November 15, 1879, Earl Granville says :—" Her Majesty's Govern- ment are unable to see. in what passed during the negotia- tions or in the terms of the decree itself anything which can be considind•as amounting to an engagement on the 1P.11; of the Khedive that the Control should be maintained in perpetuity; while on the other hand they consider that an obligation to continue under all circumstances to submit the whole administrative system of a country to the inspec- tion of two officials of foreign _nationality, selected by two _ _

foreign Governments, removable only with their consent, is one that could be asserted only on the evidence of diplo- matic engagements of the most explicit and formal charac- ter." The despatch adds:—" Recents events materially affected the aspect of the case.. The result ot the military insurrection was to virtually abrogate the control. It has only been by military intervention, in which Mance de- dined to take part, that the Khedive's. power has been re-established. and it is by the presence of British troops in Egypt that His Highness's authority is maintained pending reorganisation. Consequently it cannot be contended that former arrangements are still obligatory." ENGLAND AND THE EGYPTIAN TRIITUTP.

A London correspondent writes,—lt a just possible that when Parliament meets, Mr. Gladstone have for it a little surprise, the only parallel for which is to be found in the disclosure of the purchase of the Suez Canal Shares. It is said that Lmd Dufferin' acting under instructions from the Cabinet, has arranged for the commutation of the yearly tribute which Egypt pays to the Sultan, and which amounts to £705,000. The sum named as the purchase money is _ .

£6,000,000, and if the story is true an uncommonly good-bar- gain has been made. England will, of course, have to find the money in the first instance; but England can borrow on,terms open to no other nation, and a financial ar- rangement will be made, as in the case of the purchase of the Suez Canal ghares, in which no demand for ready money will be made upon the Exchequer. lam not in a position to say what truth there is in this report. It reaches the through a person of considerable authority, and is cer- tainly believed in by. M. Duclerc, who told my informant, . . . .

and expressed his profound admiration ata stroke at once so bold and so prudent. There is at least no improbability about it. The Sultan is his own master, and his heirs if they ever come to the throne, must lookout for themselves. A bait of six millions in ready money is more than Turkish flesh and blood can stand. It would not be the first time in which this tribute money has been trafficked in. Previous to 1866 the annual tribute paid to Egypt was £376,000. Ismail Pasha, desiring to consolidate his power, bribed the Sultan with an offer of nearly double tribute money to make the succession to the Throne of Egypt direct from father to son. The release of Egypt from this yearly drain of some- thing like three-quarters of. a million would give an enormous impetus to the prosperity of the country. If six millions be the sum paid, it would be equal to a little less than nine years' purchase, which is surely a liberal estimate of the permanence of the Turkish Suzerainty. It is stated that the scheme of repayment by Egypt extends over 21 years, which would immediately reduce the annual tax by one-half, with a prospect of its final extinction in the next generation. .Politically this step would rivet the hold Eng- land has already obtained upon the country. Having gone bail for six millions, it will be accepted as a natural con- sequence that England will kave to keep pretty close to the side of gypt, at least till the money is repaid. I sin- cerely trust that on this day fortnight we may have the report confirmed by the Queen's Speech.

A riot has taken place at Creuaot arising out of distur- bances created by some Italian workmen, which rendered the intervention of. the gendarmery necessary. The third match between the English cricketers under the captaincy of the Hon. Ivo Bligh and the Australian team was concluded at Sydney on Tuesday, the result being a victory for the English eleven by 69 runs. The New York papers report that Mrs. Langtry has been most coarsely treated and insulted during her stay in St. Louis, Mis. The journals there publiihed attacks en the actress and Mr. Gebhardt.

An elephant-keeper in the Zoological Gardens at Berlin, has been gored and crushed to death by one of the animals under his charge—one of the-pair presented to the Society by the Prince of Wales. What infuriated the brute is not clear.

The weekly health returns of the British army at Cairo show that I,44o„officers and men are sick, out of a total British force in Egypt of 12,976. This marks a general im- provement in every corps; though the cavalry still have over 20 per cent., and the artillery over 14 per cent., of their number in hospital. A revolutionary proclamation was, it is said, placarded a few days ago in one of the public gardens of St. Petersburg, a fashionable afternoon resort, in which the people were enjoined to keep clear of such places as might be frequented by th 3 Court, so that in case anything hap- pened no outsiders should be injured. MADAGASCAU. - The French Government has published the diplomatic correspondence on the Madagascar question. On the 24th ult., M. Duclsrc politely rejected an offer by Lord Granville to become the medium by which a "fresh statement" of his views might be communicated to tbe " 'lova " Government.

The preliminary proceedings against Prince Napoleon have been completed, but the question of " whether, and if so, where," he shall be tried is not yet settled. Meanwhile the bill-poster who posted the manifesto on the walls has been fined a few pounds. It is reported by the Paris—a good authority on the matter—that General Campenon has refused the War Ministry. A Berlin correspondent asserts that the friendly disposi- tion of the Powers in regard to Earl Ciranville's Note on Egypt continues undiminished, and even the Porte, he says, is not expected to offer any really serious opposition. The Egytian Gazette goes further, And claims the best authority for the statement that the Porte will in all probability agree to Lord Granville's proposals. A New York telegram says :—The Inman Line landing pier has been destroyed by fire. The National Line steamer Egypt, which was alongside the pier at the time, sustained some damage. The Gaion Line steamers Alaska and Nevada, which were at the next pier, narrowly escaped. The cargo of the City of Brussels, which was brought by the Egypt, and had been unloaded, was destroyed with the pier. Two items of-news of a 'Strikingly different character come from India. Two young Bengali ladies have succeeded in passing the B.A. examination of Calcutta University, but while this evidence is given of the progress of education and Liberal thought ha Bengal, it is reported that in Jeypore a case of suttee, or widow burning, has occurred, the victim being: the widow of the chief of the village of Utarna. For promoting this forbidden ceremony the sons and brothers of the late chief have been promptly sent to prison.

Intelligence from the &-,iudln -confirms 'the news as to the serious aspect of affairs there. It is stated that 4,000 Egyp- tian troops are at Darfour, and 5,000 more at Bars and Obeid. Although not closely invested, they are cut off , from anything but fitful communication with the outer world. The relieving force is at Khartoum, under Abdel Kader, who will now be superseded by Alaidin Pasha. Two to three hundred miles, however, separate them from the beleaguered forts, and the rebels have closed up the wells, which renders relief almost almost impossible till after the rainy season, three months hence. CwrYwaso.—Cetywayo has been formally reinstated at Ulundi as King of Zululand, in the presence of five thousand Zulus. The partition of the territory has given great offence to some of the chiefs who were present at the ceremony. The Times correspondent at Durban asserts that " it'is now admitted on all hands that Cetywayo's restora- tion was not desired by the people ;" but the correspondent, with an eye to the future, also admits that " the Zulus are so inscrutable that possibly after the installation of Cety- ' way° their attitude may change." To say that a people are " inscrutable " hardly consists with a confident state- ment of their supposed opinions. LORD DERBY AND CETYWAYO'S RESTORATION. - Lord nerhy, reifying thrnugh his secretary to the Aborigines' Pro- -I—tec-tiOn Socieiy, alled his attention to the partition of de for the return of Cety- Zululand and the arrangements... nt tht many of wayo, says, with reference to the ateme s a . those who would have been present when 5 •may° landed .4 that.a. at Port Durnford were driven away by threats, an, military censorship of the Press had been established in Zululand,- inquiry had been made of the Governor by tele- graph before the receipt of the society's letter, and he had replied that nothing was known of the matter by the authori- ties in Atai, but that the officer in command of the escort with Cetyvrayo had been asked for an explanation. It was believed that the measures for bringing back Cetywayo were well known throughout Zululand. Papers on the subject would shortly be presented to Parliament. The Calcutta coempondent of the Times, reporting the latest news from Afghanistan, confesses that it is so con- flicting as to be almost worthless. One day it is said that the Ameer's troops have been Weated by the rebellious chiefs and the bill tribes; the.next day the victory is said to be with the Ameer. The lihyber Pass has been closed to'traffic for a fortnight, owing to the action of the Shin- warria and their dispute with the Governor of Lalpoora, and large caravans are detained at Jamrood awaiting the opening of the pass. The Punjab Administration report for 1881.2 states that the Lower Khyber as far as Lundik- bana was unusually tranquil during the year, and that the experiment of entrusting the guardianship of the road to the Afredees was tolerably successful; but the state of the Upper Khyber running through the Shinwarri and Mohu- ,' med territory Was less satisfactory. The report also notices the frequent daring attacks by the freebooter chief Kamel on native cavalry pickets at Peshawur and Kohat. BALLOON AcCIDENT IN MADRID. - Captain Mayet, a Frenchman, who for two months has been making weekly ascents in a balloon, with one or more persons of both sexes, Istarting from the Retina Gardens in Madrid, and alighting in various parts of the city or the neighbourhood, made on Sunday an ascent with a workman. The balloon was tossed about by the wind, and came down. It alighted on the roof of a house fiva stcreys high, and the Frenchman, to secure the safety of his companion, risked his own life, be,

missing his hold, sell into the street below. He was mortally injured, and the placti Was almost instantly the scene of fearful excitement, the crowd gazing with horror as a priest administered extreme unction to the dying man. The bal- loon used was a Montgolfier, of large dimensions, and from it hung a basket with the other man in it, perfectly safe, and a trapeze on which the Frenchnun was accustomed to risk his life in order to amuse the thousands of people who attended his performance every Sunday.

div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.

The silk weavers in Warwickshire.are agitating for better payment. They allege that the rate of wagcs paid at pre- sent is nothing more than a starvation price, and that it is impossible to go on working for such scanty remunera- tion.

THE FORFAR FACTORY OPERATIVES.—A strike of factory operatives at Forfar, which commenced on Monday, is ex- tending, and there are now 1,900 workpeople on strike. Of six factories in Forfar, only two are now in operation, and there is as yet no sign of concession on either side. The coalowners of North Wales met on Saturday at Wrex- ham, and resolved not to make any alteration in the present rules of working as regards time at any of the collieries. It wi'l be remembered that a few days ago the men gave:notice that from the 3rd of February they had resolved to work only eight hours per da...y and five days a week. BILLS or SALE AND FAILURES,—In the week ending January 27, 1883, there were 261 bills of sale in Eagland and Wales, a decrease of 719 over those of the corresponding period of last year; and the failures gazetted numbered 236, an increase of 16. The Weis for portion of year to January 27, 18,53, are—bills of sale registered for England and Wales 964, a decrease of 2.894; the failures gazetted number 849, an increase of 13.—Stubbs's Mercantile Gazette. THE CALEDONIAN RAILWAY accordance with the arrangement between the general manager of the Cale- donian Railway and the railway enii.&;:ves when they CO- sented to resume work, 30 deputies from the men on Tuesday conferred in Glasgow with the general manager and three superintendents. The deputies stated their grievances, and these the general manager will submit for the consideration of the directors, whose answer it was promised should be given early in the ensuing month. YORKSHIRE COALMASTERS AND THE OUTPUT. South Yorkshire coalowners met at Sheffield on Tuesday to consider a circular forwarded to them by the Yorkshire Miners' Association, proposing to restrict the output of coal by work- ing five days per week and eight hours per day. The coal- owners unanimously resolved that the proposed restriction of the output of coal, as put forth in the circular, would be detrimental to the interests of masters and men, and could e BEWARE OF IMITATIONS. not be entertained. They expressed willingness, however, to Why are several Manufacturers now making meet the men and explain the reasons which had compelled them to come to this decision. Imitations of THE LANCASHIRE COAL TRADE.—AIIIIOIIgh the market THE SINGER MANUFACTURING COMPANY'S can scarcely be said to be in a depressed condition, there is a continued want of animation throughout the coal trade of MACHINES? this district. House-fire coals are only in limited demand I The Public will draw their own inference— manufacturing consumption for the time of the year, and although the requirements for GOLD IS CONTINUALLY COUNTERFEITED, are not restricted to the same extent by the mildness of the weather, common round coals BRASS AND TIN NEVER. for iron making and steam purposes also hang rather in the market. Engine classes of fuel are in moderate demand. There is no large accumulation of stocks going on at present, TO AVOID DECEPTION, but it is only in exceptional cases that pits are kept on full time. The market so far as prices is concerned is weak. BUY ONLY AT THE OFFICES OF Special quotations are, however, in many cases made for .eeee anything like quantities, and selling prices rather than list I.'llE SINGER MANUFACTURING rates to a large extent govern values. At the pit mouth the average prices are about as under: Best coal, 95 61 to 103; seconds, 78 01 to 83 3d; common house-fire coals, 63 61 to 7s; steam and forge coals, 6s to 68 61; burgy, ss; and good ordinary slack, 3s 61 to 4s per ton. Shipping has been interfered with by the recent stormy weather, and there is a good deal of coal under order for which vessels cannot be obtained at present. Steam coal delivered at Gerstell or Liverpool can still be bought at 78 6d to 7s 91 per ton. THE LANCASHIRE IRON TRADE. The recent reductions in price do not seem to have brought forward any large amount of business. A few inquiries were reported on 'Change on Tuesday, but the actual orders placed were only limited, and there is generally a continued want of anima- tion in the market. Makers, however, appear determined not to give way further, and were holding firmly for last Friday's quotations. Local makers of pig iron, who during the week have sold to a moderate extent, are less pressing for orders, and for delivery equal to Manchester their mini- mum price is 465. 61. to 475., less a for forge and foundry qualities; Lincolnshire brands remain at 465. for forge to 48s. forfoundry ; and Derbyshire 48s. 6d. to 50s. yer ton, less 21 delivered here. The recent reductions in pig iron have a tendency to cause orders for finished iron to be held back for lower prices, and although manufacturers in some cases report a fair inquiry, the weight of actual business offering generally continues very small. For delivery into the Manchester district a 10s. per ton remains the nominal list quotation for bars, but makers take 2s. 61. less to secure orders, and in some cases local bars can be bought at as low as £6 ss. per ton delivered. THE WEATHER AND THE CORN TRADE —The Mark-lane Express says:—" During the past week the weather has been variable and the temperature equally so. The general position has not improved in the least, being as bad as it was a month ago, and much more serious at the end of January than at the end of December. In addition to this feature there are now complaints that some of the early- sown wheats are losing coleur from the long-continued waterlogged condition of the land, whilst on the other hand some later-sown wheats are appearing above ground. Oppor- tunities for thrashing wheat under favourable circumstances have been few and far between, and there has consequently been no general improvement in the condition of farmers' deliveries. The advance of .a shilling per quarter estab- lished in London on Monday last on all sound parcels of English wheat has been very generally sustained in the provinces; but damp samples are neither dearer nor easier to sell, and towards the close of the week a quieter feeling has prevailed. Flour, too, has become weaker in London. Good malting barleys are more inquired for at provincial exchanges, but in London there has been no alteration. Other descriptions of native produce without change in values during the week. Trade for foreign wheats off stands in London is restricted by the higher rates demanded. Flour lifeless at unchanged rates." TILE RESTRICTION OF THE OUTPUT OP COAL IN LANCA.- SHIRE.—At some of the Lancashire collieries the restriction of the output recommended by the representatives of the miners at recent conferences has already been put in force. I At present no general announcement as to what action the colliery proprietors may take with regard to the matter has been made. Although there is no doubt that in many cases a limitation of the output would not be regarded with dis- favour, the method proposed by the men for carrying this into effect is scarcely likely to meet the views of the colliery proprietors generally. The miners propose not only to re- strict the working days to five days per week, but the work- ing hours to five per day from bank to bank, and at many of the collieries this would practically mean about four and a quarter days' actual work in the week, whilse the daymen and others engaged at the colliery, who represent about an equal portion of the working staff, would be paid for five days' work. This is a serious objection which many colliery proprietors have to the carrying out of the proposed arrangement. In the Ashton and Oldham district, where the men are working under the sliding scale, the result of the last making up of the books, which left wages un- changed, has given rise to a widespread feeling bf dissatis- faction with the system altogether. Many of the men are strongly urging the abandonment of the present arrange- ment, but under the terms of the agreement between coal- owners and the men no steps can be legitimately taken for disturbing the sliding scale until June next, when either side would be at liberty to give notice for its discontinuance. THE IRON TRADES AND THE EMPLOYERS' LIABILITY Acr.—By a scheme of mutual insurance the members of the Iron Trades Employers' Association, which includes master engineers, shipbuilders, and iron and brass founders throughout the country, have for the last two years covered themselves against claims made 43 a them by their work- men under the Employers' Liabiiitr Act of 1880. The re- sults of the two years' working of the scheme afford a. satisfactory indication of the comparative absence of dan- gerous risk connected with employment in the iron and engineering trades, and of the general care bestowed to secure the safety of workmen, which is rendered imperative by the regulations of the insurance. The basis of the rates for insurance was, in the first instance, fixed after complete statistics as to accidents had ' been privately collected throughout the various branches of the trade, but notwithstanding that, a very low scale—more than 300 per cent. below the rates asked by some of the regular insurance companies—was fixed. The association after two years' experience tied the immunity from serious claims under the Act such that they • are enabled to reduce their original rates by something ! like 50 per cent. SUBLIMITY Alm BaurrY.—ln aiming at the sublime the object of the artist is to excite the Imagination; in aiming at beauty he undertakes to satisfy it.—Sir C. L. Eastlake, P.R.A.

EVIL EFFECT OF OVERPRAISE.—I do not think a greater dmervice could be done to a man of science than to over- state his claims: such overstatement is sure to recoil to the disadvantage of him in whose interest it is made.—Professor Tyndall. GOOD WORIC.—The force that had been lent my father he honourably expended in manful well-doing. A portion of this planet bears beneficent traces of his strong hand and strong bead. Nothing that he undertook to do but he did it faithfully and like a true man. I shall look on the houses he built with a certain proud Interest. MISCELLANEOUS. Mr. W. E. Forster is at present on a visit to the Durham. The Right Hon. James'Lowther has 'oeen elected presi- dent of the Redcar Conservative Association. A movement is on foot to present Dr. Benson ,eith a pas- toral staff on the occasion of his enthronement, as a mark of welcome. A personal friend of Mr. Gladstone, who has just returned from Cannes, states-that when he :saw the Premier last he Was in excellent health. The Marquis of Bute, on Wednesday, turned the first sod on the site of the new Bute Docks at Cardiff, the day being observed as a general holiday. Mr. Fawcett left Paddington on Wednesday morning for Torquay, where he proposes staying for a few weeks. He was accompanied by Mrs. Fawcett. At the Old Bailey, on Wednesday, two men, charged with "nsniring to obtain bonds of the value of £11,500 by false pretences, were acquitted, no evidence being offered. The grand jury at the Central Criminal Court, on Tuesday, threw out the bill presented against Robert 'Cousins, one of the " Deculiar People," charged with man- slaughter. ~, A Pontypridd correspondent telegraphs that the badge of Thayer, the missing Cardiff cabman, has been found in the river Taff, near Pomtypridd. The cireumstances attending Thayer's disappearance still remain a mystery. At Chelsea barracks, on Monday, n number of men belong- ing to the Coldstream Guards quarrelled at the canteen bar, and during a fight which ensued several were injured. One, named Lowe, had a leg broken in two places, and may tot recover. There was another insubordinate demonstration of Spike 'lsland convicts on Wednesday, but it did not assume a very 'se, rious character, and the prompt appearance of a military Lome, summoned by signal, restored order in the establish- ment. The fishing at Wick on Tuesday was remarkably good, 674 crans of excellent herrings being landed, and sold at from 48s to 53s 6d per cran. A special train of 40 heavily laden trucks of fish drawn by two engines were despatched to the south. Much distress prevails amongst the working classes of Dover. On Wednesday three hundred men went to the Town Hall during the meeting of the Town Council and asked for employment. They were informed that their re- quest would be considered. The official Board of Trade report on the Fyvie railway disaster attributes the accident entirely to an internal defect in the iron girder of the bridge. The girder was honey- 'combed at the point where it broke, and the cavity held more than 15 cubic inches of water. It would have been impossible to have discovered the defect in the girder by ex- ternal inspection. A Skye correspondent points out that the farmers of the islands have had difficulties to contend with of late years, as well as the crofters. There are several with two years' wool on their hands, who cannot get dealers to give them a remunerative price for it. Farmers who years ego were getting 16s a stone for their wool now have to contend with 9s, or even Bs. THE LEICESTER TOWN COUNCIL AND FLOODS PREVEN- TION.—The Leicester Town Council have adopted a scheme for the prevention of floods in the low-lying districts of Leicester, and have instructed a committee to advertise for tenders in order to proceed forthwith with the first section of the work. The cost is roughly estimated at from £lOO,OOO to £150,000. A lady applied on Wednesday to the Court of Appeal for leave to serve a summons upon the executors of the late Lord Beaconsfield, to compel them to give her information With reference to certain memoranda which she thought might affecS her. The Master of the Rolls stated that he was happy to say the court had no jurisdiction to make such an order. A breach of promise case was tried at the Manchester assizes on Wednesday, before Mr. Justice Kay. The parties live at Darwen, and are in humble circumstances, the plain- tiff being a weaver, and the defendant an , engine tenter, earning 28s. per week. The case was devoid of any feature of interest. The jury found for the plaintiff, and awarded her the modest sum of £5. REVENUE AND EXPENDITURE.—The receipts on account 01 revenue from the let of April, 1882, to January 27th, 1883, were £67,523,629, against £67,103,445 in the coffee- Donding period of the preceding financial year. The not ex- penditure was £72,533,203, against £70,530,267 to the same date in the previous year. The treasury balances on Jan- uary 27th amounted to £1,888,427, and at the same date in 1882 to £2,466,077. At a meeting held on Wednesday evening in the large Mom of the Young Men's Christian Association, Manches- ter, under the auspices of the International Aseociation for the Total Suppression of Vivisection, resolutions in favour 01 the objects of the Association were defeated by over- whelming majorities. The audience largely consisted of medical men and students of the Owens College School of Medicine. HIGHWAY ROBBEEL—THE CAT.—A man named Mur- sell and a woman named Sherman, was convicted at the Central Criminal Court, on Wednesday, of an assault on a Man named Bowen, whom they attacked and beat and kicked in Stepney, and robbed of all tho money about him. The woman was sentenced to 12 months' and the man to 18 months' hard labour. The latter was also ordered to receive twenty lashes from the cat-o'-nine-tails. The annual meeting of the members of the Manchester Athenaeum was held on Wednesday night. It was stated by the president (Mr. S. Ogden) that for the first time in the history of the institution they had now over 3,000 mem- bers. It was resolved that 200 guineas of the balance from the soiree, held on the occasion of the visit of the Duke of Edinburgh, the Duke of Albany, and Prince Christian, Should be devoted to the foundation of a Manchester scholar- ship in the proposed Royal College of Music. The Field Marshall Commanding-in-Chief has appointed General Prince Edward of Saxe-Weimar, K.C.8., to com- mand the troops at the review of volunteers at Brighton on Easter Monday, March 25, forming the force of defence; mad Majors-General G. W. A. Higginson, C. 8., and M. G. Newdigate, C. 8., to command one each of the two opposing forces to be employed in the operations. The selection of the various adjutants, aides-de-camp, and quartermaster- generals to accompany them will be left to the discretion of the above officers. THE PREMIER AND THE EDINBURGH MERCHANTS —ln rtfehpalnykto a message of congratulation forwarded to Mr. Glad. stone by the Edinburgh Merchants' Company, Mr. Horace Seymour writes :—" I asn desired by Mr. Gladstone to you for sending him the addresses of congratulation from the Edinburgh Merchants' Company, and to beg that You will assure its members that he is very sensitive of their kind expressions. It is highly gratifying to Mr. Gladstone to learn that the principles to which he has, given support in connection with trade receive the appro- bation of so important a commercial body." THE BRADFORD CHIMNEY DISASTER.—On Wednesday evening the coroner's jury who had been inquiring into the Bradford chimney accident returned the following verdict: We find that the owners did all that non-practical men could reasonably be expected to do under the circumstances, and therefore we do not attach any blame to them or find them guilty of negligence, and we give as our verdict 'Acci- dental death.' We are of opinion that the foundation was good, and that the fall of the chimney was partly due to cutting, aided by a strong wind on the morning of the acci- dent, and we regret that the works were not stopped during repairs. A JOCKEY'S WEDDING.—Mr. Frederick Archer, the Popular jockey, was married on Wednesday, at Newmarket, to Misa Nellie Dawson, the daughter of the well-known trainer, John Dawson. The ceremony took place at All Saints' Church, which was unable to accommodate the large uunaLer of people wishing to witness the ceremony. The .o_ F. Govett officiated, assisted by the Rev. Mr. Corke; Mr. T. Jennings, jun , acting as best man. Chief amongst I)opular festivities was a substantial meal to the poor, an 'laving been roasted whole for the purpose. Mr. and Mrs. vrearcher left for Torquay for the honeymoon. The wedding elite were numerous. Tne y t_zeeza, -AND QuESTION IN SCOTLAND.—Alarming uas been received from the outer Hetrides to the that land agitation has broken out there, and the crof- cting in a body, have seized certain grazings which do not belong to them, but were regularly tenanted. They are Placing their sheep and cattle on the stolen ground in de- fiance of all authority. It is also stated that Barra men are in communication with the crofters of Glendale, who recently Created a disturbance in Skye, and against some of whom , warrants have been issued, and that arrangements have been made for establishing co-operation in their movements and their defiance of authority. The news has excited consider- 'able excitement in the north of Aberdeen. A GIRL FORGING HER FATHER'S SIGNATURE—At the Central Criminal Court, on Monday, Harriet Nntland, aged 17, who pleaded guilty last session to forging the signature 01 her father and obtaining by false pretences £l5O, was Placed in the dock. The girl's father resides in Cumber- land, and previous to leaving London he had placed in the hand of a friend the £lso—his savings. The prisoner seemed to have written a number of letters in the name of her father to the friend, representing that he was anxious to have his money. She called for it, and received it back in various instalments.—Mr. Percell said the father had been making arrangements to send the girl to America to some friends, but these were not quite complete, and he applied that the girl might be allowed out upon her father's recog- nisances, and he would take care that she was sent away.— This was allowed. ARMED Bunomens.—Baron Huddleston has shown great firmness in dealing with the "armed burglars," who were eonvicted before him of a felony at Harborne, near Birming- ham. One of the prisoners, a man named Evans, fired a re- volver twice when pursued by an officer. The first shot he fired over the officer's head "to frighten him," but the second, by his own showing, was aimed low, and the ruffian made off, believing that he had killed or disabled his pur- !tler. This belief, however, was fortunately unfounded, and it appeared that the burglar on reading an account of the affray (while he was still at liberty) said to a companion," I Missed him, thank God." It appeared that he had previously I?e_tien sentenced to penal servitude for fifteen years. Baron ddleston passed upon him a sentence of twenty years' Penal servitude, with the remark that he would have been naigned to prison for life hut for the fact that he bad fired the first shot over the officer's head. There is a distinction Without a difference between the actual and the possible sentence, Evans being already 56 years of age. His corn- Penton was sent to penal servitude for ten years. last. Shortly after mid-day, on Tuesday, a fishing boat, with a crew of four men, was wrecked at erovie. eight miles from Banff. Ttiree of the crew were drowned, namely, James Anderson and William Anderson, brothers, and Alexander Watt. The men leave widows and families. The usual Ministerial circulars in anticipation of the opening of Parliament are issued. Mr. Gladstone says in the notification to his supporters in the House of Commons that important business, "much of which has suffered delay through the special circumstances of recent sessions," will be proceeded with at the earliest moment. CIRCULATION OF FICTITIOUS BANE NOTES.—The manu- facture of fictitious bank notes is being extensively carried on in the Midlands. The notes are such good imitations that not only have commercial men been deceived, but the notes have been accepted by several banks. The spurious character of the notes was first discovered on some of them being passed to the Bank of England. The police suspect that the notes are produced and circulated by a gang of clever swindlers having agents in the principal Midland towns.—St. James's Gazette. The will of the late Anthony Trollope, the wellknown novelist, has just been proved by the two executors, Mrs. Rose Trollope, the widow, and Mr. Henry Merivale Trollope, the eldest son of the deceased. The personality is sworn at £25,892 19s 3d. The will is dated 29th October, 1878, and leaves all the property in trust for Mrs. Trollope, and provides for its division after her death between the sons of the deceased; The MSS. of the late novelist are left to the eldest son, and after the widow's death the sum of £4,000 is left to Miss F. Nightingdale Bland, niece of the deceased. AN ADROIT IMPOSTOR.—A most extraordinary case came before the Sheffield magistrates, on Tuesday. Sarah. Gosney, a woman with a good home, was charged with pro- curing money by false pretences. She has for some days past gone about at night in the rain and sleet to various mansions on the outskirts of the tewn, and, with adroitly- simulated grief and pitiful stories, worked upon the feelings of magistrates and manufacturers, several of whom gave her very substantial money gifts. The woman was afterwards found in a beastly state of intoxication. She was sent to jail for six months. William Robinson, the driver of a steam tram car on the line between Blackburn and Darwen, has been indicted at the Manchester Assizes for having, on the 7th August last, by his negligence caused the death of one William Riley. The charge arose out of an unfortunate accident which , happened to a car driven by the defendant on the day in question, when, in consequence, as was alleged, of its being overcrowdedand driven at too great a speed, it fell upon its side. Riley was killed, and several of the other passengers were severely injured. The evidence was very conflict- ing as to the main facts of the ease, and the prisoner was acquitted. A great impetus to emigration is expected to be given in the spring by the reduction of steerage fares to the United States and Canada. The steamship lines composing the North Atlantic Conference having learnt that the" non- conference " companies have been lowering the rates on steerage tickets to $25, have reduced their rates from $3l tc $2l. The companies outside the conference are the Monarch and Beaver lines to New York, the Warren to Boston, and the Dominion to Canada. All the steamship lines have found their account in attracting crowds into the " steerage ;" but the days are gone by when such enormous profits can be reaped from that source as ssere made fifteen or twenty years ago. DEATH OF LORD VAUX, OF HARROWDEN.—The death is announced of Lord Vaux, of Harrowden. The deceased peer was the only son of Mr. Charles Browne Mostyn, of Kiddington, Oxfordshire' by the only daughter and heir of Mr. George Butler, of Ballyragget, county Kilkenny. He was born at Bath in 1804, and married in 1828 eldest daughter of Colonel Arthur Vansittart, cousin of Lord Bexley. This peerage fell into abeyance on the death of the fifth baron in 1663, and the abeyance was terminated in favour of the late peer in 1838, as lineal representative and sole heir (through his mother) of Mary, the eldest sister and co-heir of the fifth Baron Vauac, of Harrowden. He is suc- ceeded by his grandson, Hubert George Charles, son of the late Hon. George Charles (who died 1879), by Mary, daughter of the late Bishop Monk, of Gloucester. Born 1860; educated at Trinity College, Cambridge. ILLING THE WRONG MAN: AN EXTRAORDINARY CON- FESSION.—Joseph Wedlake, who was arrested at Bristol, on Sunday, charged with the wilful murder of Mark Cox, has made a full confession. After being in a very dejected con- dition since his apprehension, he on Tuesday recovered his self-possession and avowed his guilt. He stated that he had made up his mind to kill a young farmer named Thatcher, who had supplanted him in the affections of his sweetheart, and on the night of the murder he hid himself in a hedge awaiting Thatcher. At about midnight the deceased came along the road on his way to the iron ore mines; where he was employed, and mistaking him for Thatcher, he (Wed- lake) struck the unfortunate man down with a heavy blunt axe. The blow had scarcely been dealt when he saw that it was Cox. Wedlake added that if his brother had not given the information he should have confessed, as he had been sorely troubled in his mind ever since. MR. GLADSTONE ON PRESBYTERIANISM AND RITUAL.— A copy of a work by the Rev. A. Duncan, Mid-Calder. en- titled "The Scottish Sanctuary, as It Was and as It Is," having been sent to the Prime Minister a few weeks ago, Mr. Gladstone, in acknowledgment, writes as follows : " Hawarden Castle, Chester, January 3, 1883.—Dear Sir,— I thank you very much for your work'on the Scottish Sanc- tuary, which I find full of interest, By no means a Presby- terian myself, I can sympathise with the high motives which,! believe, led to the movement in Scotland for increase of ritual; yet I hope this tendency will not be in- dulged without reserve, for there was a solemn and stern simplicity in the old form of Presbyterian worship which was entitled to great respect, and which was a thing totally different from the mean nakedness and the cold worldliness and indifference so widely dominant in English services fifty years ago.—l remain, &c, W. E. GLADSTONE."

ENGLISH PATENTS.—The following patents amongei others published in the Commissioners of Patents Journal were sealed during the week ending January 27th, 1833 : John Richard Hutchinson, Bury, for improvements in the manufacture of ribbed pile fabrics; Samuel Mellor, Petri- croft, for improvements in the manufacture of benzol, nitro-benzol, nitro-tolnol, and their homologues; Joseph Revell, Dukinfield, for improvements in the construction of railway chairs, and in apparatus for coupling the rails and chairs together ; Roughsedge Wallwork, Manchester, engineer, for improvements in, or applicable to machinery for the manufacture of hats ; John Hopkinson, Birstal, near Leeds, for improvements in looms for weaving; Samuel Can- liffe Lister, Manningham, for preparing and dressing waste silk; John William Fletcher, Stockport, for improvements in apparatus or appliances for use in telephonic circuits; Charles Scriven, Leeds Old Foundry, Leeds, for improve- ments in machinerY or apparatus for bending, flanging, and shaping metal. List eupplied by Mr. George Davies, C.E., Fel. Inst. P.A., Patent sOicitor, 4, St. Ann's Square, Man- chester. Tun IRISH MAILS.—The Lish Times gives on high authority the decision of the Postmr.eter-General as fellows: By the contract to expire in October next the City of Dublin Steampacket Company got £85,000 a year for con- veying the mails to and from Holyhead. The London and North-Western Railway Company get £40,000 a year for conveying the mails from Holyhead London and back. By the new contract, which has been virtually ratified, it is said that the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany undertake to convey the mails from Kingstown to Holyhead and London throughout for £BO,OOO, or £5,000 less for carrying the mails from Kingstows to London than the Steam Packet Company had got far taking them to Holyhead and back. Here is a saving of £45,000 a year in the post-office branch of the public service: However, it must be borne in mind that the Lendon and North- Western Railway Company by discontiruins their special steamer traffic from the North Wall and transferil--Le their special passenger steamers to the mail service will say _ £ll,OOO in harbour dues, as Kingstown is a free port. They will cease to run a line of steamers that don't pay, and -by placing them on the Kingstown station they expect such an increase in cross-channel passenger traffic that more accom- modation for railway carriages must be provided on the Carlisle pier. THE TITHE QUESTION AT PONTEFRACT: THE VICAR NONSUITED, WITH COSTS.—On Monday, the adjourned tithe cases, in which the vicar (the Rev. J. J. Christie) is plain- tiff against 100 defendants for various amounts due for corn rent charges, came' on for hearing. Mr. Claude Leatham appeared for the vicar; and Mr. Mellor, barrister (Instructed by Messrs. Wainwfight and Mason, Wakefield) for the de- fendants. Mr. Ke'oerry, on behalf of Mr. Bernard Hartley, one of the defendants, apologised for his having at the last court remarked "he would never pay it." This, Mr. Kaberry said, his client acknowledged was a thoughtless and foolish remark, and was said in an undertone, and not meant for the ear of the court. His Honour said it was too serious a matter for a person in Mr. Hartley's position to treat the court in the manner he did, and he could not allow it to go unnoticed. He was now, however, glad to find that Mr. Hartley amply apologised. His Honour next dealt with the preliminary objectione raised to his jurisdiction to hear the cases. He said he had looked up the law on the matter, and was of opinion that he could try them. He suggested that two cases, as against William Shay and Alfred Torr should be taken as test cases. The case against W illiam Shay, market gardener, for 3s 4d for two year's corn rent, at is Ed a year, was first called upon —The Vicar was and said that he was only inducted as vicar of the parish in June, 1878, and that the awards produced were the originals as kept in the church vestry.—Mr. Wilkinson, the vicar's agent, stated that the defendant up to eighteen months ago paid rates for the land in question, known as "Beck Field." It was contended by Mr. Mellor that the ownership of the land for which his client was charged had not been traced to belong to him. His Honour nonsuited the plaintiff with , costs, with leave to bring up the case again, and adjourned the whole of the other cases till the 9th of March.

Lid Claud Hamilton, M.P. , is reported to be indis. posed. Sir William Harcourt, in reply to a memorial, declines to interfere with the sentence of five year's penal servitude passed upon Charles Soutar for the robbery of Lord Craw- , ford's body. At Brighten, on Tuesday, John Thomas Bennett, hair- dresser, was fined £2O for having, without a license, sold beer to persons who went to his shop on Sunday mornings to have their hair cut. Notice of appeal was given. On Monday, at Bolton, Hugh Calderbank, an. operative cotton spinner, was committed for trial by ten magistrates, and also upon the coroner's warrant, for the wilful murder of his wife by strangulation at Astley Bridge on Friday

At the t.'nnual meeting oi the trustees of the. Liverpool Royal Infirmary, on Monday, it was reported that £75,000 had been promised towards the £lOO,OOO required for the re-construction of the institution. Immediately alter the re-assembling of Parliament the official correspondence on the restoration of Cetewayo and the new settlement of Zululand will be laid on the table. The good-service pension of £l5O a-year for captains, vacant by the retirement of Captain Richard Bradshaw, R.N., C. 8., on the 26th instant, has been awarded to Captain Frank T. Thompson from that date. ' The Lord Mayor of London has issued an appeal in be- half of the destitute peasantry of the island of Lewis, who are suffering through the loss of their potato crop by blight and the partial destruction of the corn crop by violent gales in October. . . Owing to the high winds which prevailed on Saturday it was deemed expedient to place policemen on duty at the new Law Courts to warn foot passengers of the danger of going under the clock at the main tower, on account of its insecurity. The Money Order Bank at Edinburgh has been compelled to go into liquidation owing to the public not allowing the orders of the bank to remain long enough in circulation to enable the bank to invest its funds. All claims will be
MR. P. RYLAND& M.P. AND HIS
CONSTITUENTS.

Mr. Peter Rylands, M.P. for Burnley, delivered his annual address to his constituents on Monday evening, and obtained a very cordial reception. He stated that though he had not been able to agree with the course which the Government took when -they first interfered in Egypt he cordially approved of what they were now doing, and hoped their action would have the effect of materially improving the position of the inhabitants of that country and enable them ultimately to have a powerful voice in the government of their native land. Alluding to Ireland he said there was a greater hope than there had previously been that through the powers which the Government now possessed crime would greatly diminish, and that criminals in Ireland would ,be taught that the arm of the law was strong enough to reach them. Notwithstanding the boons which had been granted to Ireland, the Liberal party, through whose efforts those benefits had been conferred,inet with ingratitude and hostility on the part of the Irish People. Mr. Parnell and his followers had not hesitated to call into play the most hostile and bitter feelings towards the Government, as though instead of being great benefactors to Ireland they had been hostile to its interests. Liberals, however, ought to do justice to all men, even though the benefits they con- f arred met with injury and hatred. With regard to the cry for Home Rule he was bound to say, as a Radical, that while he was willing to give the Irish people the most ample justice he would be no party to giving them anything which would separate them from the Government oi England. A vote of confidence in Mr. Rylands was afterwards nrried.
A LOCAL BREACH OF PROMISE CASE.

THE STATE OF IRELAND. THE CONSPIRACY TO MURDER DUBLIN OFFICIALS. Further extraordinary disclosures were made on Saturday in connection with the alleged conspiracy to murder Government officials in Dublin, the proceedings taking place in Kilmainham Courthouse. As the evidence adduced in the first stage of the proceedings related exclusively to the attempted assassination of Mr. Field, only five prisoners were put forward on the opening of the case. They were Joseph Brady, John Dwyer. Timothy Kelly, Joseph Hanlon, and Michael Kavanagh. The last named had been arrested since the previous hearing of the case, and, together with his four fellow-prisoners, was now charged with conspiracy to murder, and "in pursuance of that conspiracy, that on the 27th of November, they did feloni- ously assault Denis Field with intent to murder him." Mr. Murphy, Q.C., and Mr. Peter O'Brien Q.C., prosecuted. The first witness called was a young woman named Alice Carroll, who gave her evidence in the clearest manner. Under the severe cross-examination to which she was subjected, she maintained perfect self- possession. She deposed that on the evening of the 27th of November she was going down Hardwicke-street soon after six o'clock, when she saw a car, with three passen- gers and a driver, stop at the corner. The men got down and she recognised two of them as the prisoners Brady and Kelly. She saw Brady attack Mr. Field, about two doors from the latter's house, with a sword cane or a dagger. Brady knocked Mr. Field down. Another man was standing by, and Mr. Field was stabbed two or three times, and when he turned on the ground he was stabbed again, but witness could not say whether Brady or the other man stabbed him. She saw the driver of the car, and identified Michael Kavanagh as the man. In cross-examination by Mr. Killen, the witness said she did not think that the weapon she saw was a fishknife. A boy named Michael Farrell deposed that as he was passing along Hardwicke-street, about a quarter past six, he saw three men, two of them being the prisoners Kelly and Brady. He saw Kavanagh standing near a car in Hardwicke-street. W. J. Connolly solicitor's clerk, said he heard cries as he was proceeding up Frederick-street. He saw a man sitting on the flags, and a man having a bright instrument hidden under his coat passed the witness and mounted a car standing near, together with another man carrying a revolver. The car then drove away. James Egan, a provision dealer, proved picking up a hat at the scene. The other prisoners, 16 in number, were then put forward, and William Lamle, an informer, was examined. He said he joined the Fenian brotherhood in 1887. He had attended meetings of the I Irish brotherhood at various places, and named several of the prisoners who had been present. He remembered a meeting in Aungier-street, when some discussion arose about Joe Poole. At a meeting in December last, at which Joe Mullett was present, there was a conversation about Delaney, when it was said that if a fresh " vigilance " was organised, Mr. Mallen, detective superintendent, who was endeavouring to put some of them up for perjury, would be dealt wirh. Evi- dence of finding arms at Whelan's house was adduced, and, on the application of the Crown, the case was adjourned for a week, Mr. Murphy intimating that by that time they hoped to connect some of the prisoners with the Phcenix Park murders. It is stated that the criminal investigation department at Scotland Yard has despatched detectives not alone to New- castle-upon-Tyne, but also to Liverpool, Manchester, Brad- ford, Birmingham, Bristol, Wolverhampton, and other towns in the north of England and acotland where they are actively engaged in tracing out what they hope to prove to be a branch of the organisation by which the murders are alleged to have been committed. On Wednesday in London the Dublin detectives paid another visit to the Army and Navy Co-operative Store, in Victoria-street, and made further in- quiries regarding the purchases of the revolvers found with the men arrested in Dublin. They believe themselves to be in posseseion of a clue as to the buyer of the w3apons, which may lead to disclosures more startling than any that have yet taken place. Mr. Field, whose attempted assassination was the subject of last Saturday's disclosures, has left Dublin for England. The three men charged with the murder of Detective Cox have received notices of their trial. The Commission at which they will be tried opens next I Monday.

paid. a AN HEROIC Ac.—An heroic act was performed by Jessie Ace, daughter of the Mumbles Lighthouse-keeper, during the wreck of a lifeboat, on Saturday. The girl and her sister improvised a rope out of their shawls, which they threw to a drowning seaman. It proved, however, too short, and Jessie Ace then jumped into the waves and succeeded in rescuing him. THE ELECTION OF THE NEW PRIMATE.—The election of Dr. Benson to the Archbishopric was conducted at Canter- bury Cathedral, on Monday, in accordance with the cere- mony observed in electing each succeeding Primate since the days of Henry VIII. The Chapters assembled in the Cathedral library where, with closed doors, they received the letter recommendatory from her Majesty, and duly elected Dr. Benson. A MAN SUFFOCATED.—A startling discovery was made in Sheffield on Saturday afternoon. A workman named Frank Walker, employed by Messrs. Sanderson Brothers, steel-makers, had been missing some hours, and in the even- ing he was found embedded in a large gas tube. The man was lifeless, and had been suffocated. It is supposd that he , had gone up the pipe to clean it, and teeing unable to ex- tricate himself died from the gas fumes. A RUNAWAY TRAIN.—A goods train on its way to Godley Junction, early on Saturday morning, broke into three portions. Unaware of what had happened, the enginodriver proceeded to Ciodley, and soon afterwards the middle por- tion of the train dashed into the wagons behind the engine, smashing six of them. No personal injuries were caused, but both lines were blocked for some hours. The hind por- tion of the train was stopped by the guard's brake. THE YEOMANRY CAVALRY.—Major Tynte, adjutant, Royal East Kent Yeomanry Cavalry, has received a letter from the secretary of the National Rifle Association stating that the Council will allow the yeomanry cavalry to com- pete at Wimbledon this year in volunteer competitions. This will be the first time the yeomanry have been allowed to shoot for Queen's, Alexandra, and other prizes, the scores of which count for the grand aggregate. The concession, however, is only granted as a tentative measure. Just When the Army and Navy Gazette is calling upon the War Department to obtain from private inventors a new field gun the announcement that a new and powerful gun has passed a satisfactory trial comes from Woolwich. The new weapon is a breechloVer, and will be known in the service as the 22-pounder, although it is only of the same weight as the muzzle-loading 16 pounder. The gun will, it is believed, " do effective work" at a distance of three miles. A VIOLENT BLIND MAN.—John Caddy, a discharged soldier, who is perfectly blind, was committed to prison for three months at Bradford on Monday for assaulting police- men. Whilst on service in India some years ago he was condemned to be shot, but was reprieved. Shortly after- wards, being blinded by a sunstroke, he came to England. During the past few years he has committed numerous burglaries and assaults on the police, and has served a long term of imprisonment. WESTMINSTER ABBEY CRUMBLING AWAY: THE EXTERIOR To BE REPAIRED.—The Weekly journal Land announces that the exterior stonework of Westminster Abbey. which has long been a cause of uneasiness to the dean and the chapter, has now been found to be disin- tegrating so rapidly as to be almost a source of danger. I The decision arrived at by the dean and chapter by the light of their professional advice is, it is said, that there is no alternative but to reface the entire fabric of the Abbey. If it really be that there is no escape from this course, we must make up our minds to the inevitable; but the nation will demand that so hallowed a piece of national property shalt not be rudely or hastily dealt with. A sad story was told by a little boy who was put en a table to give evidence at the City Sessions, Liverpool, on Monday, against his" mother" and his brother. The woman was not his mother, but lived with his father, and it appears sent the two boys out to steal. "What did your mother say to you before you went out ?" asked the Recorder, and the little fellow answered, Go and steal a lump of print." They did so; he pulled the print down, and his brother took. it away under his jacket. The woman was sent to fire years' penal servitude, and the boy was ordered,to be detained in an industriar school until he is sixteen. The Recorder was farther of opinon that the father was not a respectable man, and that it would be well to place the younger boy in an industrial school. At the Machester Assizes, on Saturday. a married woman named Thoroley, living at Radcliffe, was indicted before Mr. Justice Kay for having written and published a defa- matory libel respecting Walter Southern. The prosecutor some time ago had The conduct of certain proceedings in Chancery in which the husband of the defendant was con- cerned. When the case was before the Vice-Chancellor an arrangement was made by council which was distasteful to the defendant, and she had persistently annoyed Mr. Southern by writing to him letters and post-cards contain- ing the language complained of. She was found guilty, but, counsel for prosecution not pressing for sentence, the judge ordered her to be liberated on giving sureties to be of good behaviour.

MURDEROUS ATTACK BY A RELIGIOUS MANIAC. At a late hour on Sunday, a young man named Snelling, a mem- ber of the Salvation Army in Folkestone, who wears the letter " S," the shield, and other regalia, went home after attending a meeting of the Army. His friends began to tease him, and he suddenly left the room. Going to an un- occupied house and shoo near the Juection Station, he smashed a large plate glass window, and got through it. Police-constable Willes, hearing the crash, hurried to the place, and found Snelling in one of the top rooms. Snel- ling rushed at Wales, and with a sharp instrument inflicted a severe gash four inches long on the side of his neck, from which the blood spurted out in a stream. Willes was assisted home, where he was attended by Dr. Bateman, and now lies in a critical state. Superintendent Taylor then had Snelling, who had locked himself in the room, arrested, and Dr. Bateman pronounced him to be suffering from acute religious mania. Attention was called recently to the programme of an asso- ciation which calls itself the English Natonal Revolutionary League, the fundamental principles of which appear to be the justification of political assassination and the repudia- tion of both God and king. An inquiry into the numerical strength of this league would in all probability reveal the fact that the comprehensive, title it has assumed covers a wretchedly insignificant organisation. It is the fashion for a few obscure individuals to take to themselves an imposing looking title, and so to endeavour to impress the public with a belief in their weight and importance. But small as this revolutionary league may be, it is a question how far its members should be allowed to abuse the cherished privilege of freedom of speech, and at a' meeting in London this week detectives atteuded to hear what the president, Mr. Oldham had to say. His doctrine is that there cannot be peace until there has been a complete social revolution. He may be permitted to hold these opinions, but not to attempt to put them in practice.
