BRADLAUGII.—At a meeting of the representatives of the railway companies having termini in London, held at the Railway Clearing- house, Euston, the subject of runaing special cheap excursion trains to London from the provinces on the date of the open- ing of Parliament, the 15th inst., has been specially taken into consideration. It appeared that the sympathisers with the member for Northampton, to the member of some thousands, were desirous of having excursion facilities ex- tended to them. On the ground that excursions run on that day might be made use of for a political purpose, the meeting passed a resolution by a majority of votes binding all companies to run no cheap excursions to London on the 15th of February. Referring to this matter Mr. Bradlaugh says :—" The refusal of the railway companies is monstrous. Trips and cheap trains have hitherto been always run for Conservative and Liberal gatheringa in all parts of England. The action of the companies will diminish the gathering on the 15th inst. by 20,000 at least, but as I expect to have fully 150,000 friends present, it will only irritate without injuring." WILKINSON v. RYLANDS. At the Manchester Assizes yesterday (Friday) week, be- fore Mr. Justice Watkin Williams, the case of Wilkinson V. Rylands was heard. This was an action brought by Margaret Emma Wilkinson against John Rylands to recover £760 and certain costs which he promised to pay if the plaintiff did not proceed further with an action against his son. Upon the pleadings the defendant denied having ever made or given authority for the making of such an agree- ment. Mr. Jordan and Mr. Smyly were counsel for the plaintiff; Mr. Russell, Q.C., and Mr. Kennedy for the defendant. Mr. Jordan said that this was a case of a somewhat un- usual character, and if his instructions were correct, a grievous wrong had been done to the plaintiff, not only by the defendant's son, but by the defendant himself. The plaintiff, who was about 22 years of age, was the daughter of Mr. G. H. Wilkinson, a gentleman who occupied a posi- tion of some respectability in Manchester. He was cashier in a large house, and resided at High Leigh, Cheshire. The defendant was Mr. John Rylands, of Thelwall Lodge, near Warrington, a gentleman of great wealth and position in the county, who up to a recent period carried on business as a tanner with his son at Warrington, besides being in- terested in a large wireworks in that town. The defendant had a son, Edward Glazebrook Rylands, who made a pro- mise of marriage to the plaintiff, and for a length of time paid his addresses to her. Eventually he seduced her. The plaintiff's father did all he could to bring about a settle- ment of the matter in the way of marriage between the parties, but as he failed in that an action for breach of promise of marriage was brought by the plaintiff against young Rylands, and the action was set down for trial at the Liverpool Assizes on the 3rd of May last. When the action was threatened the son dissolved partnership with Mr. Rylands, and went away to Australia. Under these cir- cumstances, previous to the time set down for the trial, a correspondence took place between the plaintiff's father and the present defendant. Afterwards Mr. Rylands sent a telegram to the plaintiff's father, who thereupon went over and saw him. At that time Mr. Rylands wished to compromise the matter by fiating a small annuity upon the child which had been born, some £25 a year, but the two fathers could not come to any agreement, and the interview terminated by Mr. Rylands saying he would send his solicitor to the solicitor of Mr. Wilkinson with a view to their seeing if they could come to a compromise. Next day, the 2nd May, the solicitors met, and Mr. Rylands's solicitor offered the magnificent sum of £lOO to settle the action. That offer was not accepted, and the solicitors parted on the under- standing that Mr. Rylands's attorney should see his client and be prepared to say next morning whether the case was to be settled or not. On the following morning the case came on for hearing. In the course of the opening of the action counsel read to the jury a letter written by young Rylands to the plaintiff's father of such an astoundieig character that it evidently created a profound sensation, not only in the jury box but on the bench and among the mem- bers of the bar. After this the two solicitors got together, and the attorney of Mr. Rylands offered to com- promise the matter by the payment of £5OO. That offer was declined, and then the solicitor offered £750 and costs. Mr. Wilkinson and his daughter agreed to accept that offer, the bargain was concluded, and a verdict for that amount was entered against the defendant (young Rylands) upon the record. The bargain, however, was that the action was to be stayed then and there, the plaintiff giving up her chance of the large verdict she would unquestionably have got, upon the distinct under- standing that this sum should be paid by Mr. Rylands, the present defendant. Now, however, Mr. Rylands said that he , never made such a compromise, that he never authorised the solicitor to make it, but that the arrangement was made on behalf of his son. He (Mr. Jordan) submitted that the whole of the previous correspondence and interviews pointed to Mr. Rylands, senior, as the person making the arrangement, and that Mr. Wilkinson and his daughter would never hare dreamed of making a compromise with young Rylands, who was away in Australia, and who, upon his father's own statements, was not worth a farthing. Mr. Wilkinson having been examined in support of the case, Mr. George Rideal, plaintiff's solicitor, was examined by Mr. Jordan. He detailed the interview he had with Mr. J. Rylands's solicitor (Mr. Ridgway) on the 2nd May, and said that next morning at Liverpool he again saw Mr. Ridgway, who informed him that Mr. J. Rylands had told him to brief counsel and go on with the case. Directly afterwards the case was called on. While counsel was opening the action Mr. Ridgway offered him, on behalf of Mr. John Rylands, £5OO to settle the matter. He communicated the offer to his client and Mr. Wilkinson, who declined it. Later on, counsel having read a letter by the younger Rylands, Mr. Ridgway offered £750. He did not on that occasion say on whose account he offered it, but witness inferred that the second offer was on behalf of Mr. John Rylands, as the first had been. That offer witness com- municated to his clients, who accepted it, on the understanding —as he explained to Mr. Ridgway on the first occasion—that the money was to be paid by Mr. John Rylands. Thereupon, without any evidence being called, judgment was entered by consent for £750 and costs.—Cross-exarnined : The substance of Mr. Ridgwav's communication to him early in the morning was that Mr. Rylands had instructed him to make no further offer, but to brief counsel and preceed. Under these circumstances he did not, when subsequently an offer was made, feel startled, or at the close of the business think it necessary to get any memorandum of the matter. As far as he knew Mr. John Rylarids was not in court at Liverpoel. From the fact of Mr. Rldgway's name did not appear on the present record, he inferred that Mr. Ridgway was not Mr. Rylands's usual solicitor. Mr. Russell : Upon vonr accepting the offer of £750, did Mr. Ridgway say, "Verdict against the defendant for £750 ? " Witness: I do not remember the word " verdict " being mentioned except between counsel. Mr, Russeli ; pid you hear Mr. Aepland, the defendant's counsel, say, " Against the defendant only," and did Mr. Ridgway repeat that? Witness: No; I did not hear it. Mr. Russell : Did you not hear Mr. Aspland say, "Let there lee no misunderstanding as to judgment being against the defendant only," and did not Mr. Ridgway upon that repeat in substance what he said before? Witness: I never heard such a thing. Mr. Russell: And did you not say, "We will take the judgment for what it is worth ? " Witness: No. Mr. Jordan desired to put in an answer to an interrogatory by Mee Ridgway, on the ground that he was Mr. John Ry- lands's agent. but his Lordship held that no general agency had been proved, but, in fact, the opposite. This concluded the plaintiff's case. Mr. Russell/submitted that there was no case. His Lordship agreed that there was no case, where- upon Mr. Jordan said that be would then call Mr. Ridgway to prove his anthority. His Lordship thought in his discretion that he ought not to permit that, and directed judgment to be entered for the defendant. On the application of Mr. Jordan, execution was stayed.

Another man, named Rafferty, has turned informer against the five prisoners arrested for the murder of Doherty at Carigan, County Galway. It is expected that other arrests will shortly be made for the double murder of Mr. Burke and Corporal Wallace at Castle Taylor. A Limerick correspondent.states that several detectives have arrived there to assist in detecting the branch of the Assassination League which is believed to exist there. Several arrests are expected, and considerable anxiety is felt respecting a large quantity of dynamite which was stolen some time ago. Matthias Kerrigan, his wife, and family, the principal witnesses in the Lough Mask murder case, arrived at Clonbur on Wednesday evening under a strong escort of Police. A police hut has been erected within a few yards of Kerrigan's house, and eight men of the Royal Irish Con- stabulary are in charge as special protection for Kerrigan and his family. Mr. Clifford Lloyd, special resident magistrate, has arrived in Limerick, and held at the William-street Barracks a private investigation concerning the statements of a pri- soner who has made disclosures alleging the existence in Limerick of a branch of the assassination conspiracy. It is stated that several experienced detectives have arrived in the city. The Irish Executive seem to think that they will be able to bring the Phcenix Park murders home to the perpetra- tors. There is another "informer," and this man says he was one of the party of ten who carried out the criminal design. It is further stated that three of the four men who alighted from the car in the park are amongst the persons in custody, and that the fourth man is being tracked in America. The Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland held the first levee of the season at Dublin Castle on Tuesday afternoon. There was a more than usually large attendance. The public were excluded from the Castle Yard. Sir Michael Hicks-Beach, M.P., Mr. Edward Gibson, M.P., and the O'Conor Don were amongst those present. Mr. D. V. O'Sullivan, ex-Mayor of Cork, was knighted by Earl Spencer, who was attended by the Right Hon. G. 0. Trevelyan, M.P., Chief Secretary, and members of the household and staff. INSURRECTION OF IRISH CONVICTS.—A serious emute occurred on Saturday evening among convicts employed at Haulbowline Docks, near Cork. One gang of convicts first attacked a warder named Tynan, and the insubordination quickly spread through different gangs, who also attacked the officers in charge of them. The constabulary were called out, but they, although armed with rifles with fixed bayonets, had a difficulty in holding their own, and as the riot was extending to other parts of the works the aid of the military was obtained and the disturbance quelled. One constable was struck on the head with a shovel, and several convicts and warders were hurt. DEFIANT SPEECH BY MR. Davrrr.—Mr. Michael Devitt presided at the branch meeting of the Irish National League, ' held in Dublin on Tuesday night. He observed that, while the law officers of the Crown were searching the records of the Star Chamber law in order to stifle free speech, and a judge of the Queen's Bench could think only of blasphe- mous adjectives with which to denounce his (Mr. Davit 4 language at Navan, his thoughts could not help flying away in disgust from the puny efforts of the political idiots of Dublin Castle and the bilious judgments of its Court of Castle Chamber to the homes of wretchedness along their western coast. He referred to the natural beauties of Ire- land, and to the fruitfulness of its soil; but amid so bright and glorious a landscape was, he said, the counterbalancing picture of human misery caused by inhuman laws, and of God's greatest work deformed through injustice. At that very moment there lay clasped in the deadly embrace of serpentine landlordism the lives and happiness of millions of the people, and he could not help feeling that the most godlike act man could perform would be the complete and final crushing of its hideous power.

MANCITESTER ASSOCIATION V. OUGHTRINGTONTARH (Lymrn). —These teams met on the ground of the former on Saturday. Score: Manchester Association, three goals; Oughtringten Park, one goal. Teams :—Manchester Association: Andrews. goal M'lntyre and Rouse, backs; Duerden. Middleton. Ken- nedv, Harper, Bassett, Sinclair, Hay, and Doyle, forwards. Oughtrington Park: J Smith, goal; T Thornassort and H Owen, backs; S Gibbon, E G Evans, and J Wood, half backs ; 0 G Smith, E Smith, A R Briggs, T Dodson. and E S Shaw, forwards. RUNCORN (A TEAM) V. WARRINGTON WANDERERS.—This match was played at Warrington on Saturday last, and, after a good and pleasant game, ended In favour- of Runcorn by two tries and six minor points to two minor points. Warrington kicked off, but the ball was quickly returned into their quarters by W Hughes. The game continued here for some time, and strong attempts to get in were made by H Speakman and W Wright, which were, however, frustrated by Barnes, Knowles, and Garrity. Ultimately, H Hughes obtained a try, which was not improved upon. The Wanderers next paid a visit to the Runcorn 25, Forster and Rigby dribbling in good style. Gatley, Roberts, and Gittens got the ball back into neutral ground, and, after a hard struggle. H Hughes again got over. This try was disputed by Warrington, and as neither the umpire nor referee saw it, the place kick was taken, but without gain- ing the premier point. The second half was most stubbornly contested, but at the close the seore remained unaltered. In addition to those already named, Boardman and Speakman played a capital game for Warrington, and Clarke, Ford. and Banner for Runcorn. WIDNES V. RUSHOLME.—This match was played at Rusholme on Saturday, in wretched weather. Dale, the captain of the boo., t.em. started the leather from the entrance end against a strong wind, ana the Widnes forwards playing well together soon transferred the leather well into the home team's quar- ters, Brown succeeding in crossing the Rusholme goal line, but the point was net improved upon. Walmsley, Dale, Harrop, Ireland, Morris, and Ridyard now and again made some smart runs for their respective sides. • During the second half of the game the home team, playing with the wind, had much the best of the game, and compelled their opponents repeatedly to save; Walmsley, on two or three occasions, almost getting over their lines. Nothing but minor points, however, were added to the score, and at the call of no side the Widnes con- tingent were hailed the victors by I try and several minor points, agtinst 8 minor points. Teams :—Unsholme : Dickson, back; Walmsley, Dale, and Farrar, three-quarter backs; R m- Hatett. and W Harrop, half backs; Mawrey, Emery, F Morris F Shaw, Livingstone, Twigg, Wilson, Hamilton, and Easedale, forwards. Widnes: Parkinson, back; Ireland, Morris. aad Connally, threz-quarter backs; Farrell and Ridy-ard, half basks: Mason, Brown, Fenwick, Smith, Coneannon, Killen, Grice, and Crow, forwards.

The Clisirtehatz said he had received a petition from the pronsoters of the Manchester Ship Canal Bill, which they wished the Chamber to adopt and send to both Houses of Parliament. The petition was as follows "The humble petition of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce sheweth as follows: A petition for leave to introduce to your honourable House a Bill intituled A Bill to authorise the construction of a ship canal to Man- chester, and for other purposes,' has been deposited in the Private Bill Office of your honourable House. Your peti- tioners have been informed that the standing orders of your honourable House have not been complied with in the case of the said Bill. The objects sought to be ob- tained by the said Bill are of national importance. The cheapening of inland transit is a matter of great and growing necessity to the manufacturing industries of the kingdom, in .the face of increasing competition in trade, and the increase of population. The effect of utilising and im- proving the Mersey and Irwell navigation to Manchester so as to render it nayigable for large vessels, will result in con- siderable savings in transit and dock charges, and give a wholesome impetus to the extension and improvement of waterways throughout the whole kingdom. These objects, in the opinion of your petitioners, are of such great importance to their interests, and to the general interests of the surrounding districts that they humbly pray that your honourab!e House will be pleased to dispense with the standing orders, and permit the Bill to proceed to a Select Committee there to be heard and decided on the merits. Your petitioners therefore humbly pray your honourable House that the standing orders may be dispensed with in respect of the said Bill, and that it may be permitted to proceed and be discussed before a Select Committee on its merits, and that your petitioners may have such other relief in the premises as to your honourable House may seem meet." With the view, however, of protecting the interests of Warrington, he had struck out the words "These objects, in the opinion of your petitioners," and inserted the following Notwith- standing there are provisions in the said Bill which you, petitioners consider will have to be altered or amended, still they are of opinion the general objects of the Bill." Mr. MONKS said he could support the petition amended. Mr. BLECKLY objected totally to the adoption of the petition. It was a petition presented practically to the Standing Orders Committee of the House of Com- mons, which committee was a judicial tribunal, and had to determine questions according to the rules and regulations of the House of Commons for the protection ot the public interests and properties that were interfered with by persons seeking to obtain compulsory powers to take that property from them; and those rules and regulations were framed in the interests of all such persons. If the Standing Orders Committee thought it necessary and important that the standing orders should be waived they would waive them. They knew the value and importance of the Bill, because the Examiner himself, when he had it before him, spoke of the great importance that the scheme possessed in itself; and he said also that he wished to postpone his decision until he had had 'full opportunity of considering all the circumstances. It ap- peared to him (Mr. Bleckly) an interference with a judicial tribunal, and asking them to take into consideration circumstances that did not come properly within their jurisdiction. If they were to ask a judge or jury, or any other person, to take into consideration certain circumstances that were not relevant to the point before them, they would be interfering in a way which appeared to him to be similar to what the Chamber were now asked to do. He had perfect confidence himself in the judgment of the Standing Orders Committee that if they thought the non-compliance with the standing orders was not of sufficient imPortance to re- quire that the Bill should be rejected this session they would say so, and he thought it would be an interference on the part of anybody such as themselves to ask the commit- tee to do their duty. The committee had to consider the standing orders of the House of Commons, and they would consider those standing orders alone. If they thought it necessary they would refer it to the House of Commons themselves, and some member of the House might move that the standing orders might he dispensed with, and everything would turn upon whether or not such a precedent might be created as hereafter might lead people to "The standing orders will be dispensed with, and we whl not provide such and such plans, and not do such and such things; but we will take this instance in which the stanci-
WARRINGTON CHAMBER OF COMMERCE-
ANNUAL MEETING.

Under the chairmanship of the president (Al(lerman Davies) the annual meeting of the members of the Warring- ton Chamber of Commerce was held at Bewsey Chambers, Bewsey-street, on Monday afternoon. 'There were also present Messrs. H. Bleckly, F. Monks, W. Owen, C. J. Morris, T. Jolley, J. Greening, and A. Bennett (assistant secretary).

ANNUAL REPORT. The annual report was as follows :-L" The principal sub- jects which have been brought under the notice of the Chamber during the past year are the following :—Standard wire gauge: In April a memorial to the Board of Trade was presented, praying for delay in adopting any standard wire gauge, so as to give an oppertunity of submitting such a gauge as would be most practicable for both manufac- turers and consumers, and intimating that a local committee had been appointed to report upon the matter. The com- mittee consisted of Messrs. William Carson, John Greening, Frederick Monks, Claude J. Morris and George Woods, who investigated the question, and eventually adopted the gauge of the Masters' Association of Wire Manufacturers, and recommended that the chamber should memorialize the Board of Trade to that effect. The result was the Board of Trade announced that, in consequence of representations made as to the larger sizes, it was found desirable to modify the original scale, and issue an amended scale considerably more in harmony with the wishes of this chamber. We see, however, that the Birmingham Chamber are agitating for a re-alteration, and it may be desirable for our delegates to the annual meeting of the chambers next month to be specially instructed to act in the interests of the wire trade in this locality. Navigation of the Mersey : This chamber was the first public body to memorialize the Board of Trade to require the aqueduct from the Vyrnwv in con- nection with the Liverpool Water IVorks should la; fixed at such a place, at such a depth, and in such a manner as should not interfere with the navigation of the Mersey; and acting on the suggestion of the Board of Trade, a committee was appointed to watch and report upon the matter as re- quired. Manchester Ship Canal : The plans of the ship canal are now before the public, and the attention of the chamber should be especially directed to them, so that the particular interests of Warrington may not be neglected or overlooked. Bankruptcy: The chamber has always taken great interest in bankruptcy legislation. It seems probable that a Government measure will be introduced in the ap- proaching session of Parliament, and the attenticn of the chambn should be particularly directed to it. The dele- gates to the annual meeting of the Associated Chambers, held in London in March last, were the President and Mr. George Artingstall, who gave reports of the proceedings. In the death of Mr. George Artingstall, an ex-president and one of the most zealous and useful supporters of the cham- ber, a great loss has been sustained. A likeness of Mr. Artingstall has been presented by his representatives, and is now placed in your council room. We have also to record with regret the death of Mr. John Chorley,who was a mem- ber. In response to the invitation last year, eleven new members joined, and the number of members is now forty- two. The council would again remind members to avail themselves of the facilities which are provided by the chamber for reference to the various returns, statistics, parliamentary bills, commercial journals, pamphlets, &c., which are constantly being received from Government, Parliament, and other sources. The annual statement of account is annexed. The expenditure has been very light during the past year, and a subscription of lOs 6cl from each of the members for 1883 will suffice. You may pay your subscription at your leisure, or Mr. Leigh, the collector, will call upon you in due course." 'The PRESIDENT said, in coming before them at the close of the sixth year of their existence as a chamber of com- merce, he could not help referring to the paper that was so ably read to them by the originator of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce—Mr. Bleckly—in which, amongst other things, he called their attention to the desirability of Warrington, and indeed all other towns, being represented by chambers such as that, with a view to promoting the trades in the district. At that time Mr. Bleckly called their attention to the severe competition between England and other nations in manufactures; and. he thought those present would agree with him that if such remarks were necessary in 1876 they were even more necessary to-day. (Hear, hear.) Every one must be alive to the fact that if the trade of this country was to maintain its supremacy it would have to be supported in every conceivable way. and he was quite satisfied that the existence of a chamber of commerce in a town was beneficial to the trade of the dis- trict, and that by being connected with the Associated Chambers of Commerce they promoted the interests of the trade of the country generally. But they found in their own district that there were certain manufacturers who did not think it necessary to take much interest in that cham- ber of commerce. It was possible that the monopoly which they still enjoyed caused them to think that they were not seriously affected by the competition of foreign nations; but he thought they must be quite satisfied that old and worn- out monopolies would not much longer protect particular trades either in this or any other country. (Hear, hear.) Monopoly in trade was, to his mind, fast dying out, and the race in the future would be a pretty even one; but unless they looked closely after their own interests, and availed themselves of the advantages offered by chambers of com- merce we should be falling second, third, or even fourth in the race. (Hear, bear.) He then referred to the various subjects mentioned in the report, and concluded by moving 'Lts adoption. Mr. BLECRLY seconded the motion, which was carried. ELECTION OF OFFICERS.

It would do no harm that a great work like this should be considered even more carefully, and that the promoters had been able to get it into the position it was now was a great wonder and surprise to the people who knew the difficulties. He was sure, considering it was only started about the month of June, it was not to be expected that in so short a time as this the preliminaries of so great a work would be successfully completed ; and if the Stand- ing Orders Committee where of opinion that the non-com- pliance with the standing orders was such that the Bill ought not to 'proceed this session, it Was not so serious a disparagement to it as to render any action of the Chamber necessary. He looked upon it as an objectionable thing for them to interfere with a petition or memorial of this sort with the action of a committee of the House of Com- mons which was dealing with the matter in a judicial man- ner under rules and precedents which guided their proceed- ings in reference to all great questions that come before it; and he should himself have no hesitation whatever in leaving the matter in the hands of the agents representing the promoters. The committee, knowing perfectly well the importance of it, would say to them, if they thought this non-compliance with the standing orders was not of so vital a character that they need reject the Bill upon it, they would not do it ; if, on the other hand, they thought they would create a precedent that would be dangerous in the future with such Bills as this, then they would not do it. But even then the promoters would have an appeal to the House of Commons itself, and any member could move that the standing orders be dispensed with. The House of Commons would value the judgment of the Standing Ordere Committee. It was a committee elected carefully from members of great experience, aud whose judgment he was quite sure all of them would be satisfied with in such a case as this. Therefore he thought they should object to their sending a memorial of this kind as being out of place under the circumstances. The CHAIRMAN said there were precedents where the decision of the Examiner had been set aside, and there were precedents where there had been memorials sent to the Select Committee. The Chamber were asked to send the petition on the recommendation of the agents of the Bill, and if the scheme would be of any benefit to Warrington at all, was it not their duty to send it ? Mr. BLECKLY would have been very glad indeed to have seen the matter before the Committee of the House of Com- mons this session, that they might have had it thoroughly thrashed out to see what its merits were, but at the same time he should not like the Chamber to put themselves forward. They all recollected that originally these Bills went before the Committee of Standing Orders in the first instance, but it became so heavy a business that the House of Commons appeinted these examiners to go into the technical points—not into the merits of the Bill at all—whether they had complied with the standing orders or not. If they had not complied with the standing orders then they were rejected, but if the pro- moters proved they had, the Bills went before the Standing Orders Committee. He thought they might with perfect confidence leave the matter to the Standing Orders Com- mittee. If they thought the noncompliance with the stand- ing orders was not of importance they would allow it to proceed; if they thought it was of importance they would not be influenced by anything the Chamber might say. Mr. MONKS quite agreed that if the Committee ma-de tip their minds they would throw the Bill out; but if there was no action taken they might consider the people were very lukewarm, and that the Bill could afford to stand over for 12 months. Mr. BLECKLY said he saw no objection to that. Mr. Moeiss said by sending the memorial they expressed their opinion that the matter should be pushed forward. Mr. BLECILLT said he had consulted Mr. Rylands, m.r., on the matter, and he said he did not think the Chamber could take any action to interfere with the judgment of the Standing Orders Commitee. Mr. GREENING was of opinion the petition would have very little weight, but he had no objection to its being sent. The CHAIRMAN said there were special circumstances irt connection with the matter, which the Chamber ought to know. The promoters of the ship canal scheme had all the difficulties before them before the deposit was made. The chief difficulty was as to who was the owner of the river where the canal would enter it at Garston. There were three persons who were supposed to have the ownership of the river. The Board of Trade said they were the conservator! of the river, the Admiralty also said they were the conser- vators, and Her Majasty, in the character of the Duchess of Lancaster, claimed the foreshore. Mr. BLECKLY : She's the Duke of Lancaster, although a. lady. (Laughter.) The CHAIRMAN said, therefore, if they had laid any plans the result wonld probably have been much more formidable opposition to the scheme than they had experienced. Not- withstanding what Mr. Bleckley had said, he believed when when the Bill came before the Standing Orders Committee the memorial, if sent, would have some weight with the committee. Mr. BLECKLY thought the chairman had given a wrong impression. They had noticed it was stated before the Ex- aminer they did not know what channel they were going to take, and Mr. Abernethy said it would take 12 months to make observations. He remembered that Mr. Williams said he knew the observations were in the possession of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, but it would take him many months to make observations necessary before he could say exactly which channel should be taken. The CHAIRMAN said if they did that the authorities he had mentioned would say they had no right to touch the river. Mr. BLECKLY said Parliament was supreme in the matter; and neither the Board of Trade nor anyone else could do anything. After a little further conversation, Mr. MONKS moved, and Mr. OWEN seconded, the adop- tion of the petition as altered, and the motion was car- ried.
The formal business was disposed of, and the meeting ter. minated.
"THE GREAT SEER OF ENGLAND" COMMITTED TO PRISON.

Before the Birmingham magistrates, on Tuesday after- noon, John •Hartwell, Miller-street, Birmingham, alias •"Methratton," the " Great Seer of England, philosopher, astrologer, grand master of the mysteries, and secret of the seals," alias" Anna Ross, the Seeress of New York," who has been remanded in custody, was again brought up charged with victimising numerous persons throughout the kingdom by alleging that he was possessed of the talis- manic art.—Detective Ashby testified to arresting the pri- soner at his talismanic establishment, where he found over 200 letters which had been sent with money. When arrested the prisoner said he " gave value" for the remit- tances. The officer added that the persons who had con- sulted the oracle were very reluctant to come forward and admit how they had been decieved. He had consequently summoned two young ladies, but only one was present, namely, Miss Elizabeth Grant, of Belgrave, Leicester. This witness told how she forwarded money to the prisoner, believing he was possessed of supernatural aid. In reply to the magistrate, the fair victim said the accused ad- vised her not to marry just yet, but if she would just wait a little longer she would be transformed, with a magic sur- passing that exercised in the case of Cinderella, to a very wealthy lady; that she would marry an Adonis, and that all would go happy ever afterwards.—Detective-Inspector Heiden explained to the Bench that the prisoner's career had been of a most remarkable character. For years he had lived by his professed witchcraft, except when he had been in prison. Last May he was sentenced to three months' imprisonment at Birmingham for practising the art of pal- mistry, whilst three years since he - was sentenced at the Central Criminal Court, Loudon, to 15 months' imprison- ment for a similar offence. He had also undergone 18 months' hard labour for selling indecent pictures and litera- ture in London, besides being convicted at Dayentry for for- • tune-telling.—The prisoner was committed for trial as an in- corrigible rogue and ;.vagabond, and ordered to be kept to • hard labour pending the trial. .r

Messrs. Turpie and Company, of North Shields, the owners of the screw-steamer James Turpie, have received information of a gallant rescue effected by that vessel. While bound from Genoa to Carthagena she fell in with the Italian ship Germania, of Leghorn, in a sinking condition, and dying signals of distress. After great difficulty, a communication was established between the vessels by means of ropes and life buoys, and the crew were dragged on board the steamer and landed at Carthagena. The Italian vessel disappeared shortly afterwards. Baron Pollock and Mr. Justice Manisty, sitting at the new Law Courts, on Friday, granted a rote nisi upon :he application of the Attorney-General calling upon the pro- prietors of The World newspaper to show cause why a criminal information should not be filed against them in respect of a paragraph published on the 12th inst. The paragraph had reference to an alleged elopement of a young lady of high rank with a young peer and master of fox- hounds. The application was made on behalf of the Earl of Lonsda le, and it was stated that, although his name was not mentioned, there were various facts alluded to in the paragraph which pointed to him. He all egcd there was no foundation for the statement. HISTORICLI. TRUTH AiND LEGENDLRY STORIES.—ModeII science may be able to demonstrate that many of the concep tions respecting physical phenomena dealt with in these legendary stories are utterly at variance with now welt- known facts. This may be perfectly true, but human nature is influenced in its action, quite as much as by its faiths, beliefs, and superstitions, as by the more exact knowaedge It may have acquired. Subjective truths are as true, as mere facts or actualities, as objective ones. Thomas. Carlyle forcibly expresses this when he asks, "WAS Luther s_ picture of the devil less a reality, whether it were farmed within the bodily eye or without it? " Mr. J. Green, in his 4pirMesaekrvinegs- Rocf- England," says "Legend, if it distorts facts, curately enough of the impressions of a vanished time." And thtse impressions being emotionally true, whether scientifically correct or not, have ever been ara: continue to be, powerful factors in the formation of charac- • e ro,r, aandprogressive development of humanity— morally, y, n thesocially, and politically. Our predecessors felt mt ll ' their influence and acted accordingly, and many of the presumedly exploded superstitions survive amongst the mass of mankind to a much greater degree than we often ackncw- le.dge or even suspect; although many of their more renal. sive forms may have undergone superficial transformation amongst the more educated classes.—Ancient Battle-Fields . Lanewhlre and their Associations, Charles Hardwick,.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY,, FEBRUARY 3. 1883.

THERE are fewi, if any, questions with which the member far Salford, Mr. ARNOLD, is so conversant as that relating to land, and all who know him will admit that there can be no one more earnest than he is- in his advocacy of a reform of the laws- which appertain to it Until the land of the country is freed'frorn the encumbrances with which it is now surrounded, and an opportunity is offered for its resources being fully developed, we can have, but little hope of our agricul- tural industry attaining that degree of pros- perity to which it may "fairly lay claim, ; nor can there be any chanee whatever of those who ate engaged in tilting the soil becoming its owners, though ta us it seems only right tha such a chance. ought to be afforded them. With the complexities of title to land, the difficulties and cost of transfer, and many other drawbacks which tend to hamper its cultivation, we in this country areall more or less familiar, yet to many it is a puzzle to understand why we should be less favourably circumstanced in this respect than are our friends in some of the British colonies. If in South Australia, for instance, land with an indefeasible title can be transferred in the course of a very few days at a small cost, why should it cost an exorbitant sum, and occupy

month, if not years, to transfer a similar parcel Oft land in Englan4, and that, too, with a title which is not always indisputable? Mr. ARNOLD in his researches has come across a system of transfer in Coburg, which is nearly, if not quite, all that can be desired ; and, though we are not likely to attain such i; state of perfection in our own land transactions for some time to come, there seems to us no reason why the simple method of transfer adopted in Coburg, or something akin to should not be adopted here. The facilities for the transfer of land in Coburg—over which the Duke of EDINBURG-II Will doubtless one day rule—are based, we are told, upon an accurate survey and a compulsory registration of all real estate. A legal scale of graduated fees has been fixed by the Government, pay- able for insertion on the register of all particulars ; for instance, a fee equal to 2S. per oo is levied on the amount of a mort- gage entered; a similar fee in the case cf a charge or annuity. The entry of the name of a proprietor in this register constitutes an inde- feasible title to the property entered against it, and no mortgage or claim has legal validity against the property unless it be duly inserted in the register. The ease with which, as a consequence, a purchase or transfer can be effected may be told in the words of the English Secretary of Legation, who writes : " If I wished to purchase a piece of land here (in Coburg) to-morrow, I could quite safely do so without the assistance of lawyer, solicitor, or notary. Having purchased for a few shillings the necessary sheets of the survey map, I could ascertain from them the corresponding numbers in the register, which I might consult free of cost on satisfying the Registrar that I had a bona fide interest in doing so. For a very small fee, I could obtain certified copies of the entries that interested me, and from them satisfy myself as to the title of the owner or owners, the intrinsic value of the land, the price paid by the last purchaser, and all the debts and mortgages on the property. After coming to terms with the present proprietor as to price, the sale would be recorded in the customary simple form, a copy of which I could easilY procure, ana this would suffice to satisfy the Registrar Lefore whom we should both appear in person. The seller would surrender his title to me orally in the Registrar's presence and give consent to his name being replaced by mine in the Registry. I should then paY the Government tax (about five-sixths of the whole 'cost) for the declaration of con- veyance, and the fee for the entry of mY name, particulars of sa'e, price given, and InY limitations of title." Under such a system there is no necessity for either party being troubled with a bundle of bulky and often unintelligible deeds, and, as an example of how it works, it is mentioned that a purchaser of an estate worth £lB,OOO had his first inter- view with the owner on the Saturday, while on the following Monday the conveyance was completed. This, to us, is somewhat remark- able, but we think it will be still more remarkable to most of our readers to • learn that the purchaser's costs and fees in this transaction were only about £r 00. A reforni in the transfer of land in England is one of the reforms of the future. It is probably too much to hope that it will be carried out during the approaching session, but it is one of those things which cannot be long delayed. It is a question which rises above all party considerations, and it is one the importance and necessity of which has been recognised by both political parties. Here it is a dis- puted point whether for the purposes of a transfer there should be a registration of deeds or a registration of title. The pre- ponderance of evidence is unquestionably in favour of the latter mode as being the least likely to lead to insecurity, involving less expense, and being altogether the simpler method of the two. It is the mode adopted in the most of the British colonies, and it has always been found to work well. A register of deeds, as Lord CAIRNS says, would lot, simplify title—which is the essential element in a purchase—the least. It only puts on formal record a multitude of deeds and con; veyances of the extent and complexity o' which there is already so much reason tn, complain. One of the evils of the system o'• conveyancing now in vogue in England IS. thus described by the Royal Commissioners in their report on this question: "When a contract (to purchase) is duly entered into, the investigation of the title often causes not only expense, but delay and disappoint' ment, sickening both to the buyer and the seller. The seller does not receive his money, nor the buyer his land, until the advantage or pleasure of the bargain is lost or has passed away." The sooner, therefore, a system is' adopted which will obviate evils of this ' nature, the better it will be for the parties immediately concerned; but more especiallY will it be to the advantage of the countrY generally, for once the restrictions upon land are removed, much more of it will be brought under cultivation, thus hastening the time when we shall be less dependent than we' are at present upon other countries for much of our food supply. If Mr. ARNOLD Carl br any possible means succeed in establishing the Coburg system of transfer in England, he will confer a great boon upon his- countrY- men.

At the weekly meeting of the Halton Parish Church Mutual Improvement Society, on Tuesday Mr. Thomas Miller read an essay on "Armstrong." Mr. J. S. Jeasock presided. FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE IN LANCASHIRE.— There were up to Wednesday morning over 30 farms on which foot-and-mouth disease existed in Lancashire and over 100 animals were affected. The disease principally prevails in the Salford and West Derby hundreds. Every effort is being made to prevent the spread of the contagion, which has greatly extended within the past few days. RUNCORN MADRIGAL CLUB—On Monday next this so- ciety will give its third concert of the season in the National Infant Schools. The principals engaged are Miss Emily Stewart, Mr. E. Batty, and Mr. C. Powell, who, with the chortle' will form an effective company, and it is to be hoped. that the public of Runcorn will evince a greater interest in the performances of the society than they did on the occa- sion of the last concert. HERR COHEN AT WIDNES.—Herr Cohen, phrenologist, has been lecturing in the Drill Hall, Widnes, during the past week, to large audiences. The lectures have been of a high moral character, including lessons of conduct, tleought, agpiration, improvement, and godliness. Next week Herr Cohen continues his lectures in Runcorn, where no doubt they will also be well attended. Full particulars respecting the lectures will be fund hr our advertising columns. THE MANCHESTER AND LIVERPOOL DISTRICT BANKING COMPANY, LIMITED.—In their report the Directors of this company state that the gross profit for the year ISB2, after providing for all bad and doubtful debts, is £312,385 14e. 10d. The nett profit is £187,158 19a. sd. The dividend of 15s. a ' share and bonus of ss. a share, declared by the half-yearly meeting in July, amounted to £90,500, and the Directors recommend a further dividend of 15s. a share and bonus of ss. a share, which will require £93,500. This leaves a b dance of £6,158 19s. sd. to be added to the reserve fund, which will then amount to £731,045 Bs. Bd. THE LONDON AND NORTH-WESTERN RAILWAY AND CONTRACT TICKETS.—The third-class contract ticket arrangements came into operation .on Thursday on the London and North-Western Railway, and at the same time other important changes were made in the issue of first and second class contract tickets. The number of applications for third-class contracts has been very considerable, and many persons who had second-class contracts falling due have made application for third-class tickets, notwithstand- ing the reduction which has been made in second-class rates. These, combined with other new regulations, have caused an unusual amount of work in the department through which the tickets are issued, and it is probable that some applicants will be temporarily inconvenienced thereby. One of the new regulations is that no contract ticket will be issued for a less sum than £3, except in the case of scholars and apprentices. TEMPERANCE LECTURE AT WIDNES. OR Thursday evening a lecture, entitled "Home Rule," was delivered in the Waterloo-road National school, in connection with the Widnes branch of the Church of England Temperance Society, by the Rev. R. Posta.nce, M.A., vicar of St. Barna- bas, Liverpool. The Rev. J. Wright-Williams, vicar of the parish, presided, and there was a crowded attendance. The lecturer divided his subject into four heads—forbearance, thrift, love, and t nnperance, which he contended was essential to every happy house. He defended the " double plank" in the platform of the Church of England Temper- ance Society, and while speaking as a total abstainer ad- mitted that in the past incalculable mischief had been done by intemperate advocacy of temperance principles. On the motion of Mr. Kilcross, one of the vice-presidents of the society, seconded by Mr. Frank Kay, secretary, a vote of thanks was accorded to the lecturer. A number ef pledges were taken, and collection was made to assist in defraying expenses. WIDNES OWNERS' AND OCCUPIERS' ASSOCIA.TION.—Yes• terday afternoon a meeting of the members of Widnes Owners' and Occupiers' Association was held in the officers' room of the Drill Hall ; Major Cross presiding. A dis- cussion took place with regard to the action which should be taken at the next election, and Mr. Gossage, in the course of a speech, said the public of Widnes had got the idea that that association was composed of manufacturers only. This was most misleading, for the fact was that it was purely and solely a ratepayers' association, and every fatepayer had a right to become a member by conforming to its rules. The candidates they had nominated and suc- ceeded in carrying at the poll showed that it was not a manufacturers' association, for they comprised medical men, tradesmen, and owners not engaged in manufactories. A commenittee was appointed to draw up a circular, and was to be sent to each ratepayer, setting forth the objects the association had in view, and the local measures that met with their approval. LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE ENTOMOLOGICAL SOCIETY.—Die annual meeting of this society was held on Monday evening, in the Free Library, the president (Mr. S. J. Capper) in the chair. Mr. Sidney Slater was ballotted for and elected a member of the society, and Messrs. E. Nelson and G. T. Shaw and Miss H. Joimson were proposed for membership. The officers elected for the current session were Mr. S. J. Capper, president; Mr. Robert Brown, vice- president; and Dr. J. W. Ellis, honorary secretary. The President then gave a short address, in which, after thank- ing the 'members for his re-election, he referred to the ento- mological work done dur:ng the past season. The past year had been a most prosperous. one, 15 new members having been elected. He belies ed this was a greater num- ber than in any previous year. Seven members had left through removal from Liverpool and other causes, and the society now numbers 67 against 59 members at the begin- ning of the year. At the eleven meetings which had been held, 13 papers had been read, most of which had evinced a considerable amount of care, thought, and talent in their preparation. The Secretary then read the annual report for 1882, and the financial statement showed a good balance in the hank. Mr. E. R. Billington read a paper entitled "Four- teen days in Trinidad," in which he detailed his experiences, entomological and otherwise, in that charming West Indian island, describing very vividly, and occasionally with much humour, its fauna and flora, its scenery, and the character and mode of life of its inhabitants. A short discussion ter- minated the proceedings. CONCERT AT ELLESMERE-STREET SCHOOL, RUNCORN. In aisi, of the fund for repairing Ellesmere-street Methodist Free Church, a work which was resolved upon some months ago, an entertainment was given in the schoolroom on Mon- day evening. Mr. J. R. Frith performed the duties of chairman, and before calling upon the choir to render the glee " Queen of the night," addressed a few observations to the large company which had assembled. The enter- tainment, with the exception of a reading by the Rev. J. Billington, was entirely musical, and was on the whole successful. Miss Curzon sang with good taste the song "Mother's treasure." Misses Ashbrook and E. White were very successfel in their performance of a piano- forte solo, and Mrs. Carr's interpretation of the song "Beautiful dreamer," was very enjoyable. The choir, under the conductorship of Mr. Holford, sang the glee "To the top of the diem "in good style, a remark which ale° applies to their rendering of " Excelsior." The first encore of the evening was secured by Mr. J. T. Moore for his rendering of the amusing song "What an afternoon." At a later stage in the evening a similar honour was awarded to Mr. J. Halford, who sang "Liberty Hall" in capital style; to Mrs. Newell, for her rendering of the sweet song " Killarney ; " and to Mr. R. Moore for his vocalisation of the popular song "The anchor's weighed." Mrs. Newall responded by slnging " Home 'sweet home," in a manner which callell forth hearty applause from the audience. An encore was awarded to Mr. James Marlow for his skilful execution of a solo on the violin, and he responded by repeating a portion of the piece. The programme also in- cluded the song "Why chime the bells ? " Mrs. Curzon; 11 duet, "All's well," Messrs. T. Parry and R. Moore; and the song, "When the swallows homeward fly," by Miss Jones.
