div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 3, 1883. WIDNES LIBERAL ASSOCIATION. F THE WIDNES WOUNDING CASE.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 3, 1883. WIDNES LIBERAL ASSOCIATION. F THE WIDNES WOUNDING CASE.

ANNUAL MEETING. The annual meeting of the members of Whines Liberal Association, held their annual etesting in the Office, s'-room of the Dill Hall, on Tweedy evenirg. Mr. Eustace.: Carey presided, and there were also present Captain Wareing, Messrs. 1) Wriger, J. Taylor, Pankh us% S. U ems, J. Morrison, Ward, Heslieth, D. W. Hunter, Has, ca,-d, H. B. Shores (secretny), (Re.% Mr. H. B. Snores it:t the minutes of tee I ist meeting, which were conli: ei,d. During the election of hon. officers Mr. Carey retired, :pet Captain Wareing took the chair during his absence.— r. ESKETH moved that Mr. E. K. Muspratt be re-appointed to the presidency of the Association.—Mr. J. Monnisoet said he had great pleasure in seconding the motion. Mr. Muspratt was a most advanced and enthusiastic Liberal, and one of the most prominent pioneers of Liberalism in South West Lancashire. He was, besides, always ready to help the town of Widnes by every means in his power ; and he (Mr. Morrison) hoped Mr. Muspratt might long continue the head of the Liberal organisation. (Hear, hear.)—The motion was carried by acclamation.—The next business was the election of vice-president, and the CHAIRMAN said Mr. Carey had occupied the post last year in connection with that of honorary secretary, and he thought it desirable that he should be re-elected. He understood that Mr. Carey, in case they wished to re-appoint him, had intimated that he was prepared to accept the office.—Mr. WARD moved, and Mr. Doweinn seconded, a resolution that Mr. Carey be re-elected vice-president, and it was unanimously adopted.—Mr. SHORES remarked that since Mr. Martin Taylor resigned the secretaryship, the labours attached to the office, which were of a difficult character, had been performed by Mr. Carey, who had spent a great deal of time upon them.—The CHAIRMAN and Mr. Monuisoer bore testimony to the extent and value of Mr. Carey's services; and on the motion of Mr. WRIGHT, seconded by Mr. JOHN 'fAvLon, he was re- appointed to the office.—Mr. Carey then took the chair. He said he was much obliged to them for the kind manner in which they had re-elected him to these offices, and for the courteous expressions which fhey had use He could only say that if he could do anything for the 'Liberal party of Widnes, he should always be most happy to do so, as far as his small powers would allow him.—Mr. Robert Shaw was appointed treasurer, on the motion of Mr. JOHN TAYLOR, seconded by Mr. PANKHURST.—On the proposition of Mr. WRIGHT, seconded by Mr. WARD, the following gentlemen were elected representatives of the Association on the Connell of the National Liberal Federation :—Messrs. E. K. Muspratt, E. Carey, H. Shaw, T. S. Timmis, Martin Taylor, Thomas Snipe and Dr. O'Keefe. Mr. E. K. Mus- pratt and Mr. Carey were appointed representa- tives on the executive of the same organisa- tion, on the motion of M. HUNTER, seconded by Mr. S. Owens.—The CHAIRMAN explained that any person paying £5 5s to the Sothh-West Lancashire Liberal Association had a right to sit upon the Council of that organisation, and it would therefore be for the meeting to elect two per- sons who did not intend to subscribe that amount.—Mr. S. OWEN moved, and Mr. NEWALL seconded, that Mr. John ; Taylor and Mr. Henry Brunner be re-elected in that capacity. The motion was carried.—Mr. Muspratt and Mr. Carey were re-elected representatives upon the Executive of the South-West Lancashire Liberal Association, on the motion of Mr. HESKETH, seconded by Mr. STOUT.—The SECRETARY (Mr. H. B. Shores) read his annual report.—Mr. CAREY moved, and Mr. PANKHURST seconded, a motion that the report be adopted, and it was carried.—lt was decided that the annual meeting should be held in Simms Cross Board Schools in February, and it was stated that Mr. E. R. Russell, editor of the Liverpool Daily Post, and Mr. Bosom- worth, of the Junior Refor n Club, had promised to be present on that occasion.—Mr. J. MORRISON suggested, in view of the probable extension of the franchise to the counties, that the Association should do something towards educating the people of the district in the true principlep of Liberalism. The Tories had not at present any programme to put before the country; whereas the Liberals when they were in Opposition were always urging upon the attention of the Tories certain reforms, which they considered should be carried out, and if that party would not carry them out, to make room for one that would. The Liberal party was now in power; they had a programme of reforms which they thought necessary for the benefit of the country, and he should like those reforms explaining in a course of lectures. A similar policy had been adopted in other parts of the country, and he thought a course of lectures would be of great benefit to the townspeople. He saw no reason why they should not be successful.—Mr. S. OWENS regarded Mr. Morrison's suggestion with favour, and remarked that he thought the formation of a club would conduce to the accomplishment of the desired end. In Penketh and Earlestown, places much smaller' than Widnes, they had clubs, and he thought that either a Liberal Club ot some other mode of educating the people would kle to their material advantage in Widnes —A long discussion took place on the subject, with the result that a small committee was formed to organise a series of lectures. The suggestion as to a club was not dealt with. •

DEATH OF MRS. PERCY.. Widne's has acquired an unenviablle notoriety in conse- quence of the many crimes of violence that take place within its boundaries, and another tragedy, ef a most harrowing de- scription, has to be added to the long list. Mrs. Margaret Percy, after lingering in a state of almost complete uncon- sciousness for about a month, succumbed to the injuries, which, it is alleged, were inflicted upon her by her husband, on Thursdcy evening, about half-past five. Additional hor- ror is lent to the affair on account of the age to which the chief actor in the tragedy and his victim have attained, William Percy being 72 years of age, and the deceased 68. The facts of the case will, no doubt, be fresh in the minds of our readers, but we may just briefly repeat them. On Satur- day, the 7th January, Percy, who is a person of intemperate habits, left his farm, in Gorsey-lane, Widnes, to go to the town. He returned about 11 o'clock the same night in a state of intoxication. Incensed at something. which took place he, in his drunken state, struck his wife a violent blow on or about the head. The suddenness and force cf the blow made the poor woman reel, and she fell into a chair. Margaret Roach, a servant, inter- fered on her mistress's behalf, but the violent actions and threatening language of Percy alarmed her for her own safety, and she ran hurriedly from the house. As if with a settled purpose to commit some deed, Percy locked and haired the outer doors, both back and front, and then was enacted a scene of horror which human eves did not wit- ness. Percy and his victim were alone, but the servant, Rorch, standing at the door outside heard the sounds of a struggle taking place within, and her mistress's shrill cry for help. • No help was at bpd, and the lonely spot on which the farm stands precluded' the possibility of the ser- vant obtaining any. At length the sounds of contention ceased. Roach crept into the shippon where she slept all night; and the silence of the night, which had been so rudely broken, once more reigned. About eight o'clock on the Sunday morning Roach gained access taithe house. She discovered her mistress lying on the kitchen floor, in a pool of blood, her countenance disfigured and discoloured, and her hair clotted with blood. The furniture and the fire irons were cattered about the room in confusion, everything tending to show that a terrible struggle had taken place. The poor woman was placed on a bed, temporarily erecte,d in the kitchen, and here for a period of 25 days she lay in a state of semi- unconsciousness, when on Thursday evening she died. Dr. Cooper, who had attended her throughout, attributed her state to concussion of the brain, but a post-mortern exami- nation of the body was made yesterday by that gentleman and Dr. McLennan, who will relate the results to a coroner's jury to-day (Saturday). Percy was apprehended OA the Sanday following the occurrence on the charge of unlaw- fully wounding his wife, but it is highly probable that he will be now arraigned on the more grave charge of murder. A great difficulty in the case is the fact that Mrs. Percy was never able to give an account of the brutal treatment which resulted in her death. Percy, who, not- withstanding his age, is a vigorous man, has not exhibited much feeling in regard to the matter, and when brought be- fore the magistrates has assumed an air of indifference. Ten days ago, however, when Inspector Barnett was repeat- in, a statement which had been made to him by Percy, the latter seemed stung to the quick, and declared excitedly that the evidence against him was false. The statement which thus excited him was to the effect that he had said that his wife had a bad temper and "many a one would have killed her before this." On Wednesday last, when he was brought before Mr. W. L. Evans and Mr. E. K. Muspratt, and formally remanded, he apparently took no interest in the proceedings, and made no observations. He was to have been taken before the justices last night on a "graver charge" than that of unlawfully wounding, but no magi- strate coming forward he was detained in the cells, and will be charged to-day. Afterwards, the inquest will be held, when, no doubt, further light will be thrown upon an occurrence which has had a most terrible ending.

div.head: HOLY TRINITY CHURCH, RUNCORN,
div.p: HOLY TRINITY CHURCH, RUNCORN,
ANNUAL TEA MEETING.

The congregational tea party, in connection with Holy Trinity Church, was held in the schoolroom, on Tuesday evening. About 150 persons partook of the good things provided. Subsequently an entertainment was held, pre- sided over by the vicar, the Rev. W. Preston, M.A., and the other rev, gentlemen present were Canon Barclay, M.A, G. Carson, A.K.C., and D. Llewellyn. During the evening the band of the Orchestral Society executed several pieces with good style and finish, and were loudly applauded. Mies Glover sang the song "At the ferry," very tastefully, her full soprano voice being heard to great advantage. " The Frenchman and the flea powder," a humorous recitation by the Rev. G. Carson, evoked a hearty encore, which was, how- ever, not responded to. Miss Pierpoint, who has a contralto voice Of much power, was highly successful in her interpre- tation of the song " Auntie "•, and Miss Tomlinson per- formed a violin solo, in which she exhibited a skill and a delicacy of touch which was deservedly applauded. Mrs. Morton sane. " Steering " with deep feeling, and she was heartily applauded by the audience. Mr. R. Pierpoint's ability as a cornet player is well known, and bis execution of "Ii Trovatore " was a fine piece of instrumentation. He received an enthusiastic encore, to which he responded. Miss Harrison executed a solo on the pianoforte in good style, after which The Rev. W. PRESTON, M.A., delivered an address. • He congratulated those present on the harmony that existed in the church, Which he hoped might long continue, but he complained that although the evening congregation was very fair, the morning congregation was not satisfactory. He should like to see a much larger attendance. The small attendance at the Lord's table caused him sincere sorrow, and he had started a Communicant Association in order to bring more forward. The Sunday schools, he was thankful to say, costinned ba a flourishing condition, and he wished to return his heartiest thanks to their self-denying and hard- working superintendents, Sunday school teachers, ladies and gentlemen. (Applause.) He looked upon the Sunday schools as one of the grandest organisations for bringing up the future generation in the ways they should go. (Applause.) The work at Mill Brow, which was not at the west end of Runcorn, was being carried on by his disinterested and hard-working young men. The Sunday school there, conducted by Mr. Wm. Cunningham, was admirably at- tended. (Applause.) During the past year the district visitors had made 4,000 visits. Speaking of church affairs, Mr. Preston complimented Mr. Annett, the choir master, and Mr. Jowle, the organist, on the efficient state of the new choir, the old choir having resigned in consequence of an action which the churchwardens felt constrained to take in connection with the organist. The day schools, the rev. gentleman said, still retained their great efficiency, and in consequence of tbe teaching staff not being sufficiently large, the managers had to refuse numbers of boys and girls who went week after week. Mr. Annett had started a select class, and he urged them, if they wished to give their children a sound education, to send them to that gentlemen. The Young Men's Christian Association, of which Mr. Hy. Hankinson was the secretary, was progressing, and the Bible class conducted by Mr. Llewellyn, was very well at- tended: The latter gentleman's cottage lectures were also very much appreciated. A plot of vacant land near the church had been an eyesore to him for a long time past, and it had been his desire ever since he came to Runcorn to take the matter in hand. He did not say it boastfully, but thankfully, that he had never taken anything in hand that he bad not carried out, and, God helping him, he would carry out this special worke It had been decided to pur- chase the piece of land, which was a source of danger to the church, for a churchyard. They could obtain the land from Sir Gilbert Greenall for a mere song, but it would take about £l2O to cart away the rubbish upon it and rail it round. He had raised in a single week £3O or £4O. He had made a very good start, and he thought it fair to call upon them and others to help him and the committee. (Ap- plause.)

The programme was then concluded as follows :—Heim- liche liebe, " Gavotto," Orchestral Eand ; song, "The pilot," Mr. Littler; glee. "Oh, who will o'er the downs so free," the choir; song, Miss Pierpoint ; pianoforte duet, "Fandango," Misses Harrison and Tomlinson; song, "Stars the night adorning," Miss Glover; recitation, Rev. G. Car- son; song, "True till death," Mrs. Moreton; duet, Miss L. Robinson and Master Owen; song, Mr. Sharrocks ; guar- tett, "Sleep while the soft evening breezes blow; "National Anthem, Orchestral Band.

On the motion of the Rev. D. LLEWELLYN, a vote of thanks was accorded to the ladies who had presided at the tea tables, and also to those ladies and gentlemen who had contributed to the evening's entertainment.

A WEDDING INTERRUPTED: THE BRIDEOROOM ARRESTED.—A wedding party at Sheffield met with a grievous disappointment on Thursday morning. A local schoolmaster was about to lead to the altar a wealthy widow. Three carriages and pairs were at the door of the bride to convey her and her friends to the church, and a cab went for the bridegroom. As he was about to step into it be was arrested on a charge of felony and conveyed to the police station. There was great disappoint- ment when the news of his arrest reached the bride and her friends. It appears the pair intended going to Tor- quay for the honeymoon. The intended bride on Thursday evening was stated to be very ill, and under medical treat- tnent.

div.head: WIDNES PARISTI CHURCH TEA PARTY.
div.p: WIDNES PARISTI CHURCH TEA PARTY.

On Wednesday evening, the annual parochial tea party of Widnes Parish Church, was held in the National school. The gathering seemed to have lost none of its popularity, judg- ing by the large number of persons who partook of the sub- stantial tea which was provided. The following gave dona- tions towards the expenses of the tea :—Widnes Metal Com- pany, Golding, Davies, and Company, Vickers and Son, W. Pilkington and Son, Widnes Alkali Company, Messrs. Handley and Beck, and the fsllowing Kil- cross, Crawford, Wright-Williams, Matthews T. Davies, Boardman, Faulkner, Littler, Briscoe, Henry 'Mather, Jos. White, Aukers, A. M. Wharton, Treacy, senr. and junr., Lord, Imison, and Smith. Mr. Birchen and Mr. Atherton were also donors. After tea the entertainment was held, the vicar, the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, presiding. The room was crowded to excess, several la,undred persons being presont. Before the excellent pro- gramme, which had been arranged, was proceeded with, the Chairman gave a review of the work"which had been accom- plished in the parish during the past year. Whether they were fast people or slow people, all their energies should be naturally round their church, and they might fairly con- gratulate the church officers upon the improvement that had b..n wade to tue cnurcnyara by the erection of a new wall. The gates were yet wanting, but he understood the officers had done all they could to have them put up in time, but so far unsuccessfully. He hoped they would be up before the Ist of April. Great tact was required on the part of the officers in their management of the chnech, and he thought they were to be congratulated from the churchwardens downward upon the smooth way in which things had worked. He would propose, second, and carry himself that the very best thanks of their united body be given to the church officers for their work during the past year. (Ap- plause.) They had to congratulate their !school mana- gers always excepting himself (applause) and thelr school teachers, and he would add their scholars, for the way in which the schools had been conducted, an for the success they had, as a rule, achieved, and for the vitality by which they were surrounded. He paid a compliment to the clever and talented master, Mr. Crawford. ' He referred to the self- sacrificing labours of the glee class and the choir, observing that the baton bad passed from Mr. Treacy, senr., to Mr. Crawford, and he went on to speak of the quiet, but very effective labours of the district visitors, to whom he paid a fitting tribute of praise, expressing the fervent hope that their ministrations would be productive of increasing good and increasing comfort to those with whom hey were brought in contact. (Applause.) He acknowledged the obligations those present were under to the members of the Church of England Temperance Society, and to members of the congregation for the aid they had given in arranging for the tea party. A working men's mission, conducted entirely by working men, had been successfully carried on every Sunday night during the past twelve months, end other missions had been conducted every Sunday morning and every Sunday evening. Noble class-rooms had been added to the school, and further ex- tensions were contemplated. Speaking of the proposed church at Anderson's corner, he drew an amusing picture of the slow progress that was being made, but added that the church had not bean forgotten. He expected that it would be commenced by some sign in the course of next month. The contracts had been sent in, but there was a little indecision about accepting them. A large sum of money would be required for the completion of the church, and he trusted all present would he ready when the collec- tion went round. He had received 10 from Mr. Frederick Neil, £lO from his mother, and from his brother Charles, and he thought these were kind and generous people. (Ap- plause.) The members, he thought, had every right b be very well satisfied with the work which, by the grace of God, one and another in connection with the church had been enabled to do. If stagnation be a sign of death, certainly there was no sign of death about the schools or the church. Ile could only bear testimony to the fact that there were far more men. engaged in doing God's work in the parish in various ways than there had been for some years past. These were men who were not accustomed to do so, and men who were work- ing as only working men could do. He hoped that next year would see a great many more things done more class rooms raised,--11 new church built-4he architect had said if they would only furnish him with money enough he would finish it next November—but in the meantime en- deavour to fill the mission rooms. (Applause.) The following programme was then gone through in very creditable style: "Happy moments," Mr. Mason; glee, "Blow gentle gales," song," It is easy if you only know the way," Mr. Winkworth •' song, "Ye banks and braes." Miss Fairley ; "song, "The village blacksmith," Mr. Wilkin- son; song, " What are Englishmen made of," Mr. Davies; glee," Come o'er the brook ;" "Strangers yet," Miss A. Purver ; song. "The pilgrim of love," Mr. Large; song, "Shy Robin," Miss Fairley ; song, "Measure your wants by your means," Mr. Davies; "The bashful man," Mr. 'nelson; quartette, "Wrecked hope," Miss Fairley, and Messrs. Bate, Large, and Wilkinson: song, "The pilgrim fathers," Miss A. Purver •, song, "The midsbipmite," Mr. Wilkinson; song, " The chase," Mr.. Walker; song, "Tom Bowling," Mr. Large; song, "Roses," Mr. Mason; eong, " Hope on," Miss Purver ; song, "The pilot," Mr. Walker; glee, "Now by days retiring lamp," Miss A. Purver, Miss Lord, and Mr. J. B. Imison.

On the mution of the Rev. Mr. DUGGAN, curate, a vote of thanks was Passed to those ladies and gentlemen who had subscribed towards the annual expenses of the tea meeting, also to those ladies who had prepared the tea, and to those gentlemen who bad arranged the room. Mr. W. TREACY (secretary) moved a vote of thanks to the chairman, of whom he spoke in eulogistic terms. It was carried with acclamation, and the entertainment concluded.

The Press Association learns that the vacant county court judgeship at Clerkenwell has been accepted by Mr. A. Geddis, Q.C. A gang of burglars is at present infesting Oldham, al- though the police have already broken up one party of them. A house in Hobson-street has been entered, and £32 belonging to a friendly society carried away; and on Friday morning the Derby Hotel, Manchester-street, was broken into and £99 taken from a safe. The police, how- ever, have succeeded in capturing the depredators, and the safe which was carried away has been recovered. Sir Stafford Northcote has sent a circular to his political supporters urging them to be present at the opening of Par- liament. The letter was written on board the Pandora, off Messina.

div.head: DISTRICT NEWS.
div.p: DISTRICT NEWS.
ALTRINOHAM.

SERIOI7S CHARGE AGAINST CATTLE DEALNIIS.—WiIIiam Rowbotbam and James Rowbotham, cattle dealers, and James Bsooks, were charged at the Altrincham Police Court on Saturday with committing perjury at a magis- terial inquiry at Lymm on the 19th inst., and also with eon- lipiring together to commit perjury. Mr. Hockin piese- ented, and Mr. P. Davies, Warrington, defended the prisoners. The case, which occupied the Altrincham Bench three days in hearing, the preliminary investigation only terminating at half-past eight on Saturday, arose out of one heard at the Lymm Petty Sessions, in which James Rowbotham was the defendant. The evidence given on that occasion injuriously affected the character of the then complainant, a girl named Nelly Newton, and two married women residing in the neighbourhood.—The prisoners were committed for trial at the Chester Assizes. ASHTON.

• THE NORTH ASHTON BRASS BAND.—The annual ball in connection with the North Ashton Brass Band was held on Monday evening last, at Holy Trinity schools, Downall Green, which had been kindly lent for the occasiOn by the Rev. W. J. Melville rector. There was a goodly number of persons present, and the company very much enjoyed them- selves, everything passing off successfully. DISTRIBUTION .OF THE ASHTON CHARITIES. A special meeting of the trustees of the Ashton Charities was held at the Local Board offices, on Saturday afternoon last, for the purpose of distributing the charities. There were present Messrs. Valiant, Clarke, Gaskell, Richardson, Livesley,- Aspinall, Knowles, and Melling. Out of the 300 applications received for assistance and relief 151 of the most necessitous and deserving cases were selected at a meeting of the trustees, held a few weeks ago, and these persons were asked to attend the special meeting held on Saturday last. Each person entered the room in turn, and what it had been decided to give them was banded over. To the aged people four yards of ,red or white flannel, or eight yards of twilled calico was given, whilst a few old men received a coat or trousers, as they were most in want of. A number of lads had suits of velveteen given to them. The work of distribution occu- pied some time, and Many of the recipients expressed themselves as very thankful for what they had received. About twenty yards of the fencing surrounding the Recrea- tion Society's ground at Ashton was thrown down by the recent storm, and in Garswood Park branches were lopped off as if they had been cut off with an axe. The wall in question is brick built, and stands about eight feet in height. Some of the windows of the Congregational school, Gerard- street, were blown in, and besides the inconvenience of the gales in blowing off slates, many of the residents in Ashton had their cellars flooded with water. In many in- stances there was a depth of three or four feet, and several of the publicans had barrels floating about. One gentleman was unable to supply his customers with sherry, owing to the barrel having floated beyond his reach, and another, in answer to an application for stout, remarked somewhat brusquely to a new comer, " Thou'll get none here." It appeared that in going across the plank to his stout barrel he had made a false step and measured his length in the water, and was under the impression that his latest customer was expectant of a repetition of the escapade. THE SAVAGE ATTACK ON A FIREMAN AT ASHTON. Robert Eccles, colliery fireman, Ashton, was charged on remand at the Wigan County Police Court, on Friday last, with committing a violent assault on George South- worth, also a colliery fireman, Long-lane, Ashton, on the 30th ult.—Mr. Superintendent Weir prosecuted, and Mr. Leach (Messrs. Scott aid Ellis) defended.—Prosecutor said about half-past nine o'clock on the night named he saw the prisoner in the Star public-house, in Ashton. Witness left the inn shortly before 11 o'clock, and when he got near Nicol-lane on his way home, he overtook the pri- soner and William Howard. He said " Good-night "to prisoner, and was going on when Eccles said " Thou'rt pique- ing again." Piisoner then struck him over the mouth with his fist and knocked his bat off. He picked his bat up and went walking on followed by the prisoner. He told Eccles that if he could not go along the highway without being attacked in such a way he would be obliged to summon him. Prisoner thereupon struck witness on the side of the head and knocked him down. As he was raising his head to get up, Eccles gave him a violent kick on the left side of the head, and on getting up he found that he was bleeding very freely. At that time James Berry came up and picked up witness's hat and put it on his bead. He also assisted him home. Witness lost a considerable quantity of blood, and was attended by Dr. Latham. He was still under that gentleman's care.—Corroborative evidence having been given, prisoner was committed to the Sessions for trial, but was admitted to bail.

div.head: CONGLETON.
div.p: CONGLETON.

At the Manchester City Police Court, on Friday, Thomas Hall, formerly in business as a corn miller at Odd Rode, Congleton, and Forge Mill, and his son, Thomas Henry Hall, were charged with conspiracy under the Debtors' Act, and the former was also charged with certain other offences under the same Act, he being a liquidating debtor. After the case had been partly heard, the further examination was adjourned to February 8. FRODSHAM.

LOCAL SUCCESS.—It gives us pleasure to announce that the name of Master W. G. Turton grandson of W. G. Gibson, Esq., Overton, and pupil of the Ray. R. P. Rorwiok, Prod- sham, appeared in the list of successful candidates at the late examination of the College of Preceptors. FEODSHAm LITERARY AND DEBATING SOCIETY.—A meet ing of the above society was held in the girls' schoolroom on Monday evening, when the vicar (Rev. H. B. Blogg) pre- sided, and a paper was read by Mr. John Jones, assistant master at Overton School, on the fo'lowing subject: "Which has been of the most service to mankind, printing or steam?" The essayist in an able Manner reviewed the history and progress of printing and steam, and the chairman, the Rev. A. P. Reynolds, and Mr. Wallace took part in the discussion which followed. A vote of thanks to the chairman, proposed by Mr. C. E. Linaker, concluded the meeting. RECHABITES MEETING.—The Frodsham tent of the Order of Rechabites held a meeting in the Town Hall, on Friday eveiaing, but, in consequence of the unfavourable weather, there was only a moderate attendance. Mr. William Farish, of Helsby. presided, and a very interesting programme had been prepared, which consisted of recitations by Forrester Nicholson, F. Hougle, W. Sutton, B. Robinson, G. Webb, John Beard, and T. Lloyd. These juvenile reciters showed considerable merit in the respective pieces, the first-named being worthy of special notice. Mr. Hinde and Mr. Thomas, of Norley, each gave a good practical address on the advantages of temperanceond the temperance choir rendered excellent service, accompanied on the harmonium by Mr. Aston. A vote of thanks to the chairman and speakers, proposed by Mr. Thomas Hour.th, seconded by Mr. William Booth, brought the meeting to a close. HAYDOCK.

William Hunter, collier, Gerard's Bridge, near St. Helens, was fined 40s. at the Wigan County Police Court, on Mon- day, for stealing a cage and two larks from the dwelling- house of Thomas Boby, collier, Billinge-Chapel-End, on Sunday liorning. LOWTON.
CONCERT AT LOWTON PARISH CHURCH_ SCHOOLS.-

ith the object of raising funds to be devoted towards the purchase of school furniture and hooks for the Sunday school connected with Lowton Parish Church, a concert was held therein, on Monday evening. There was a fair attendance. The vocalists were Mrs. Seton (Lowton Grange), Miss Turner, Mrs. Jones (Newton), Dr. Mapei (Golborne), Mr. McClure (Wigan), Dr. Coombs (Wigan), and Mr. H. F. Gooch (Newton). The programme was a capitally selected one, and many of the pieces were exceedingly well given, those by Dr. Coombs and Mr. McClure creating the greatest enthusiasm. NANTWICH.

The first statutory meeting of the creditors of James Heap, residing at Mill-street, Nantwich, and carrying on business at Nantwich,Winsford, and Farnworth, near Bolton, manufacturing and retail clothier, was held on Wednesday at the offices of Messrs. Edward Heath and Sons, solicitors, Manchester. The statement of affairs as read by the receiver, Mr. William Griffin, accountant, showed liabilities £1,775, and assets £678. An offer of composition of 5s in the pound was made, but refused, and liquidation was there- fore resolved upon, Mr. James Eckersley (Astbury and Eckerslev) accountant, Cross-street, Manchester, and Mr. W. O. Clough (Armitage, Clough, and Co.), accountant, Huddersfield, being appointed joint trustees. witk a com- mittee of inspection. The principal creditors were repre- sented by Mr. H. Claud Lisle (Nantwich) and Messrs. Heath and. Sons (Manchester), solicitors; and Messrs. Eckersly, Tilzey (Guardian Society), Griffin and Black, accountants, Manchester; Mr. Clough, accountant, Hudders- field ; and Mr. Jones, accountant, Farnworth. Messrs. Heath and sons were entrusted with the registration of the resolutions. The proceedings were transferred to the Man- chester County Court. OVER, •

ST. JOHN'S CHURCH.-0; Friday evening last, the annual tea meeting connected with St. John's Cliurch took place in the National School, which was beautifully decorated for the occasion. Tables were given by various ladies. The attendance was good ; the chief families in the district were represented, incluaing Lady Delamere, Mrs. Turner (Over Hall) and party, Mr. ff. J. Falk and party, Mrs. Okell, Mrs. Cooke, Mrs. Ninis, kc. During the evening songs were sun; by Mr. Leigh, Mr. J. Hall, and Mr. Cromack. Miss Woodvatt sang "No, sir," and in response to an encore gave "Baby mine." " Good-bve," sang by Miss Turner, received such a hearty encore that she complied, and sang "The three maids of Lea." The Misses Okell played a pianoforte duet very nicely. A violin solo by the Rev. E. Woodyatt, accompanied by Mrs. Woodyatt on the piano, was so heartily applauded that he gave another solo. Mr. G. Hamlet gave a piccolo solo, and for an encore a cute solo. The usual votes of thanks and the National Anthem closed a very pleasant evening. GOLBORNE.

THE PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAZAAR AT GOLBORNE.- The bazaar held in the Primitive Methodist Chapel. Edge Green, Golborne, last week, on account of the opening of which appeared in our last issue, resulted in the anticipa- tions of its promoters being considerably exceeded. On the Thursday, there was a crowded attendance, but not much business was done on the Friday. At the conclusion of the sale on the Saturday it was found that a quantity of goods had not been disposed of, but it has not yet been decided what shall be done with them. It will probably prove of considerable interest to state that the stall in charge of Mrs. Sproston, Mrs. it. Johnson, Miss Twist, Miss E. Sproston, Miss Knowles, Miss S. Critch- ley, and Miss S. Ince realised the sum of £l3 12s 3J ; the stall of Mrs. Crewdson, Miss Sproston, Miss Sutton, Miss A. Walker, Mrs. J. Prescott, and Miss J.

llnce realised £l7 7s 11d; the stall of Mrs. Boydell, Mrs. IVO Whalley, Miss Darlington, Mrs. Latham, and Miss A. Fres- cott realised £5 6s 7d; and the "glass stall "of Mr. :Ind Mrs. Potter raised £4 lOs 2d. The refreshment stall in charge of Mrs. Sharpe, Mrs. Oldfield, Mrs. Ridyard, Mrs. M. Knowles, and Mrs. A. Knowles realised £7 2s SM. The sale of tickets at the door brought in £4 12s 84 ; the " art" gallery £1 7s 10d; "dips," £1 8s 3d; and the weighing machine. Sc. In addition to these sums the choir by sina- ing at Christmas raised £5 163 71c1 ; tea meeting and subscriptions, £lB 15s 3d ; the Rev. R. Crewdson's account: cards, £l2 4s; books, £1 13s; tickets. £2 2s 54; dona- tions, £8 13s sd. These items added together make a total of £lO4 18s 114 raised in connection with the bazaar. It is a most gratifying and pleasing sum, and the trustees can- not but feel thankful to all those who so willingly and kindly assisted them.

SERVICE OF SONG AT GOLBORNE.—The want of more convenient accommodation in connection with the Golborne Independent Methodist Sunday School has been long felt, and an effort is being made to raise funds to make the necessary alterations. On Wednesday evening a service of song, entitled "Gems from the life of John Ashworth," was given in the chapel, High-street, the proceeds being devoted to the object just named. There was a very good attend- ance. Mr. Lee, evangelist, of Stubshaw Cross, read the con- nective pieces, the musical part of the service being excellently carried out by the choir under the efficient leadership of Mr. John Openshaw. Mr. Joseph Openshaw ably presided at the harmonium. The service was very much appreciated, and unusual interest was taken in it as it was the first of its kind at that place of worship. The service was concluded with singing and prayer. GOLBORNE CONSERVATIVE CLUB: LECTURE ON IRE- LAND,—A few weeks ago we announced the postponement of a lecture on "The Poetry and Literature of Ireland," which was to have been delivered by Mr. Walter Pierce, of Liverpool, in connection with the Golborne Conservative Working Men's Club. On the original date fixed Mr. Pierce could not attend threugla ill health, though he promised to give it on some future date. This promise was fulfilled On Wednesday evening last, when he gave his lecture in Mr. Brewis's schoolroom. There was a large attendance, and Mr. W. H. Arnott occupied the chair. In addition to Mr. Pierce, there were also on the platform the Rev. J. Smith, rector of Lowton, and Messrs. John Brewis, junr., Richard Fairhurst, and Woolacott ; Captain Locte and Major Parker (the latter of Liverpool). In the curse of his lecture Mr. Piercelgave some interesting details relating to the early history of Ireland, from the most remote period to the act of union, ISM. The stirring incidents at various periods were graphically described, and the Irish character deliene- ated with taste and humour. The great orators of Ireland and the poetry and literature of the country received a due share of comment and description.

TARPORLEY. The Cheshire magistrates have passed a sentence of three months' imprisonment on James Midgeley, a joiner, for stealing ornaments from Oulton Hall, Tarporley. Midgley had been courting the housemaid at Oulton Hall, and hear- ing that he was also paying his addresses to another young woman in the neighbouring village of Weaverham, the housemaid went to inquire. On her entering the young woman's house the mother said Midgley was courting her daughter, and that they were engaged to be married, at the same time pointing to a number of handsome presents he had made her. These presents the housemaid recognised as ornaments stolen from Oulton Hall, where Midgley had been employed. .The housemaid had him arrested. It then transpired that he was a married man with one child, and that he had also become "engaged" to two other young women in the same heartless way.

LATEST NEWS.
The Ontario Legislature has been postponed. Mr. 6allin, Republican, has been elected senator for Min- nesota.
The Governor of Madras has presented the insignia of the Order of the Star of India to the Maharajah of Travan- core.

The Duke of Albany installed Lord Brooke, M.P., yester- day, at Cold'ester, as Provincial Grand Master of Free- masons for Essex. • Cardinal M`Cabe is lying ill at his residencb, Monks- town, Ireland. His Eminence is labouring under physical prostration, but no serious apprehensions are entertained.

A telegram from Sligo yesterday morning states that the gunboat Redwing, with Her Majasty's Law Inspectdr on board, made an ineffectual attempt yesterday to reach Lillis- murray Island, off Sligo coast, where it is said the inhabi- tants are dying for want of food. The waves were running mountains high.
A Madrid telegram states that the Spanish Congress on Thursday rejected a motion authorising the most favoured nation treatment to countries which might concede commer- cial advantages to Spain.

The authorities at Inverness have received a reply ta their request for military, in order to enable them to repress the outbreak among the Skye Crofters. It is understood that the Government have refused to allow soldiers to be employed on this duty. The Procurator Fiscal has gone to Barra, where another outbreak has been reported.

-Yesterday, Dennis Grimmand, aged 43, while working at the molten iron pit in the Blochairn Ironworks, Glasgow, fell into the pit amongst the boiling iron, and he had to be rescued by a fellow workman by means of an irbn hook. He was carried, fearfnlly burned, on stretchers, to the Royal Infirmary, and he is not expected to survive. PANIC IN A FACI'ORY: TWENTY-THREE WOMEN

CRUSHED TO DEATH. A Bombay telegram dated Thursday, says :—A terrible catastnophe occurred here to-day. An alarm of tire, which was wholly groundless, was given at a wool-cleaning factory, and the work-people made a rush to the door. Twenty-three women engaged on the premises were crushed to death in the thr.ng of people who were struggling to escape. WITHDRAWAL OF AN ERRONEOUS STATEMENT. In a 'speech delivered at Dumfries last week Colonel Alexander, M.P., stated that Admiral Lord Alcester had asked permission to land a force at Alexandria immediately after the bombardment, and that his request had been re- fused by the Government. The gallant member was yester- day informed by Mr. Campbell-Bannerman, secretary to the Admiralty, that no such request had been preferred, and he has accordingly publicly withdrawn the statement, coupled with an expression of regret for having made it. MAN-OF-WAR'S BOAT CAPSIZED. NARROW ESCAPE OF A COMMANDER. While Her Majesty's ship Dasher was lying in Alderney Harbour during the recent gale, the captain's gig, which was returning to the steamer, was capsized by a sudden squall, and Commander Charles Reade and ten of the crews were percipitated into the sea, which was running very high, spars, arc., were thrown from the Dasher, an ultimately all were saved but one seaman, named Rrice, twenty-four years of age. Several had narrow escapes, one man saving him- self by climbing the floats of the paddles and the captain was rescued by a sailor who plunged from the deck cf the Dasher and caught him by the hair as he was sinking. The party were immersed seven minutes, but it was some hours before all were entirely resucitated.

DISPUTE ABOUT A QUARRY AT RUNCORN.

FARRELL v. GOEST.—This was an action to recover dam- ages for the non-fulfilment of an agreement to deliver certain goods. According to the pleadings the defendants admitted the agreement, but denied the refusal to deliver up the goods. Mr. Addison, Q.C., and Mr. Little were for the plaintiff, and Mr. Gully, Q.C., and Mr. Segar were for the defendants. Mr. Addison stated that plaintiff was Mrs. Elizabeth Far- rell, a widow whose husband died in January, 1881. Up to the time of his death, and for some time before, he had worked a quarry on the west side of Runcorn Hill, which had been let to him by the agent of Lord Cholmondeley under an agreement to pay royalty for the stone that was got. When the husband dicd he left everything to his widow and his only child, a lad of 18 years of age, and she continued to work the quarry as her husband had done. The particular part which she worked was the northern part of the west side of the hill. Some six months before Mr. Farrell died the defendants, Messrs. Guest, who were father and son, began to work the southern part of the west aide of this quarry; and when they found that the widow was going on as before they cOnceived a notion th tt they would make it so unpleasant for her that she would be obliged to go. In 1882, therefore, they began to interfere with her wot kings. They threw rubbish up, and blocked the only way to her workings. They also enclosed a crane so that it could not be got away The pl.intiff began Cr, qllrry on the east side of the hill, and the defendants also interfered with her there. Under these circumstances a dispute arose, and an agreement was ulti- mately come to between the parties with regard to the quarry on the west side of the hill, and that certain matters were to be left to arbitration; but with these they had nothing to do in that case. Subsequently another agree- ment was made that within a fortnight after the Ist Septem- ber the defendants should give up to the plaintiff the stone which she had quarried on the eaet side of the hill, which was worth about £2O, and also all her tools and material, together with a-crane, which, as it were, had been impri- soned. The arrangement was that the defendants should lift the crane from the quarry and place it on the edge of the highway, where the plaintiff could find it and take it away. Under these circumstances, and within a few days of signing that agreement, the plaintiff sent her son to the de'endants to say that she would send next day for the crane. The defendants, however, said that the tools must remain where they were until the plaintiff herself came. In the meantime the plaintiff had taken another quarry, and she required all her tools and implements for the pur- pose of working it. Next day the plaintiff's son went with a cart and a number cif men to remove the tools, but they found that the crane had not been removed to the edge of the highway. The defendants refused to give the articles up unless the plaintiff came for them herself and gave a written receipt for them. The plaintiff then consulted her solicitor, and on the 14th September she went to the defendants' with a written demand to give up the articles. The defendants, however, said that they would give them up if she paid £lO. Later in the 'day the defendants reduced this amount to £5. This action was then brought to recover damages for the detention and the value of the stone which had been quarried.

His Lordship: The question between you is one of damages if there is no refusal now. The plaintiff, Mrs. Elizabeth Farrell, spoke to her having gone to the defendants with a written demand for the goads and their refusal to give them up, first without the pay- ment of £lO, and after wards £5. If she had the possession of her tools she could have taken another quarry and worked it.—ln cross-examination by Mr. Gully, plaintiff said that it was no business of the defendants, under the agreement to put the tools and plant on the highway—it was only the crane and the gearing which was to be put upon the highway. The defendants did not ask her when she saw them to give them notice before they could remove the things, nor did she ask them to collect the whole of the tools and place them upon the highway. The defendant did not say to her that it would take some time to collect the tools, and that he must be paid for it. The plaintiff's son, Arthur George Farrell, George Higgins, and William Wright, labourers, in the plaintiff's employment, spoke to having gone for the articles with a lorry, and that the defendants declined to let them have them.

Mr. Joseph Burton, the plaintiff's solicitor, was also called. He explained the steps which he bad taken to get the defendants to give up the property. Mr. Gully, in opening the case for the defendants, said that this was really a fight about costs, and he could not help regretting on the part of both sides that some arrange- ment had not been made. It would have prevented a waste of time and money in prosecuting that action. The goods were there in the quarry, they had never been used, and the defendants denied that they ever refused to give them up. There was one thing in this case which was quite clear, that if the solicitor for the plaintiff had waited for an answer to the letter which he had written, an end would have been put to this dispute. He wrote a letter to the defendant's solicitor on the Bth September ; but without waiting for a reply he went to the defendants in person. Such a proceeding, of course, precluded all further corres- pondence, and the next communication which the defen- dants had was a notice that a writ would be issued. His (Mr. Gully's) learned friend had opened his case by iniply- ing that the defendants were the persecutors of this widow ; but he had put forward no evidence at all which supported such an imputation, and he gave an entire denial to the statement which bis friend had made. The contention of the defendants was that they declined to give up the articles without some authority from the mother. At first the defendant asked for £lO if he was to undertake the collec- tion of the tools and materials, and to bring them down to the edge of the highway with the crane. He might have been asking for too much ; bit that was not a wrongful detention. She might have said that she would collect the articles herself. Afterwards the defendant reduced his charge ta £5 which the plaintiff agreed to pay, and that the defen- dant understood to be the result of the conversation which took place on the 14th September. The defendants offered to have the crane ready for the plaintiff on the 15th Sep- tember, and she went away under the impression that she would send that morning and pay £5 for collecting the things, and for the interruption of the work in the quarry; but she never sent for them at all.

William Guest, one of the plaintiffs, detailed his inter- views with the plaintiff. In cross-examination, he said that there was nothing in the agreement which required him to move the articles without being paid for it. He did not know that the son acted for his mother.

At the conclusion of the defendant's evidence, Mr. Gully said he thought that the evidence put him out of court. The defendant was evidently charging for remov- ing, goods which he was bound to deliver for nothing. The parties then agreed to a verdict for £lOO, which would be reduced to £1 if the articles were delivered.

WANTED, A PILLAR BOX. Sir,—Tho requirement of a letter box in the vicinity of \ ' Duke's Field has not unfrequently suggested itself to my mind i and if I were asked where would be the most suitable spot 1 to fix one, I should at once say the bottom of Ashriclge- I street, opposite the recently made bridge slope. We read i from time to time of boons being conferred upon the town I in the shape of free libraries, sick accident hospitals, mor- tuaries, Szc., but I think the inhabitants in the locality ' I alluded to, would in all probability, consider a letter box an inestimable boon, especially when the elements are some- what unfavourable, as of late. It is a very unpleasant task, sir, to run snorting in a blinding hail or snowstorm on a dark night to the General Post Office, a distance of not less than three-quarters of a mile, in order to post a letter. There are only three general or public letter boxes in the town— exclusive of the Post-office—namely, Higher Runcorn, Waterloo Bridge, and Canal-street, and when the distance of the two latter from the General Post Office is taken into consideration, I think you will agree with me, sir, that the people in the Duke's Field district are equally as much en- titled to the privileges appertaining to a letter box, as , those living in the neighbourhood of Canal-street or ' Waterloo Bridge.—Yours truly, J. GATES. Runcorn, February 1, 1883.

LEssom p.m TIM YOUNG.—The Mote and the Beam— the illustrations of the proverb are endless. Young people especially ought to remember it. There are no critics of human character half so severe as those whose own char- octer is as yet unformed; none who denounce human im- perfections with such an air of infallibility as those whose inexperience of life disqualifies them for forming any true conception of the infinite varieties of human temperament and the infinite varieties of temptation by which human vytue is tried. To young people life seems extremely simple. As soon as they hear a stranger speak, they know everything about him. A sentence is a complete and final revelation. A single action is sufficient to glorify a man, or to condemn him to perpetual infamy. They seem to think it possible to judge character as corn merchants judge a sack of wheat, by looking at a sample which they can take in their hand, or as tailors judge a piece of cloth, by ex- amining a pattern three Inches square. They will find by- and-by that most men are not of the same quality all through, and that they are not all of a piece. Human character is very complex. In most of use the base and the noble, the selfish and the generous, the courageous and the cowardly, earth and heaven, are strangely mixed. Even when a man's life is over, the whole story told, the com- plete evidence pat in, it is sometimes hard to give a verdict. But young people are prepared to acquit a man or to hang him as soen as he is in the dock.—R. W. Dale in "Good Words" for 17 ebruary.

THE AMERICANS AND ENGLISH PLATE GLASS. Sir,—l wrote you a letter some few weeks since on the American people and plate glass. I have had a letter from that country saying it is true that their in'ention is to beat the world ; that at the present momeat, this great firm, which will, I believe, be called the Alleghany Company, are in a position to sell 50,000 feet a week that is, if they had it. I have given the glass manuticturers a hint through I your valuable paper, that for the future they must look east ' for trade. This great firm or glassworks will be able to beat any glassworks in Europe, even when the Americans allow England to send its glass into that country free of duty. For this reason: their works are situated at a place called Hite, Alleghany county, P.A., near Pittsburg, with the railway running at one side of the works, and the Alleghany river on the other. Not enly this, but it is seated on a bed of 80 acres of coal, into which wells have been bored. From these wells gas springs up over 50 feet high to heat their furnaces and annealing kites. I myself have seen this place, and I know it to be true. No one that has been to America will attempt to deny that in Pittsburg there are mountains of coal almost as large as England it- self. Yes, Mr. Editor, America is the future country for glass making, for, not only coal have they got at this great glassworks that is to be, but splendid limestone as well, for I have seen it and used it at a place 50 miles from Pitts- burg. They say glass making is only in its infancy. This I deny, for England has gone from a perfect state of making glass to an imperfect state. if anyone asks me to prove this, I will ask him to look back 18 years, and compare the glass that was being made at Ravenhead then, and the glass beihg made now, and then say if glass making is only in its infancy. I was told by a German chemist that plate glass was first made in France in the year 1668, at a place called St. Gobins, which was the only place that made it for nearly 100 years. This valuable plate glass was thought BO much of, that an Act was passed prohibiting anyone to make it, only the noblemen of the land. It is not much unlike that in England. This profitable business is only in the hands of the few, and those few are in our midst. Look at the great Pilkington's glassworks 30 years since, or even 20 years since, and look at it to-day. It has a railway running past, and one of their own all over the works, I cannot say there is a river running through the works, but there is what was once a valuable canal. I say with truth that there was better and cheaper glass made 18 years since than there is made to-day, and yet peopli will say that the man who made that glass is out of date. They lie, and the truth is not in them.—l am, &c', JAMES SEDDON. Milk-street, St. Helens, January 29, 1833.

"THE TWO PATHS. "—LIBERALISM—CONSER VATISM. Sir,—A most important feature of our every day life is the political atmosphere by which we are surrounded. It is quite impossible for anyone possessed of the slightest amount Avitality to avoid connecting himself with one of the two great parties, who, in their turn, govern this nation for weal or for woe. Previous to the Reform Act of 1832 a very few families kindly spent of their wealth and devoted their time for the good of the cornmanity. The passing of that important Act made it possible for a still larger section to take part in the all-important business of politics. From 1832, until the passing of the Ballot Act, a most important interval in the nation's history, occurs a period during which more political life was infused in the nation's blood than at any other given period. Nearly all the manufac- turing systems or me Coutiwy umlet went. 4 ,vtuplcto transformation. Instead of the trade of the country being I carried on in the house of the worker, or in the little work- shop behind the house, great manufacturing centres sprang up, men were compelled by the very force of circumstances, over which they had no control, to work together in large communities, and the workshop became the political arena wherein "our masters" prepared themselves for the time when household suffrage would make them a power in the State. It required but the ballot to complete the enfran- chisement of those resident in our cities and towns. Men.do sot, with equanimity, see power slip out of their possession, especially when it adds so largely to their social position; consequently the fifty years, during which Mr. Gladstone's political life forms so prominent a factor, have been years of keen struggle betwixt those who had power and those who felt the need of it. Warrington, previous to its emanci- pation from Tory misrule, may be taken as a fair sample as to what Tory dominance really meant. On market days and other special occasions, to receive a nod of re- oognition was deemed all that was required. To sit at the bead of the table at ordinaries, and move amongst the far- mers at agricultural shows was surely condescension enough horn one who sacrificed the comforts of home for the discom- forts of the best club in London. To pass 20 years in silent meditation in St. Stephen's, interspersed with silent intervals at Walton Hall, as the acme of Tory representation. But all things change. Old ideas give' place to new, and now one of the chief requirements of a member is that he shall have an active political brain; that he shall also be able to make his constituents aware from time to time of the direc- tion in which that brain is working. To bring other men as speakers on the political platform, and merely rise and nod and bow, and say "Them's my sentiments," is not enough. The people's welfare requires that we shall have men at the front full of vitality—not mere money bags and political fossils. Mr. T. Ashcroft, with a frankness that is quite re- freshing, complains of being "sold." If Mr. Ashcroft would only study the constitutional history of his native town, leaving for a time that of the kingdom, he would become aware of a feature that is'inseparable from Toryism—that is, the necessity,from the very nature of things, of the political party in the town that has lost power and knowing it will never return, being compelled to sell their more stupid sup- porters. Toryism never had real honest life in it, and Whig- gory differs little from it. Legislation for their own class was always their object: Mr. Ashcroft says further that they must "strive to make converts," but converts are not to be made by—farces. Converfs can only be made by argu- ment, and I appeal to all Englishmen, and ask Where shall we find Tory argument ? Lord Carnarvon made a rash statement when he said that the Conservatives had the largest portion of the literary intellect of the country on their side. I hope, Mr. Editor, you will kindly give our friends the enemy full liberty in I your paper to advertise their new magazine the National Review, price half-a-crown, which will appear next March ; and we shall see what literary skill will do in converting Liberals into the ranks of those who learn nothing and forget nothing. We need not wait for this intellectual giant. Let anyone take up the current Nineteenth Centypy, and enough may be found to satisfy all who care to inquire as to which of the two paths, Conservatism or Liberalism, it is desirable to follow. Two writers, Henry Cecil Reikes and • W. St. John Brodrick, make an earnest effort, not exactly to make converts, but to prove how useless and disorganised the Cocservatives are, and hew the leaders of the party in St. Stephen's are imitating the leaders at home here, viz., selling their supporters. It seems as if the party bad thrown the proud position of being Her Majesty's Opposi- tion to the winds, and become so demoralised that to be termed a Tory wift shortly be a synonym for a Toady. Lord R. Churchill states that "The business of an Opposi- tion is to oppose." Mr. Raikes, terming this a bald truism, goes on to state that it must keep itself in " good fighting trire, so that it may avoid at once the extremes of ridiculous extravagance and despicable weakness," and while he deplores that "an exuberant verbosity has been dedicated ever since the death of Lord Beaconsfield, to the celebration of his career," he denies his tactical skill, and says that "it was his unfailing audacity that rendered him indis- pensable." So we see two prominent features set up for Tory workingmen to fall down and worship : one is the , destruction of all that is good by Lord Randolph's party and the memory of Lord Beaconsfield's "audacity." There are few men belonging to either party but must earnestly desire that the Opposition in the House shall be of a healthy, vigorous character, and although it may not be altogether necessary for them to have a declared policy, it is clearly to be desired that they shall not be mere obetructionists. Mr. Broderick states that "Wanted, a policy!" is a terrible drawback to Conservatives at the present time. lam not so sure of this. Had the Tories a policy, they would cease to be Tories. The very few instances in the past in which they have carried measures are in no sense reassuring. The Agricultural Holdings' Act was a failure because it was a dishonest measure. The Public Worship Regulation Act is a failure, because it is doing nothing but breed law suits. When Mr. Broderick goes on to sketch a policy, then we see how little the people are cared for. Such mottoes as specify the work of the future are not to be found. Free land and cheap food, electoral reform, justice to Ireland, and comity franchise and redistribution of seats are not even thought of. I dare say your readers remember the timid inquiry put to the Conservative leaders respecting workingmen candidates for Parliamentary honours. They will also remember how indefinite the answer was. Had Liberals cared to go about their business in this fashion, we should never have had the intellectual treat recently enjoyed in the Public Hall by all those who had the pleasure of listening to Mr. Broadhurst.

With the singing of this song and "Auld Lang Syne the audience whiled away three - quarters ot an hour, as the proceedings did not com- mence until 7-45-15 minutes after the ad- vertised time. When the meeting did commence it soon became manifest that the assembly was not entirely com- posed of Conservatives, but the numerous dissentients were very orderly, and although there were several cries of "put him out," no notice was taken of them, and the "great Conservative meeting" quietly terminated. Sir Gilbert Greenall presided, and there were also on the platform Sir Robert Peel, Bart., Mr. Wm. Beamont, Mr. Robert Davies, Mr. Peter stubs, Colonel Bell, Colonel Greenall, Mr. John Fairclough, Mr. Robert Pierpoint, Dr. Brabazon, Mr. John White, Alderman Webster, Alderman Harrison, Alderman Kean, Councillors Bolton, Burgess, J. Pierpoint, Taylor, Whittle, Woolfall, and Wright; Rev. Canon Guest, -Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Rev. J. Ward, Rev. S. Wilkinson, Captain Litton, Captain Reynolds, Captain Nicholson, Captain Bolton, Captain J. C. Ridgway, Messrs. W. H. Brook. J. R. Buckton, W. Carson, Vera Davies, Richard Fairclough, William Fairhurst, D. W. Finney, H. J. Gaskell, John I Harding, John Hatton, Robert Heaton, John Hall, H. N. Houghton, W. D. Jeans, R. J. Wynne Jones, G. T. Moore, N. B. Percival, George Powlson, L. W. Reynolds, R. W. Rowson, William Sharp, William Silcock, jun., C. Spinks, James Smethurst, W. D. Thurnam' James Tinsley, Josiah Whittle, Arthur Whittle, John Hampson (Conservative agent), and others. The CHAIRMAN said they had now a grand and glorious spectacle. They were met together as Conserva- tives. (Hear, hear.) They were met together as Liberal Conservatives. (Hear, hear.) They were Conservatives who desired and wished to stand by and to maintain the valuable and fundamental principles of the ancient consti- tution. (Cheers.) When he said that, he meant to say they were resolute Conservatives. But they were not bigots. They did not resist and should not resist changes—changes brought about by change of thought, change of opinions; but they would stand by the ancient lines of our constitu- tion. (Cheers.) He said they had before them a noble and a most grand meeting—(hear, hear)—but they all knew that there was never a day of entire sunshine. They had on the present occasion, he was sorry to say, their disap- pointments. Uhey bad not with them—but he intended to be with them—their respected friend Colonel Blackburn—(cheers)—a man of whom they did not think more highly than he deserved to be thought of. They all regretted the unavoidable absence of Colonel Black- burne, and he regretted very much indeed also the absence of a near and dear relative of his own. He was sorry his nephew, Edward Whitley, of Liverpool—(cheers)—was also unavoidably absent ' • but he knew that he might say, , both in the name of his friend, Colonel Blackburne, and in ' the name of his relative, Edward Whitley, that they were good for another day. (Cheers.) Both of them, when they wanted them, would be present. He was sorry to say also I that they had unavoidably absent that night a gentleman I whom Sir Robert Peel knew, Mr. Knowles, of Wigan. (Cheers.) They had also another gentleman unavoidably I absent, Mr. Pickmere, the late Mayor of War- rington. Now, it was not his intention to speak at length at the present moment, but if, at the termination of the meeting, there was either time or opportunity for him to speak, he should be very glad indeed to have the privilege of speaking to them. (Applause.) But he would say what they all felt. He believed they rnrfertly wearied of the present Administration. (Applause.) He believed that the present Administration had only been successful in one way. They had been very successful in promising a great deal, and had fulfilled none of those promises. (Laughter and applause.) The Govern- ment promised them peace. One would have thought when Mr. Bright left the Administration upon that principle, that we should have had a settlement of all debateable warlike subjects. They also promised that we should have economy. Their economy had been shown in a very increased expenditure, and they had blessed them with an additional income tax. (Applause.) He concluded by reading Colonel Blackburne's letter, which was written that morning, and addressed to Captain Reynolds. Colonel Blackburne stated that his night's expedition to Leigh on Tuesday had increased his cold, and general feeling of un- comfortableness, that he dare not carry out his engagement at Warrington that afternoon and evening. Would he kindly inform Sir G. Greenall how much he felt the neces- sity of arriving at that conclusion. He hoped Captain Reynolds would assure his constituents and friends he much regretted being absent from the gathering calculated to prove so useful to the leaders of the Conservative party. Mr. R. DAVIES said they must be labouring at that moment under feelings of disappointment that whereas they expected to see their friend and neighbour, Colonel Blackburne, they only saw the familiar face of one of their own townsmen. They had that night a very varied programme, and he thought he should not anticipate the remarks which they would hear from those who had to follow him; but he should confine himself to a few comments upon what took place in that hall at the Liberal meeting last week. (Applause and voices: "Give it 'em hot," and "Dress 'ern down.") He called it a Liberal meeting, but that word was scarcely uttered throughout the evening. Every one present seemed to glory in the name of Radical. (Applause.) Some of them went so far as to invite the appellation of Socialists—(applause) —and any me who would read through the speeches and take away the thin veil which hid them, would see at a glance that the doctrines of Socialism were those doctrines which were advocated from that platform in the presence of three members of Parliament last week. (Applause.) But he confessed to a very great feeling of disappointment. He wished this country to be well governed whether it was governed by a Conservative or a Liberal Executive. (Hear, hear.) It was their object to get a good Government. They preferred good statesmanship to political feeling, and he wished there was more of it. (Hear, hear.) Bet as it was, what did they find? Theylfound Sir William Harcourt in 1878 declaring that the motto to which Sir Gilbert had already alluded—of the Liberal party was " peace, retrench- ment, and reform." (Applause.) He looked in these speeches for some indications of peace. He found that in Ireland, in spite of the boast which was made u, on that plat- form, after a period of inaction which became one of anarchy and utter lawlessness—he found Ireland at this moment, instead of being in a state of peace, suffering under one of the most stern and arbitrary Acts which it was possible to put in force in any country governed as we were, by a Parliament. (Hear, hear.) He did not complain. What- ever measures were necessary for the peace of the Kingdom, those they were all bound to support; but these extreme measures had been rendered necessary by their inaction—(applause)—and their powerlessness to begin with, until the people actually thought that no law could ever touch or reach them. Then they found in the speeches of their political opponents the war in Egypt was very lightly passed over. He did not think that ever Lord Beaconsfield, assuming him to have been as rash as he was said to have been, would ever have brought this nation into that war. (Hear, hear.) So much for peace. Then he looked to see if he could find anything of retrenchment. He saw the national expenditure had risen he thought—if his figures were correct—from £80,000,000 to 84,000,000, and would go on increasing; and he found, first of all, that Mr. McMinnies, the honourable member for Warrington— (laughter and voices: "He's not member," and "Dress him down")—admitted the fact, but he said he could not help it. (Laughter.) What did the Liberals send him to Parliament for if he could do nothing? He had done nothing —(hear, hear,)— and he said nothing. (Applause.) He had no doubt that the audience then expected to hear from the lips of Mr. Broad- hurst, the labour representative, some comfort. What did Mr. Broadhurst say? He said "the expenditure is large, but return a majority of us to Parliament and it will he larger." (Laughter.) They might suppose he was mis- quoting him, but anyone who would take the trouble to read the speech would say that he was not. Mr. Broadhurst said there were many things which were required which would cost money, and he could hold out no hope of a re- duction in the national expenditure. So much for retrench- ment. He was not going into the wide question of reform, but he said the greatest monopoly of the present time—the Corporation of London—was absolutely force from the attacks of Mr. Gladstone, that those who called so loudly for reform when they were out of power. They came next to the doctrines that were advocated in that hall, and they were—as those present might suppose—disband the army and navy, and we should have no wars and less expenditure. Did any sane man, looking at our position in Europe, and looking at the stite of Europe, when he came to sit down calmly and consider, approve of that sentiment? The next was we must have legislation about the land. That was the text of the whole of their speeches. He wanted to know what the land was? The land was part of the material wealth of this country. It might have got into hands in too large quantities,
