the most extraordinary siagech that ever: was delivered in that hall, and almost any other. He did not like to be per- sonal, and he should not say who it was any further than that it was a gentleman of the name of Jones—(loud laughter)—who hailed from Wales. (Laughter.) That gentleman had a peculiar idiosyncracy. A cathedral town made him poorly. When he got to St. Asaph the sight of lords and bishops upon the platform quite upset him. He did not think so much of Wales as he did of England, but he frequently took air upon his native mountains. He thought Mr. Jones was like Commodore Rogers. He was a man exceedingly brave, and climbed up exceedingly high rocks —rocks that were quite perpendicular. (Laughter.) This Mr. Jones, amongst his other discoveries, had found out what Would cure bilieusness—(laughter)—a very bad attack of biliousness. He supposed he must have been at Chester and dropped across the bishop, or the dean, or the precentor, or the beadle, or perhaps had seen the tower of the cathe- dral, for as he was going home he had a bad billious attack; but as he was passing the gates of Hawarden Castle his wife said to him, " Here comes the grand old man.' " (Laugh- ter and cheers.) He must not garble this. He must not be charged with telling it as Mr. Jones did not. "I had been," he said, "in Montgomery, and I had a terrible bilious attack'. My good wife said to me, 'Here is Mr. Gladstone.' 'Where is he ?' and in a moment my bilious attack was gone, and I have never felt one bit of it from that day to this." (Laughter.) When he read this, he thought what would become of Mr. Cockle and his antibilious pills. (Laughter.) Well, Mr. Jones was the gentleman who said that the clergy were to Toryism what liquid was to water, and he went on to say that he should not give them a quotation in Welsh, because he was afraid they might suspect he was a classical scholar. (Laughter.) He (Mr. Davies) was very much surprised at this; but when he turned to another part of his speech he found that he was half an Irishman and half a Welsh- man, and he did not think anything more about it. (Laughter.) He saw that Mr. McMinnies went a great length to thank him for coming from Rhyl to make that speech. He did not think he need. It seemed to him, speaking politically, Mr. Jones was ready to go anywhere and to say anything. If he were in Ireland,, he would put himself by the side of Mr. Parnell ; and if he could only get Lord Randolph Churchill on the top of Plin- limmon they might imagine what would follow. (Laugh- tei.) That was the mixture of doctrines that went down last week in that hall. He was very much amused—so much so indeed, that when he went to bed on Saturday night —he didn't often dream—but he had a very disagreeable nightmare. (Laughter.) He thought that he was some- where near the Hill Warren, and at the very top of the beacon—the ordnance mark—he saw the Rev. E. Lloyd- Jones, of Wales, making a speech in Welsh, with Mr. Par- nell as chairman, and on every fifteen acres, which was the quantity of land that INlr.Broadhurst gave to each of them when the new division took place, stood the owner. The hon. member for Warrington stood in the middle of his. The hon. member for Burnley in the middle of his, the hon. member for Stoke was in the middle of his, and there were a number of other local celebrities whom he could not re:ognise, for he awoke, and, behold, it was a dream ! (Laughter and applause.) He concluded by moving the ' following resolution :—" That this meeting is of opinion I that the Government has forfeited all clhims to the confi- dence of the country by its mismanagement of Irish and foreign affairs, by its neglect of pressing domestic legisla- tion, and by the extravagance of its expenditure, which far exceeds that of any previous Government in this country." (Applause.) Mr. P. Sruns briefly seconded, and Sir ROBERT PEEL supported the resolution. He said he was glad to see that the operative classes largely predomina- ted in the meeting, ana no was graa mere pa,lo.raely to address his remarks to them, not from purely party, but from a national point of view. Like his honourable friend the member for Newcastle, Mr. Cowen—(applause)—on occasions of great emergency he preferred national interests to the consideration of mere party expedients. It had always been the policy of the Conservative party in this county to give a general and generous support to any Government which might support to some extent the principles which they advocated, and the last advice the late Lord Beacons- field gave to his party was that no premature attempt should be made to embarrass the Government. (Hear, hear.) He believed that their Radical opponents in Warrington had been recently very active and energetic, and they must be active and energetic too. (Hear, hear.) They had plenty of materials to work upon, and the better cause of the two. Conservative and Constitutional principles had solely and only in view the real interests of all classes of the commu- nity, whilst their Radical opponents were always stiff in their opinions, and most intolerant in the application of new-fangled experiments and of rash innovations. All over the country the popular forces were being marshalled. Why should they not enlist them upon their side, recruit them to their party ? If they stood aloof and were indif- ferent, their opponents would gain the monopoly of political power, from which it would be very difficult to displace them. Never in his recollection was the opportunity more favourable. Never was the situation more grave: never was the occasion more inviting to criticism. The Prime Minister had emigrated—(laughter)—not abdi- cated—(renewe(l laughter)—that, indeed, would be a great misfortune to the Coalition Government, for they would fall to pieces directly if they had not Mr. Gladstone's guiding influence. If the Premier were indisposed, they would all feel sympathy for him; but the morning papers told them he was in excellent health, and the only bulletins received were bulletins of fetes and picnics and big dinners. (Laugh- ter and applause.) 'Uhe Prime Minister of this great country had literally emigrated at this moment. He began to think that Dr. Andrew Clark was a bit of a tactician as well as a practitioner, and he had no necessity to call in the cele- brated Dr. Gull. (Laughter.) Dr. Clark saw there were breakers ahead in Midlothian, and knew that the Prime Minister would be a good deal "heckled" when he went there. (Laughter.) He knew there were a great many Radical promises that had never been kept—(hear, hear) —and that the orthodox Presbyterians of 'Midlothian might be very anxious to know something about the Vatican treaty of which they had heard lately. Therefore, Dr. Clarke apparently forbade the Premier from going to Mid- lothian where they certainly would have had a second bombardment of Alexandria. (Laughter.) However, speak- ing seriously,here was the Prime Minister deserting the helm of the vessel of State at the very moment when Parliament was going to meet, when Cabinet Councils ought to be held, and when he ought to be superintending the machinery for the coining session. Mr. Gladstone had relinquished the post of Chancellor of the Exchequer at a time when the finances of this country, owing to extravagant mismanagement, were in a very unsettled state. At no period within the last 50 years had it been more important for the Prime Minister to be directing the councils of the State. But the Government was carried on upon the co-operative principle—that was to say, all the profits went to the shareholders, and the public had to pay cash for the in- estimable blessing of trading under those auspices. The co-operative principle of the present Government was its concessions and coercions. The moderate Liberals coalesced with the extreme Radicals in order to turn out the Bea- consfield Administration; but what a pitiful state of things they had had since! They had two or three interests now at the helm of the Government—the Whigs clinging to office and the Radicals wanting to get rid of them, which they probably would do before long. Whilst these two parties—the moderate Liberals and the extreme Radicals —were clinging together, they had threwn over altogether the famous battle-cry, "Peace, Retrenchment, and Re- form," and there was hardly a shred of it left. (Ap- plause.) Where was the peace since this vacillating Government had blundered into war in Egypt? (Hear, hear.) He called that no peace—it was a peace with dishonour—where a humiliating peace was made, as in the case of South Africa and Afghanistan. (Hear, hear.) As to retrenchment, the expenditure of the country was heavier than it had ever been before. Comparing the expenditure of the first three years of the Beaconsfield Administration with that of the present Government he found that for the year ending March, 1875, it amounted to 74 millions; 1876, 761, millions; and 1877, 78 millions; whereas for the year ending March, 1881, the ex- penditure reached 83 millions; 1882, 8572 millions; and for the year which would end in March next it would not be less than 87 millions. The expenditure was therefore over ten millions more in 1883 than in 1877. (A voice: "What did you do with our six millions surplus ?" and cries of "Put him out "and "Ask Peter Rylands.") The Govern- ment had promised to deal in the coming session with three great measures of reform—county government, the Corpora- tion of London, and parliamentary reform. He would ad- mit that it appeared to him to be the mission of the present Parliament to deal with an extension of the franchise, and he did not think that question could be postponed. (Faint applause.) With regard to parliamentary reform, he recom- mended his Conservative friends to be prepared and not indisposed to deal liberally with a measure of that kind, be- cause he thought the time had come when it would have to be dealt with; but at the same time it was absolutely neces- sary that the question of a redistribution of political power should be very carefully considered by the House of Corn-

promote the freedom and extension of trade, and he defied any one to discover a single instance in which he gave a vote that was not in the direction of free trade and for the interests of the labouring classes. (Applause.) The meeting then terminated, Mr. W. Johnson, who presided at the organ, playing the National Anthem.

France, and they had adopted violent measures in Ireland, where they had interference with freedom of contract and toleration with attacks on life and property. He took a hopeful view of Conservative political prospects at this moment. He thought the country was with them; at all events, they had a golden opportunity now, which should not be lest. (Applause.) Lord Hartington had asked at Bacup whether the Conservative party intended to oppose a blind and desperate resistance to advance and progress of -all kinds, or to build up a future upon the fothadations of Tory democracy and imperialism. He would reply that they had never opposed resistance to advance and progress of all kinds—(applause)—and they did not accept the term "Tory democracy" or "Democratic Toryism." The Conservative party had undoubtedly at heart the honour and glory of the empire and her true imperial interests, vast and enormous as they were, and they did not mean to deny that Imperialism in that term was not one to their advantage. (Applause.) The function of the Opposition at the present moment was to adopt an atti- tude of persevering activity. Democratic Toryism was a transparent sham. It could leave no hold on the country and could not promote the Conservative and Constitutional principles which they advocated. The Liverpool election showed that 26,000 electors remained unpolled because they declined to accept the principles of Democratic Tory- ism which were put forward. But what was the result of the elections that had taken place since 1880? During the past year there had been 25 elections, and the balance of parties remained unchanged; but since the general election the Conservatives had gained 14 seats, which counted 28 upon , a division. (Applause.) He agreed with every word in the , resolution, condemning, as it did, the Government's extrava- gant expenditure, their mismanagement of affairs at home, and their vacillating and uncertain policy abroad. (Loud lapplause.) The resolution was carried. Captain REYNOLDS moved the next resolution, "that the lbest thanks of the meeting be given to Sir Robert Peel for 1 so readily acceding to the request of the Conservative As- sociation to visit Warrington, and for the excellent address he has delivered." (Applause.) He said Sir Robert Peel when he arose said he was a stranger in that room, but the name of Peel had lived in the hearts of the Lancashire people now for a great number of years. (Applause.) When Sir Robert Peel spoke of his father, the name was , like magic, and every man in the room, whatever his prin- ciples were, felt that the name was an honour to the coun- try. To-morrow Warrington would know the present g.intle- man through every house in the town, and he hoped it was nut far distant when they would see the honourable gentle- man again where he ought to be, that was, in the House of ICommons. (applause.) He thought it was a liberty—per- haps Sir Robert did not think so—to write to Sir Robert to ask him to come to Warrington to address them that even- ing. (A voice: "Could get nobody else.") f that room had been three times as large they would have filled it. Sir Robert, with great readiness, replied, "If I can do you any good in Warrington I shall be very happy to come." (Applause.) And he had come down to do what he (Captain Reynolds) asked them to do as chairman of the Association, that was, to use patience. Now that they were not represented in Warring- ton—that was, their party was not represented—it was by patience, faith, and organization that they were determined to wrest this borough out of the bands of their opponents. (Applause.) Lie believed at the present moment there was an undercurrent of feeling against the present Administra- tion, and asked them all, whether as Toriesor Radicals,what, as workingmen, had the present Government done for them? Had they had one single thing cheapened by the present Government? Then they as men knew where the shoe pinched, and they would say, "I will have this shoe kicked off." (Applause ) There was a feeling gradually stealing over them and the next time they went io tine ballut thcy I-foul:I ltiantv haw to vote. The resolu- tion was one that they felt, and they would spring on their legs when it was put before them—to thank this gentle- man for coining down to address them that night. (Applause.) Mr. ROBERT PIERPOINT seconded the motion. He said they would be astonished if Sir Robert Peel did not prove to be a gentleman of great political ability and good oratory. If he did not do so he would not be the worthy son of a great sire. (Applause.) He was sure they were all exceed- ingly obliged to Sir Robert for coming down to give them that address to which they had listened with much interest. He ventured to state that no speech delivered at the meet- ing held there thu other night could compare with the speech to which they had just listened. (Applause.) There was one speech—and that he would say was of considerable ability, although it contained no principle with which he agreed—which seemed to him to be far above the rest, that was the speech by Mr. Broadhurst. As to the other speeches, one came down upon the audience in that room perhaps like the floods which were visiting us now—like the long pent•up rain of years gone by. (Laughter.) They had seen the honourable member for Warrington returned to Parliament like most Liberal members were returned, full of promises ; and those promises had been like many Liberal promises, not yet performed. Pass- ing to the conduct of the Government, he said it came into power on the platform of peace, and had gained its popularity by war. As to Ireland, that country had not improved since the Liberal Government came into office, but it had improved in the last few months. It had not im- proved because of the quack remedies which were put for- ward by the Government. (A voice: "Old Marwood has done it.") He believed order was preserved in Ireland by perhaps one of the most able lieutenants that had ever been in Dublin—(hear, hear,)—but behind the Lord Lieutenant of Dublin came the shadow of Marwood the executioner. (Applause.) Any man could govern a country by what was next to military law. They had got in Ireland the severest Coercion Act that had ever been passed for Ireland in the present century. Govern it! Of course they could Iby means like that. Do not tell him it was ' the Arreas Act or the Land Act that was ' bringing peace; it was the police and Marwood. (Ap- , plase.) div.head: DARING BURGLARY AT NEWTON.
div.p: DARING BURGLARY AT NEWTON.

Sometime between Sunday night and Monday morning last a most daring and successful burglary was committed at the extensive printing and stationery establishment of Messrs. George McCorquodale and Co., Newton-le-Willows. On Monday morning it was discovered that during the night time an entrance into the building had been effected, that the drawers and offices had been completely ransacked, and also that a sum of money had been abstracted. An examination of the premises showed that the burglar or burglars had gained an entrance through one of the windows of the manager's office, ito the right of the front door. Strange to say, how- ever, a safe in the office bore no appearance of having been tampered with, but the office door, which had been locked from the outside, was burst open by an iron " jemmy," which the depredators afterwards left behind them in their flight from the building. The cashier's office appears to have next claimed attention, and several drawers therein were prized open, the marks corresponding to the iron " jemmy " already mentioned. In the drawers were a variety of documents, but these were left behind apparently being considered of no value to those in search of booty. A couple of valuable knives belonging to the cashier (Mr. Davidson), and a sum of money—about £2 it is believed—were, how- ever, taken away. The thieves next visited the general office, and after bursting open the desk of Mr. A. C. McCor- quodale, J.P., ransacked the papers therein, but found no cash. The desk of Mr. Jeseph Woods also suffered the same fate, but strange to say a parcel containing 15s of copper which the thieves must have missed was left untouched. The desk of the postage clerk was also prized open, and a large sum of money—about £4—was abstracted. A lame parcel of postage stamps and a bundle of post cards were left behind, thus giving the impression that money was the only object of the thieves' visit. On the discovery of the robbery the police were communicated with, and an inspection of the premises resulted in the dis- covery of the iron " jemmy," and footprints were also \ I observed about one portion of the grounds. Since then P.E. ' Commins has been energetically prosecuting inquiries into : the burglary, but as yet no apprehension has been made.
ELOPEMENT FROM ST. HELENS.

A somewhat painful, and, as far at least as the two chief actors are concerned, a very foolish elopement took place at St. Helens, about a week ago. The errant damsel, or rather matron, is a person of about thirty-five summers, the wife of the landlord of a small public-house situate not far from St. Thomas's Church, and it is said she still retains some of the personal charms of youth, as she undoubtedly does no little of its folly. Her accompanying swain is a young knight of the razor, about fifteen years her junior, who was a frequent visitor at the house, and seems to have used his opportunities so skilfully as to have very effectually drawn her allegiance away from her lawful lord. It is said that one-half of the world is ignorant of what the other half is doing, and it cer- tainly seems that the husband in the present case had been very imperfectly acquainted with the predelictions and doings of his wife. On more than one occasion, it is said, she and the young barber have been seen together at the St. Helens theatre, yet not the least suspicion had been aroused in the mind of the confiding husband. On the day in question, however, matters were brought to a climax. The husband, in the pursuit of his work as a painter, went to Prescot in the morning, but before going out he noticed his wife to be somewhat perturbed at something. In answer to his affectionate queries as to whether anything was the matter with her, and his offer to stay at home if such was the case, she kissed him with more than usual ar- dour, but said it was not necessary for him to stay at home. During the morning the young gallant was noticed at the house, and probably all the necessary preliminaries were then arranged, for in the afternoon a cab came to the door on which a trunk was placed by Mrs. , assisted by the cabman. She then, doubtless feeling some relentings at the heartless act she was about to commit, kissed her children, telling them that she might not see them again, and giving them some coppers, after which she got into the cab and was whirled away to the station where she was met by her youthful lover. The 'husband, on getting back home in the evening, of course missed his help-meet, and ascertained by further inquiry that she had gone to Liverpool in the company named. Next morning he went there, and succeeded in finding out where the silly couple had stayed together during the night, but unfortunately or fortunately, as the case may be, they had flown before he got there. He then very wisely gave up the search and returned home, to ruminate over the inherent fickleness of the daughters of Eve.

ANNUAL MEETING OF MEMBERS. The annual meeting of the members of the Earlestown and District Liberal Club, for the election of officers for the ensuing season, the passing of accounts, Sze., was held in the news-room of the club on Tuesday evening. There was a very large attendance of the members, including Charles Pilkington, Esq., J.P., and Messrs. P. M. Campbell, W. H. Dagnall, G. F. Aveline, P. Hall, John Ball, and Thomas Howard (secretary). Mr. Pilkington, J.P., was unanimously elected to preside.

THE STATEMENT OF ACCOUNTS. Mr. HOWARD (secretary) read the annual statement of accounts, which showed that the income for the year had been £l2O 12s. 71d., and the expenditure £129 195., leaving a balance of £3 Gs. 41-d. due to the secretary. In addition however, a number of bills were left unpaid. Amongst the receipts were: Billiards, £69 lOs 4d; subscriptions and en- trance fees, £lB lOs 6d ; honorary subscriptions and dona- tions, £2O 18s 6,1; sale of newspapers, £2 13s 3.1. d. The expenditure included the following items : Caretaker's salary, £29 3s 4cl; gas, water, and poor rates, £l3 19s 4d; newspapers, £ll us sd; interest paid to shareholders, £5 15s. The accounts had been audited and found correct by Messrs. Thomas Lambert and James Duxbury.—The CHAIRMAN did not think the statement a very bad one considering all the circumstances. Many, and in fact most, of the clubs during the first two or three years of their establishment had to struggle for an existence. So far he thought they had struggled very well. (Hear, hear.) With the exception of one or two small honorary subscriptions all the money had been raised by the members themselves, and he thought that was en- couraging.—Mr. JonN BALL moved that the accounts be passed as read. He thought the decrease in the receipts from the billiard-table would almost explain away the little loss on the year's working. Then with regard to the accounts there was one thing he would like to point oat, and that was they still had the value of their money. The changes that had taken place in connection with the-billiard- markers would also account for the deficiency.—Mr. P. HALL seconded the motion, observing that every member of the club ought to go in for turning the balance to the other side of the account.—The CHAIRMAN asked the auditors for their report. Mr. DUXBURY said he and Mr. Lambert had carefully gone through all the books and documents in the possession of the secretary, and so far as they were aware the statement before the meeting was quite correct.—After some further discussion the accounts were passed as read.

div.p: RUNCORN YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN i ASSOCIATION, ANNUAL MEETING. T.lit lanual meeting of the members 44. Raman Youttt 'Wes Vhristian Association, was held at the Cocoaelbrims, on gonday evening. Tea was provided by Mr. Moore. Dr. Vteele, president of the Association, presided over the pro- ceedings and amongst those present were :—The Rev. Canon Barclay, M.A., Messrs. John Simpson, S. C. Beckett, W. Shaw, S. Coventry, J. D. Jones, W. Johnson, F. J. Norman, &c. After prayer, Mr. C. Nickson, the hon. sec., read the fol- lowing report :—" It is exceedingly gratifying to be able to report that the past year, from a financial point of view, has been a very successful one. The embarrassments by which the Association from its commencement has been crippled, never pressed more closely than at the end of 1881; and the committee having received intimation that no further special help might be expected from our late president, whose valued connection with the Association, and his generous support will long entitle him to our respect and admiration, it was evident that there must be a speedy collapse. Christ- mas saw us with a debt of £49 6s. 7d., and the outlook was so gloomy and cheerless that the committee abandoned all hope of being able to carry on the work of the Association successfully, and passed a resolution to close the rooms. Each member of the committee pledged himself to stand by the tottering and enfeebled institution until every liability was honestly discharged, and every preparation was made for a respectful, but sorrowful inter- ment. It is possible the committee never had to perform a more bitter task, but the affairs seemed to imperatively demand that it should be per"orrued. It is only fair to state that this resolution was not unanimous, and when submitted to the judgment of the general meeting its expediency was questioned, and what is always better than apathy in times of difficulty, the members generally awoke to the peril in which the Association was placed. After six years of in- cessant toil, the impending dissolution was regarded as a great public misfortune, and ev n at the eleventh hour it was determined that one more struggle should be made. It was pointed out that if a strenuous effort were made to in- crease the income, and some step taken by which the ex- penditure could be reduced, the work of the Association might still be carried on. To carve out a new path may be perfectly easy it the hands of the workers are unfettered, but how te accomplish the object of clearing off the debt which burdened the shoulders of the committee was a matter which could not so soon be settled. A feW, weeks passed over, during which period several meetings were held, and ulti- mately we resolved to leave the commodious premises at Camden buildings, occupy the rooms which were offered at I a fair rental by the Coffee and Cocoa House Company, and renew our appeals to the public. Owing to the publicity given to the critical state of the Association, public interest was awakened in our favour, and while members were devising means to con- tinue the work, a generous public was breathing on the dry bones and they quickened into life. In the endeavour to pay off the old year's deficit and provide for the working expenses of another year the smile of Providence rested on the work, and the year's success attests to the earnest effort and the liberality of the public. It was with no little re- gret that the committee acquiesced in the decision of Mr. Robert Shaw to resign the post of president, which he had held since the formation of the Association. The commit- tee feel bound to place on record the since; a esteem in sihich he is regarded by them, ard to express their indebted- ness to him for the valuable assistance which he has con- stantly rendered. In seeking for a gentleman to follow Mr. Shaw it is fortunate we were able to obtain the consent of Dr. Steele, of Heath House, to become the president of the Association, and, in terdering him their thanks for the labours he has never shrunk from performing in the welfare of the Association, they desire to express their confidence in him and the respect they feel towards him as the head of the institution to which they believe he is fondly attached. Allusion has already been made to the occupation of the present rooms. The Coffee and Cocoa House Company met the committee kindly and fairly, and the members as- sembled in the new premises for the inaugural meeting on the 27th February. Owing to the kindness of several gentlemen the committee were en- abled to provide a gratuitous tea for about 80 members. The vicar, who has ever evinced the liveliest sympathy in the work of the association, presided and delivered the opening speech, and from the success of the proceedings the committee pictured a period of prosperity, I and a departure from the sluggish waters in which they had been helplessly drifting for so long. The roseate picture which fancy then drew has been realised by facts. Instead of the usual soiree a successful concert was held on the 30th March, which yielded the handsome profit of .£7 18s 6d. The committee desire to thank all those who assisted in this undertaking During May the committee endeavoured to secure a piece of land for the purposes of a gymnasium, but they were unsuccessful. They feel that if a pece of ground could be got, and a certain proportion of the funds devoted to the formation of a gymnasium to which the public would be admitted on payment of a nomi- nal subscription, they would be meeting a long-felt want, and materially strengthening other departments of the asso- ciation. In August the committee also considered_a sugges- tion to establish a centre of the St. John's Ambulance Association in Runcorn, but at that time could not on several grounds carry out the idea and they take this opportunity of thanking at least one medical man who offered his aid.'" The report then referred to the annual fruit banquet, by which £5 83 ld was added to the funds of the Association; and to the annual pic-nic to Weaverham Wood, the committee expressing their thanks to Captain Clark, of Weston Point, and to Mr. and Mrs. Sanderson, of Weaverham, for their kind aid. The report continued :—" Many members will no doubt share in the regret of the committee that they had not been able to devote much attention to evangelistic work. The meeting will have gathered by this time that thii is owing to the weakness of the funds, and not from any lack of spiritual zeal. Every effort in which we have been engaged has been controlled by pecuniary considerations, and the committee think you will agree it was better trt get out of debt than to deal in uncertainties, and possibly increase the liabilities. A committee, consisting of Mr. J. H. Humphreys, Mr. W. Shaw, Mr. George Howard, Mr. W. H. Rogerson, and the Rev. Ryan Williams, is formed for the purpose of arranging to resume evangelistic labour as far as the funds of the Association will permit, and now the debt is paid off we hope this committee will shortly be at wcrk. The reading- I room has been well supplied with newspapers, magazines, I and a class of wholesome literature, and members have I made profitable use of the rooms. Our thanks are due to Mr. John Simpson, the editors of the Runcorn Guardian and Examiner, Christian Commonwealth, snd Christian Age, for their gifts of books and papers; to Mr. J. A. Smith for a contribution box, and to Mr. George Yarwood for the decoration of the room. The library comprises more than 500 volumes. At the beginning of the year. the ittee decided that members should be entitled to. die the library without charge. Up to the time of th fah- ment of the Free Public Library, many p,rsons availed themselves of the advantages of the Association Library, but since July the books have been comparatively little used, and early in December, Mr. Langshaw, our esteemed librarian, having resigned his post, the committee dec'-''d for a time to close the library. No doubt this me-ong will be able to make such arrangements that the oenefits of the most valuable adjunct of the Association eery not be entirely wonderful increase of 2 lost. The past year has witne„„, members. At the close 1881, the number on the roll (honorary and ordinanr) stood at 64. Ry the end of March it rose to 165. owing to removals, withdrawals, and deaths, it at 135, which marks an increase over 1881 of now ste-ds 71. :or the formation of a Literary Improvement Class, a ~ommittee consisting cf Messrs. E. Rhodes, F. J. Norman, J. A. Smith, and W. H. Rogerson, has been formed. A com- mittee consisting of Mr. W. Shaw, Mr. J. D. Jones, and Mr. F. J. Norman, has been appointed to form a Rambling Club; and to carry on temperance work, a committee, consisting of the following, has been entrusted with the arrangements:— Messrs. S. Coventry, W. Shaw, W. H. Rogerson, and J. H. Humphreys. The committee hopefully look forward to the co-operation of the members in the several branches of useful work." After referring to the successful treat to aged folks, and the treat to children, the report concluded:—" To sum up, the committee have paid off the debt of nearly £5O and provided £7l for the expenses of the Association. With the sum collected for the aged people's treat, the total income of the Association has been upwards of £l6O. In 1881 our receipts from all sources were £4B, a total increase of £ll2. In closing, the committee earnestly trust that the public will continue their support. The institution is the only one possessing the combined ad- vantages of a reading room and library in a town of 15,000 inhabitants, and the committee feel it is shedding a beae- ficial influence abroad. With the same support and sympathy the committee hope to extend the usefulness of the Asso- ciation and to leave imperishable lustre on the annals of the town."

Mr. S. C. BECKETT (hon. treasurer) read the financial statement which showed that the income for the year was £l2l 14s. id., which amount included £4l 6s. subscriptions from honorary members, and £37 33. 11d, from active mem- bers, and £9 7s. donations. The expenditure amounted to £l2l 143. id., less £4 16s. in the hands of the treasurer. Mr. Beckett remarked that he bad never before had the pleasure of presenting such a favourable statement. The debt of £49 6s. 3d., in which the association commenced the year's work bad been paid off, and there was a balance of £4 16s. (Applause.) he ebe aotespsofced Association Dr. STEELE delivered an address. He congratulated the gtooi nthg e o n o o boardergy of members on the improved position which held, and said he must conufeehssautshti' afthtwhobawneneurse presidency he felt very m sinking ship. (Laughter.) v the committee, the ship had weathered the storm, and he hoped might yet weather any storm that might be ahead of the members. (Hear, hear.) He noticed with much pleasure that the committee intended to do something in keeping with the Christian character of the Association. Some people had objected to the name Young Men's Christian Association, because they stated there was no Christianity about it. They might admit that partly, and he was sorry to say they must also admit that, there was little Christianity in the world. We all called ourselves Christians, but the were very few real Christians; and nomatter what name the society might be called by, if it was doing nothing else, it was providing a place where young men who came into the town could read the papers and were provided with wholesome recreation, and tended to prevent the fulfilment of the truism that "Satan finds some mischief still for idle bands to do." He regretted that the funds of the Association had not permitted the committee to maintain a smoking room, and he was rather

afraid that tl,'-' ..er lnability to provide this convenience had I caused B..fnie dissatisfaction. The members must remember, ho- --etret) that the Association must cut their coat accord- \ \ing to the cloth. He concluded by wishing the Association 'evet- prosperity. (Applause.) Mr. SuersoN said he had great pleasure in moving the adoption of such a capital and satisfactory report and finan- cial statement. It was very encouraging to find there was some life left in the Association, and someone who would breathe on the dry bones of such an institution as this to try i to • bring it to life again, and put it in a position in which 1 something for which they had worked might be accorr.-- t plished. He thought that those who took the matter in hand and were determined, if possible, not to allow this institution to pass away as so very many institutions in Runcorn, more or less like it, had done, deserved their very hearty thanks. He had lived in Runcorn many years, and he sometimes brought to mind the Mechanics' and the Literary Institutes which had existed at one time and an- other, and notwithstanding the efforts of those who wished to support them, had passed away. The Literary Institute was the last of the kind. It seemed little more than a year ago that he thought the Young Men's Christian Association was to go with it. They had arrived at a better state of things, and he trusted the Association was now being placed on a footing which would ensure its success, and that they might look forward to the future with a greet hope that it would accomplish something very satisfactory. Mr. Simp- son referred to the chairman's excellent services as presi- dent, and entered into a review of the report, throwing out several valuable suggestions with regard to the working of the Association in which he felt a deep interest, and said he would be glad to do anything in his power to promote its welfare. (Applause.) The Rev. Canon BARCLAY seconded the motion. He ob- served that he hardly knew any institution in Runcorn with the exception of the Savings Bank, which could present such a favourable balance sheet as it had been their pleasure to hear that night. (Applause.) He might say as regarded the treat to aged people that he had come in for a great deal of honour which he didn't deserve. Through the kind- ness of the committee of the Association he was asked to be a sort of gentleman usher to the different perons who enter- tained the people, but having taken so prominent a position, he could only say that he knew of nothing that had transpired for many years in Runcorn which had called forth so much gratitude from the guests as that particular treat. Many old men and old women who he did not know had thanked him personally for the very excellent treat they had had. He told them that they were not obliged to him, I but to young men who paid respect to age as well as beauty. (Laughter.) He thought it was one of the bright features in the management of the Association that they arranged that treat so well, The Rev. Canon referred te the generosity of the Runcorn public, who had never failed him on any occa- sion. Some one had made a remark that one great cause of the diminished intemperance of the ccuntry,or the increased temperance,whichever they pleased to call it,was not merely the result of moral and religious motives, but because the people were beginning to find that drinking intoxicants did not pay—that they could make their money go faither and get a great deal more enjoyment from their money by spending it in a different way than in the alehouse and the gin palace. (Hear, hear,and applause.) He had no doubt there was a great deal of truth in that. They ought all to try to make their way in the world, and to really Nacl truly spend their money in a way that would bring them most benefit from it. He referred to the free breakfast, and said he thought that if in future a general intimation were I made that it was hoped that parents who I were in a position of life to give break- fasts at home would not avail themselves of the invitation, he did not think the committee would be over- burdened as they were on the last occasion. Referring to the accusation that the Association was of a non-Christian character, the speaker remarked that if they announced that there was a Young Men's Christian Association, it was an inducement to strangers who came into the town to go to a place where they would find a comfortable room to read in, ana at the same time meet with a cordial welcome from the members. (Hear, hear.) This was a work which the Free Public Library would not affect, and he advocated that a theological discussion class should be held regularly in con- nection with the Association. He thought in that way they could keep up the Christian character of the Association. (Applause.) The motion was passed. Mr. J. D. Jones moved that the best thanks of that meeting be given to Dr. Steele for the able manner in which he had discharged the duties of the presidency during:the past year, and that he be re-elected for the ensuing year. He spoke in high terns of praise of the manner in which Dr. Steele had performed his duties. Mr. J. A. SMITH seconded the resolution, which was car- ried, and the Chairman having replied, the following gentlemen were elected vice-presidents, on the motion of Mr. J. A. Smith and Mr. S. Coventry:—Rev. Canon Barclay, M.A., Rev. W. Preston, M.A., Rev. J. E. Robinson, Rev. J. D. Thomas, Rev. J. Jones, Rev. J. Billington, Messrs. R. Shaw, J. Simpson, J. Meadowcroft, J. 0. Jackson, G. S. Hazlehurst, C. W. Hazlehurst, W. B. Gibson, T. Handles', W. Whitaker, J. Johnson, J. H. Humphreys, C. Wigg, G. L. Davies. . The Rev. Canon BARCLAY proposed the reappointment of Mr. C. Nickson as hon. secretary, speaking of that gentle- man's abilities in the most eulogistic terms. The motion was seconded by Mr. JOHNSON, and supported by Mr. BECKETT. Mr. NICKSON, who was received with hearty applause, declined the office on the ground that his many other press- ing duties would not permit him to give the necessary time to the work. The meeting would, however, take no denial, and he was reappointed, with Mr. Kirkaam Evans as his assistant. Mr. S. C. Beckett was appointed treasurer on the motion of Mr. Joixempar, seconded by Mr. NICKSON. The Rev. Canon BARCLAY moved a vole of thanks to the chairman, whom he congratulated upon the set of members he had ruled that evening, who were more orderly than the members he sometimes had the pleasure of presiding over at the other end of the town. (Loud laughter and applause.) Mr. BEcirerr seconded the motion, which was carried with acclamation and the meeting separated. We may state ;hat it was decided to obtain a higher class of literature than had formerly found a place in the reading room, an in future the Nineteenth Century, Harper's Monthly, Cornhill, Longnians, stc., will be found there.

div.head: WIDN LS WESLEY/INS AND THE BLUE RIBBON ARMY.
div.p: WIDN LS WESLEY/INS AND THE BLUE RIBBON ARMY.

On Tuesday evening a meeting was held in Lacey-street ' schoolroom, with the object of forming a Weoeyan Methodist Blue Ribbon Army in Widnes. Tbcre was a moderate attendance. The Rev. R. HP presided; and the Revs. J. Tesayma.n, George 14—a, and Mr. T. S. Swale occupied seats on the platfi.,,A. The CHPIEMAN, in epening the proceedings, expressed his pleasure at mp.ting those present on such an interesting occasion. Tney would observe that the notice calling the meeo,.g spoke about gospel temperance. He believed that 6ospel and temperance ought never to be disunited; they ought to work together, as one helped the other. There were many in that audience who knew the blessings of the Gospel, and the advantage of temperance, too. He believed the time was coming when they would have a temperance society in connection with every Wesleyan congregation. (Hear, hear.) They had bands of. hope in connection with the majority of their chapels, and they now felt that they needed some organisation for their boys and girls when they attained an age at which they could not be admitted into the former society. A society, too, was wanted in which the fathers and mothers could be enrolled members. The form that the temperance movement was taking at the present time was 'at of the Blue Ribbon Army, and they we. :epared that evening to give the coloured ribbon to anyone who would accept it, on condition of course, that he or she signs the abstinence pledge. de thought there was an advantage in wearing a coloured ribbon, because it helped a man to adhere to his pledge with greater steadfastness. The chair- man expressed the opinion that teetotalism was an aid to trade end commerce, and described the temptations which a young man who was a convict to teetotal principles would escape on leaving home, and the greater confidence his parents would have in his virtue. He believed that nothing would be more advantageous to the inhabitants than a general adoption of , the blue ribbon in Wid- nes, for it would reduce the taxes consider- ably.—The Rev. GEOZIDE Hem (of Runcorn) advert:d to the great advancing strides the Wesleyan denomination had made in teetotalism, and remarked that he considered it one of the good signs of the times. He attributed the splendid majority by which the Rev. Charles Garrett was appointed to the presidential chair to that gentleman's well- known temperance principles; and he advocated the use of the blue ribbon because of the temptations from which the wearer was saved thereby. He quoted statistics to show that if the money invested in the drink trade were put to some useful manufactory, it would give employment where at present there was none, and give a spirit of vitality where at present there was only lethargy.—Addregses were also delivered by the Rev. J. TESSYMAN and Mr. T. S. SWALE, and it was decided to form a branch of the Army, and a committee was formed for thepurpose of organising it'

THE SUICIDE IN A RAILWAY CARRIAGE BETWEEN WARRING lON AND RUGBY. PAINFUL REVELA,TIONS.—TUE RESULT OF FLIRTATION. On Monday, Mr. Poole resumed the inquiry, at Rugby, into the circumstances attending the death of James Vt'tlaen, aged 24 years, late steward of the steamship Celtic, of the White Star line, whose body was found in a first-class com- partment, on the 20th inst., on the arrival of the up limited scotch mail at Rugby Station. It was reported that the \contents of the stomach had been analysed, but without find- ing any trace of poison.—The deceased's aunt, who identi- fied the deceased, said the scent found on him was German cologne. Deceased was her nephew and her adopted son and had been employed at chemical works at Runcorn. She last saw deceased on the 17th inst. \She had no idea that he was going to leave Liverpool. He had had a week's holiday while the ship was in dock, and would have joined it azain had he been alive. She knew in December last that 1 e ;tad formed an acquaintance with a young lady, and she advised him to be careful. Before Christmas he said the young lady was Ada Adams, and that she was favourably disposed towards him. He said she was once a barmaid at Crew's Hotel, Liverpool, and that she had told him she was the daughter of a colonel, and would come into £B,OOO at the age of twenty-one; but it transpired that she had at present only 5s a week, and was freqaently travelling about from place to place. The yortng woman had informed him that it was the wish of her friends to put her in an asylum, so that they could get her money, and it was to avoid them that she kept moving about. After this explanation deceased decided to marry her, and a telegram was received from Stafford for the parties to proceed there to sign papers as to the disposal of the property ; but the young woman said she had to proceed to France. Deceased saw her off at Lime-street Station, Liverpool, but as the train started he saw two gentlemen gat into the same compart- ment as the young woman, and from what he saw he was in- duced to get into another carriage, and ride as far as Edge- hill, when he got into the same compartment with her, and they had a row on their journey to Warrington. On leaving there she promised-to telegraph when she got to London, which she did. A few days after he was surprised to find her again at the hotel, and she aczonnted for this by saying she had broken a blood-vessel at Crewe, and had to return, although she had telegraphed from London. Subsequently the girl told the deceased that she must break off the engage- ment on account of her health, but would like to correspond with him as a friend. She thought the girl's behaviour h.,d great influence on him, but did not believe he put an end to himself. Some of deceased's relatives had died suddenly. Ada Adams, a prepossessing young lady, stated that she lived at Crew's Hotel, Liverpool, and was visiting there as Mrs. Crew's friend, but was not there for more than three weeks at a time. She had been there since the 6th inst. She did not work unless she chose. Her father died when she was young, and she left her mother because she married again. Had known deceased about two months. He wished to marry her, and she allowed hinkto pay his addresses to her, thinking he might get tired. Jhe did not consider her- self' engaged to him. The letter produced was in her hand- writing. She last saw deceased the Friday before he died, when he remained about an hour; but they did not quarrel, nor had they ever done so. Had she chosen to marry him she could have done so any day. When they parted they were good friends. He told her he was going to London, but this did not annoy her. He sent a telegram from Warrington, saying she had failed to fulfil her errand of mercy. After pressing on deceased's part, she said she would marry him if he would wait six months. He visited her nearly every evening. Deceased objected to wait so long. She did not know what deceased was, and although she promised to marry him she never intended to do so. She supposed the person deceased wished to "meet either in heaven or hell" was herself. She saw in the papers deceased was dead, and guessed it was him. They said at the bar that she was to be blamed for his death. Deceased told her on the Friday night that if she did not go to Warrington that night he would kill himself. She refused to go, and did not think he would carry out his threat. She had been engaged to be married on another occasion. Deceased had never said he was jealous, and had never asked her to be "off with the old love before she was on with the new." She had a private income, and went where she liked. She did not think deceased knew she had an annuity, which had been given her by an old lover. This old lover was still alive. She swore positively that there was no engagement between them. The telegram from War- rington stated that he had waited anxiously for her, but she had failed in her errand of mercy ; he should not fail in his, and hoped God would bless her. She wrote to the deceased, calling him "her dearest." He wanted her to go to Warrington so that they could be married next day, but the banns were not published and they had no licence. She was very shocked to hear that deceased committed suicide, but she did not think she was to blame. She was twenty. She did not know deceased's mind was unhinged; she really knew very little about him. If shelled met the deceased in 1 the street she would have passed him by without speaking. —The Coroner said he did not believe that.—By the Jury : It was six weeks since she gave deceased up, and he knew the reason why. She was aware deceased carried a revolver, but he had not threatened to use it.— William Matthews, Runcorn said deceased told him in December that he was to have been married, but the young lady had refused him. Deceased had borrowed £l5 to make Miss Adams a handsome present, provided she accepted him.—Mrs. Wilson, the aunt, said deceased had told her that he intended to give up the sea and live on the interest of £B,OOO, which belonged to Miss Mains.—Miss Adams said she was satisfied deceased did not put in end to himself on her account. She had been from Liverpo3l six weeks, and he had taken other young ladies to bills.— The Coroner thought it was no use to pursue the inquiry further, and advised the jury to return an open verdict, which they did; and the Foreman expressed We disap- proval at the wa'y in which Miss Adams 1-.. d given her evidence. —

The LECTURER said it would not be difficult to show that the question they had associated with the name of Richard Cobden was one of pressing importance to all who desired the welfare of the human race. Few would deny that peace was a desirable thing, and that war was one to be avoided. It was not generally recognised, perhaps, that the prepara- tion for war in time of peace was only second in disaster to that of war. It was calculated to cost Europe somewhere about five hundred million pounds per year to uphold her armaments. It was an enormous sum, and it should be borne in mind that it had to be raised by the industrial classes. It was also calculated that out of every sovereign raised by taxation 15s. went for the war system. He had no objection to war being costly; he even wished it were more costly, for it seemed that some people who had no conciences had pockets. (Hear, hear.) He asked the audience to consider this enormous waste of wealth—how civilization was kept back, and people kept in degradation and misery through it. If only one half was devoted to the advancement of mankind, to the development of trade, art, and science, what a happy and contented people we should find everywhere, to say nothing with regard to the diminution in the slestruction of life and property. All this preparation and expenditure of life and money did not answer ;it did not bring peace or confidence. Europe was now bristling with armed men, and all this show of armaments, instead of maintaining peace tended to create war. The question was, what could be done to remedy this state of things. Was the sword to go on devouring for ever? were they to sit down and let it go on gathering strength and hindering civiliza- tion and christianity ? or was there a better way of settling international disputes when they:arose than by going to war over them? A man whose life had been devoted to this question had taught them that arbitration and law were bet- ter than violence and brute force. The lecturer then pr.- needed to speak of Richard Cobden, who, be said, was born in 1804, at Midhurst, Sussex, a place which had already been associated with eminent statesmen. When be was 10 years of age he was sent to one of those wretched schools where he was ill-fed, ill-taught, and ill-used; and it was not till 1819 that this state of things came to an end, when he was sent to a London warehouse, where he devoted himself to hard work and hard study. On leaving the warehouse he became a commercial traveller, and in 1830 he commenced business as a calico printer. It was about 1838 that John Bright came over to Manchester and had his first interview with Cobden, his object being to invite him to a meeting at Rochdale on education. Cobden knew something of educa- tion by its absence in his early life, and he consented to go. He went, and lodged at old Jacob Bright's house. Some time after he went to America, and it was here where be issued those treatises which are said to contain his first notions re- garding the Corn Laws,and in which he pointed out that our foreign policy had tended to create a kind of chronic hos- tility between France and England, and he protested against the notion of regulating the balance of power, ridiculed the arguings of diplomacy, and asserted England's mission to be the avoidance of war and the ex- tension of commerce. Another fact that he pointed out in the policy was that the Jingoism cost the nation £14,003,000. The lecturer wished it only cost that amount at the present time; but Jingoism was no new thing—its history had been written in blood for centuries past. In 1836 Cobden published a pamphlet on Russia, which con- tained a strong arpiment in favour of non-intervention in foreign quarrels and foreign affairs, He said that Russia was accused by us of being an aggrandizing people, but he said that for every league Russia had annexed England bad annexed three; and further, it was important to bear in mind with regard to Russia, that she owed her extension less to her own ambition than to her interference of her neighbours. The lecturer said that we are accustomed to speak of Cobden as a great free trader, but he was more aptly described by a Frenchman as an international man. He did not go into that memorable struggle against the Corn Laws merely to release the springs of industry and to make a roaring trade, but rather to blend into one great federation the nations of the world. In 1849 Cobden brought forward in Parliament a bill for submitting inter- national disputes to arbitration instead of war, and in the dnhate that followed, the practice of private duelling was alluded to, and it was pointed out that it had a great hold of a prominent section of the English society. The lecturer said we needed in these days to be reminded of the practice. But how had this been got rid of? It was not by passing an Act of Parliament, but by rousing public opinion against it. It was a fact that the men who fought duels were not brave men, but rather men who were afraid of people thinking they were aliata. oa th.e war was international duelling. In a private duel one man was praced on one side and another man on the other, and the signal was given to fire at each otber; but in war perhaps 50,000 were placed on one side and the same on the other, and then they were told to go at it and destroy their fellow creatures, and when this was done a number of men would sit down and make lexplanations. A more common sense way would be for men to sit down and make explanations before going to war. (Applause.) Cobden urged the plan of two nations making a special treaty that if any dispute arose between them they should refer it to arbitration, and Lord Derby also ad- vocated this. The lecturer referred to the many other pub- lic movements in which Cobden took an active and pro- minent part, and said that the last time he appeared before a public audience was in 1864, at Rochdale, after which his health gradually failed, and on the morning of the second of April, 1865, he died at the age of 61, in the ripe- ness of his mental powers. He was missed, but his works would remain, and his triumphs were not like military achievements, but were indelibly stamped on the annals of time. The lecturer had pointed out some of Cobden's re- form work—how he planted the spirit of non-intervention, holt he laboured to bring nations together in friendly inter- course, how ha strove to show that "peace on earth and goodwill toward men" was both sound gospel and good common senge, and he therefore submitted that Cobden's work was one of estab:ishing peace and law in the earth. (Applause.) A vote of thanks to the lecturer, proposed by Mr. JEFFREYS, and seconded by Mr. GLARE, brought the pro- ceedings to a close.
NEW FREE ItETHODIST CHURCH FOR MIDDLEWICH.

The ceremony of laying the foundation stones of a new Free Methodist Chapel at Middlewich was performed on Monday last. For a quarter of a century,. or thereabouts, this body has been dependent upon the society of Friends, who have a meeting house there called the Bank Chapel. This the Free Methodists have had for their religions ser- vices, and though it is far from modern in its appearance and internal arrangements, and requires much more heat to make it comfortable than is at their command, yet it has served them well, and been the scene of many happy ser- vices. But for years the society has been wishing and praying for a chapel of their own; and probably would have gone on so for a long time more had not one of its members, now no more, promised them £2OO. This caused the circuit to take the matter up, and the more so when to that another friend promised the land, and likewise the balance of £2OO when he saw the thing fairly moving. Plans were submitted, estimates sent in, and a chapel begun capable of meeting the growing wants of a thriving congregation in this old town. Being the centre of the Winsford and Sandbach circuit, it is the general meeting place of the societies, and will prove a great addition to the circuit in its future operations. The land will allow of extensions when required, so that as far as this society is concerned the best of prospects is before them. The morning fixed for laying the stones began most inauspiciously, but at noon the weather cleared up, and continued fine through the whole service. There came friends from all parts of the circuit, and when the hymn was given out by the superintendent, the Rev. W. T. Symons, there was a good gathering. The Rev. J. K. I Walker (Independent) offered up prayer, after which a chap- ter from the dedication of the Temple was read, and 6 stones were laid by Mrs. R. Atherton, Mrs. Robt. Stubbs, Mr. John Aspey, Mr. John Buckley, M.R.C.P., Mr. Wm. Dale, and Mr. Reuben Stubbs, for the aforesaid two friends. Mr. R. Atherton, and Mr. J. Dean, and other friends laid bricks, after which the Rev. N. Fysb (Northwich) delivered an address on points of history and worship among the Free Methodists, which, with the one by the Rev. A. Holliday, detailing.the polity, doctrines, and church government, rendered a com- plete resume of the whole matter, and added much to the interest of the ceremony. A public tea was partaken of in the Wesleyan School (kindly lent for the occasion), after which there was a public meeting in the Town Hall, under the presidency of Mr. R. Stubbs (Winsford), who was sup- ported on the platform by the Revs. A. Holliday, N. Fysb, W. T. Svmoris, J. K. Walker, J. Wright, Mr. J. Buckley, F.R.G.S., Mr. W. Pool, 4lkc. The Chairman, in the course of the evening, detailed promises and gifts for the new chapel, as follows :—Two friends, each £200; E. H. Moss, Esq., J.P., £10; Mrs. R. Atherton, £lO 10s. ; Mr. John Aspey, £10; Mr. W. Dale, £10; Mr. C. Allen, £10; Mr. D. Harding, £5; Mr. S. Pickstock, £5; Mr. R. Stubbs, £5; Mr. J. Buckley, M.T.C.L.., X 5 ss; Mr. J. Latham, Li; Miss E. Smith, £2 55.; Mr. R. Atherton, £1; Mr. J. Dean, .£1 ; collections, £s` 16s. sp.

Two women named O'Neill, mother and daughter, have been arrested at Greenock, on the charge of murder of a boy two years old, the son of the latter. It is alleged that the women, while drinking heavily, had thrown the child down.

liHE EXAMINER SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 3, 1883. LECTURE ON RICHARD COBDEN. -- Under the auspices of the Warrington Co-operatiye Society, Mr. W. Pollard, of Manchester, delivered a lecture ' in the Co-operative Hall, on Monday evening, entitled "Richard Cobden, the Apostle of Peace." Mr. T. Birchall (the president) presided. There was a moderate attendance. The CHAIRMAN, in introducing the lecturer, said Richard Cobden was essentially an economist. One of his greatest objects was to teach the nation to practice sensible economy, and to mind their own bu;, but this wae no easy matter for he had to combat all kinds of absurd arguments. The 1 testimonies paid to the worthiness of Richard Cobden, im- mediately after his death, were such as were paid to only a few men. It would be difficult to determine which of the two great political parties paid the greatest honour to his memory after his death. His whole 'career was spent in teaching men abe honourable, and to pursue a course of integrity in all things, and he was essentially an apostle of peace.

WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The monthly meeting of this Aultiorily was held yes- terday at the Workhouse. Present: Messrs. W. Darbysbire (in the chair), Houghton, Humphreys, Gibson, Kilshall, Cooper, Roberts, J. C. Sutton (clerk) S. Sutton (assistant clerk), J. H. Gornall (medical officer), W. Owen (surveyor) and a. Rawling (nuisance inspector). S°4l.". WASTE DEPOSITS. Mr. RAWLIN.7, reported that in that portion of the Asthorit ';s district in the township of Warrington, on the y Nyt'a side of Lovely-lane, a large quantity of soap waste was being deposited to fill up the brick pits in Mr. Job Swales's field after the clay had been removed for making bricks. This waste was very offensive when first deposited, and also very injurious to the brickwork in connection with the Authority's sewers which passed through this land, and the ground over and around them was being filled up with this waste. He found that the brickwork of sewers in Wright-street, Dale-street, and Edward-street in the Sankey district, where the land was filled up with soap waste' was crumbling faster a great deal than that .of the sewers which were not built in that material. The tenants of the houses in Dale-street, built on waste, also complained of dampness in the floors and foundations of the houses.— After a short conversation, the Surveyor and Inspector were directed to take steps to protect the manholes of the sewers. HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT. The MEDICAL OFFICER reported that during the month ending 31st January, there were 41 births-24 male, and 17 female; and 20 deaths-12 male, and 8 female. The ex- cess of births over deaths was 21; the death rate 19 2. There had been six deaths from zymotic diseases, three being due to scarlet fever, and one each to rheumatic fever, croup, and diarrhcea. One case of scarlet fever had been admitted to the Fever Hospital from Penketh. SURVEYOR'S REPORT. The Surveyor reported as follows :—During the month inspections have been made of Mr. Bostock's 'houses off Lovely-lane, Warrington, and of Mr. Jameson's houses, Liverpool-road. Certificates for habitation have been given to Mr. Jameson for four houses, Liverpool-road, and to Mr. Bostock for Lye houses, Percy-street, Lovely-lane. The owners of properties in Jockey-street have commenced to make the street in accordance with the notices and specifi- cations issued by the Authority, and the work is receiving my superintendence as it proceeds. the owners of property in Warburton-street have not yet commenced.. Mr. Thomas Seed submits plans for four houses at Penketh, which are in accordance with the bye-laws. The certificate of approval should be issued subject to the positions of well and cess- pool being also in accordance with the bye-laws, Mr. Seed having, subsequent to his deposits of the drawings, and on my pointing out what was necessary, purchased sufficient land to enable him to comply wit'l the bye-laws. Messrs. Ashton and Woods having commenced additions at the farm of Mr. William Haslarn, Burtonwood, without having previ- ously submitted plans, I have written to say plans are re- quired unless they can claim exemption under the clauses in he bye-laws. This was all the business.

div.head: BAD MEAT AI 'WALTON.
div.p: BAD MEAT AI 'WALTON.

On Tuesday, as Daresbury Petty Sessions, before Messrs. Edward dr (venal! (in the chair), James Marson, Robert Pierr,lnt, and W. C. Jones, Joseph Maddock, land- lord of rse Stag Inn, Walton Inferior, was charged with havlag on his premises, on the 22nd December, about 401bs. or diseased meat, for preparation for the food of man.—Mr. Percy Davies appeaaed for the defendant.—Mr. Farrington, the inspector of nuisances, stated that he went to the de- fendant's premises, and in a slaughter house he found two pieces of beef and the lungs of a cow, in all about 40:bs. From the appearance oc the meat he concluded that it was diseased, and seized it, and after it had been seen by a magistrate it was destroyed. He reported the case to the Sanitary Authority, and he might say that much sympathy was expressed for the defendant, as it was thought that he was ignorant of the meat being on his premises.—By the Clerk : He thought that the cow had suffered from tuber- culous disease, and that from the appearance of the intes- tines it was in the last stage of consumption, and was not I fit for the food of man.—Mr. Mies, after congratulating I Mr. Jones on his first appearance on the bench,l said the defendant bad on his premises a slaughter house that was used by several persons, and could he speak he would say that he knew nothing about the meat being on his premises. He (Mr. Davies) would bring witnesses to show to whom the cow belonged, from whom it was bought, and who brought it from Warrington to Walton. Thomas Holcroft was in the habit of buying what were called " big " cows for the purpose of selling the skins, and he had a general permission from the defendant to use the slaughter house. He bought the cow from a respectable man named Hedgcock, of Warrington, and gave £1 for it. Holcroft, never dreaming of anything like the present pro- ceedings, got Mr. Norman's man to help him in driving the cow from Warrington to the Stag Inn. On the way they called at Mr. Bradbury's, and the latter was informed by Holcroft that he intended to kill the cow, and that if he wanted any pig or dog meat he should have some. Brad- bury said if he would bring the meat he would pay a reason- able price for it. Holcroft then went on, along with the Inspector's man to the premises, and the cow was killed and skinned, and he (Mr. Davies) understood that it was also boned. Holcroft took as much of the flesh back with him to Bradbury's as he could get on the handcart, and received Es for it. The bones were sold to a bo re dealer in Warrington for 55., and the skin was sold for • ' t 15s 6d, so that a profit of only 8s 6d was made. The defendant knew nothing of the meat being on his premises, or of the cow having been killed thereon, as he had given Holcroft a general permission to use the slaughter-house. The meat had been on the premises a week before it was seized, and it was therefore evident that it was not intended for human food, or it would not have been allowed to remain there so long.—Holcroft was called, and his evidence confirmed the foregoing statement.—By the Bench : The reason why he brought the cow from Warrington to Walton was that they had no public slaughter-house at the former place, and he had no place of his own where be could have killed the cow. He did not ray a word to defendant about the meat being on his premises.—The Inspector of Nuis- ances, in support of the charge that the meat was in pre- paration for human food, said that the lungs were pared. The meat could not have been at the place a week, as the lungs were perfectly slimey ; had they been there more than 2 or 3 days, they would have been dry.—Mr. Davies said he could not call Mr. Hedgcock, as he was ill, but if the Bench would grant an adjournment he would bring Bradbury and Hedgcock as witnesses.—The Clerk said their evidence would not make any material difference in the case, as they would not be able to prove that the cow and the meat were the same. He need not point out to Mr. Davies that it was for him to prove that the meat was not intended for human food.—Mr. Davies, after consulting with his client, said that he could not offer any further material evidence, and he would ask the Bench to deal with the case.—The Bench said the defendant bad rendered himself liable to a penalty of £2O. As he had undertaken to cease using the building as a slaughter-house, he would only be fined 20s and costs. —Mr. Davies said the defendant undertook not to nse the place as at present, with the understanding that if any butcher wished to use it as a permanent slaughter-house' defendant would be able to let it as such after applying to , the magistrates.—The Clerk: Of course, in that case, he ' must apply to the magistrates.

div.head: ST. PAUL'S AND ST. BARNABAS' CHURCHES.
div.p: ST. PAUL'S AND ST. BARNABAS' CHURCHES.

ANNUAL TEA MEETING. This popular tea meeting took place on Moaday evening at the Warrington Public Hall, and was as well attended as in previous years. The usual entertainment was given after tea when there was a crowded audience. Sir G. Greenall presided, and he was supported by the Rev. S. Wilkinson, Rev. E. St. A. Duke Messrs. T. Jolley, T. Sutton, T. Morris J. Smethurst, /c. The :CHAIRMAN said-he was sure that was a most excel- lent and satisfactory meeting—(hear, hear)—excellent and satisfactory to his mind because it expressed the affecqon those present felt for the vicar of the parish. (Hear, hear.) He was one of those who always liked to see due and proper affection between and amongst those who were associated to- gether. When he came into the room he asked how many years it was since Mr. Wilkinson and he first sat down to tea there, and he believed ten years had passed since Mrs. Wilkinson put the first sugar into his cup of tea. (Laughter.) He was thankful that God had kept the Vicar amongst them so long, and he was glad to be with him when he was surrounded by such a concourse of friends as he saw before him. He had no intention whatever of saying mere. He never spoke because the vulgar and illiterate said he could not speak. (Loud Laughter.) It was the vulgar, the unre- fine,i, and the coarse who condescended at any time to per- sonalities. (Applause.) The Rev. &Wilkinson afterwards addressed the assembly He said he was very thankful indeed to say that during the past year the same kindly feeling has existed between the pastors and the people that had existed for the last ten years, and in the name of the clergy of the parish he wished publicly to thank all those kind friends who had rendered them such valuable and real help in the work of St. Paul's parish during the past year. He was not going to mention names, but he must thank the officers of the church, the members of the choir, the district visitors, and the host of good friends who helped them in the schools, in the socie- ties, and in every kind of work. When he told them they had something like 200 churchworkers, those present saw they had occasion to be very grateful indeed to the laity for the kind help they rendered. They had met that night as a parish consisting of two churches—St. Paul's and St. Barna- bas', and while they remembered that was a parcchial gathethig they must also runitial..er tlxat 'Limy wovo ahurch of England gathering as well, for they were proud to ack- nowledge themselves members of what he believed was the purest church on earth. He believed, notwithstanding all the imperfections of the clergy, and all the imperfections of the laity, the Church of England at the present moment was doing her duty better than she ever did before. He be- lieved her clergy were more zealous, he believed the services of their churches were more reverently conducted, and he believed the agencies employed by the Church of England for winning souls to Christ were more efficient and more numerous than ever they were before. Of course they knew it was always hard to judge exactly as to the success of their work, yet to a certain extent they could judge of the outward success which followed the labours of the clergy and laity, because they must remember if the clergy had to work alone they would do very little. They had, as he had said, no less than 200 men and women who were able to help them in every kind of good work, and to those they returned their most sincere and hearty thanks. It was now just 17 years since he first came with his dear wife into that neighbourhood, and he was thankful to say that during that period the Church of England had been able to do great and glorious work. If, for instance, they took Warrington as the centre of a radius of something like eight miles they would find that during the last 10 years no less than £60,000 had been expended in church buildings and in church repairs, which they must acknowledge was a large sum; and if they Went back a few years earlier they would have to add to that a sum of £12,000, which had been spent upon another church, so that they might fairly sty that within the last 20 years something like £102,000 had been spent upon the erection and repair of churches. That was not all. A great deal of money besides that had been spent upon the erection of schools, and also upon the erection of parsonage houses. If they took the schools and parsonage houses, all they had to do was to go to Walton, whei e Sir Gilbert Greenall resides, and there they would find a beautiful school and beautiful parsonage that had cost £5,000 or more, besides all the churches that had been erected. (Applause.) That was a most satisfactory state of things, and he was sure they thanked God for enabling the Church of England to do so much. Coming to the parish of St. Paul's, he said since he had been at the church they had had between 3,000 and 4,000 baptisms, about 1,200 mar- riages, and about 1,000 young people confirmed, and they had bad various other successes for which they ought to be very thankful. During the time he had been at St. Paul's they had raised for church and school, and other parish pur- poses in various ways, no less a sum than £2s,ooo—(ap- plause)—and they had been instrumental in spending many thousands of pounds in the erection of a new church, in the ' conduct of their schools, and in many other works they had undertaken. He might mention that the parochial schools were in a most satisfactory condition, and he held in his hand I the last report of Her Majesty's Inspector, which plainly set I before them the admirable condition in which the schools I were at the present time. They had by God's help done I something, but there was a great deal more that they wanted ,to do. They wanted schools at St. Barnabas', and a mission I room at Bewsey. He was thankful to say that during the Ipast year they had had a lady at work in Bewsey—Miss McKenzie—who had done a wonderful amount of good, and , he hoped that the work which had been begun so success- fully would go on and prosper. In conclusion he said be was sure there was no parish so well blest with officers, and he expressed his belief that the work would go on and prosper. (Applause.) The Revs. E. ST. A DUKE and H. G. SMITH also gave brief address. An excellent programme consisting of songs, duets, quartettes, and glees—in which the following took parf : , Mrs. Lawless, Miss Smith, Miss Beddard, Miss Williams, • Messrs. Josef Cantor, Reddish, Lawless, SherloCk, and • Potter—was then proceeded with, and gave the greatest satisfaction.

Beans tended downwards. Maize was again variable in condition and price, and was generally held for fully previous rates.

ASSAULTING HIS MOTHER.—A man named Redfern was charged at Warrington Police Court, on Monday, before Alderman Pickmere and Mr. Fairclough, with having been drunk and disorderly in Erwood-street, on Sunday night, and also with having assaulted his mother.—P.S. Spinks said Mrs. Redfern's daughter met him in the street about 10 minutes to 12 on the previous night, and told him the pri- soner was assaulting her mother. He, along with another constable, went to the hour fi.nd found prisoner and a woman named Margaret Fleming I.e. "qrs. Redfern, who had been hiding from her son, came into the house, and he noticed that she had a wound near the eye, and was covered with blood. Prisoner, in his presence suddenly took up a candle- stick and struck his mother with it, and witness then took him into custody. Margaret Fleming then broke the win- dow with her hand, cutting herself in a dreadful manner, and before she could be taken to the Infirmary nearly bled to death. It was doubtful whether she would recover.—Pri- soner was committed for two months with hard labour. LECTURE ON CHARLES KINGSLEY BY THE REV. THOMAS RIPPON.—On Saturday evening last, the Rev. T. Rippon, of Warrington, delivernd a lecture on Charles Kingsley. in the Wesleyan School-room, Penketh, before tne members of the Mutual Improvement Society. Mr. Robert Garnett presided. The lecturer, after a few introductory remarks, referred to Kingsley's parentage, and remarked upon the great debt he owed his parents for the training he received from them. He also alluded to his precocious youth, looked at him as a school boy, traced him through his university course, and then spoke of the 'nfluence for godd he received from reading books such as those by Carlyle, Coleridge, and Maurice. Looking at Kingsley as the rector of Eversley, the lecturer dealt with him as the speaker and faithful pastor, and said that in discharging his duty as rector of the parish he went down to the lowest without losing his self-respect, and went up to the highest without staining his surplice. In criticising his teaching as a preacher, the lecturer said Kingsley was a preacher for the times, nay, rather a preacher for the coming times, in that his life work was just beginning to appear and repeat itself; that England was in the springtime of Kingsley's sowing; that the seeds he scattered in lectures, novel, and sermon, were beginning to appear in blossom, presaging a harvest which to those 1 who ate thereof was life. The lecturer then spoke of Kingsley as the distinguished novelist and assayist, and in support of ,his ability as a poet recited " The poacher's widow." Referring to Kingsley as a politician, the lecturer said he viewed politics from a standpoint other than that of a party standpoint. As to his relation to the chartist agita- tion, having a profound sympathy for the working classes, he showed sympathy for those who suffered, but whilst he would burn with indignation that they should. thus suffer, he was faithful in reproaching them likewise. After advert- ing to Kingsley as the national scientist, as the educational reformer, and as the sanitary reformer, the lecturer gave a picture of his home life, and wound up by referring to Mr. Gladstone's lecture on Dr. Hoek, in which Mr. Gladstone held up the subjcct of his lecture as a hero, and in which he said that a hero was none the less a hero because he was a Christian, or a classical hero • and for Kingsley the lecturer claimed the same degree of reasoning. He would urge upon those present to learn of Kingsley, to follow in his steps, and they would be counted worthy of Christian ' knighthood • the age wanted heroes, and Heaven wanted souls, then they should acquit themselves like men. The meeting concluded with the usual votes of thanks.
